The investigation of exotic physics beyond the Standard Model can be aided by examining the characteristics of B^0_s mesons, including their lifetime and decay properties. To achieve this, an study is being proposed that involves accurately measuring the lifetime of B^0_s mesons through a detailed analysis of several decay channels, utilizing data from the LHCb experiment at the European Organization for Nuclear Physics research CERN. This research involves evaluating various theoretical approaches that influence quark masses and strong interaction forces, utilizing recent advancements in theoretical calculations. Based on current theoretical predictions and experimental limitations, it is estimated that future measurements of B^0_s lifetime and its oscillation period will improve significantly, allowing for the constraints on exotic forces to be strengthened. Specifically, it is forecast that the range of possible values for exotic force strengths will narrow to values that are 10 to 30 times stronger or weaker than present limits, following a similar pattern to the constraints derived from the most recent LHCb and CMS measurements. This study is part of a larger investigation that also evaluates the potential for measuring the difference in lifetime between B^0 and B^0_s mesons, as well as the characteristics of Lambra and B^0_s^* mesons. If implemented, this research is expected to make significant contributions to our understanding of exotic forces even before the arrival of the upgraded LHC. If necessary improvements to the current setup are made, it is projected that this study will result in a publication-worthy finding facilitated by the established collaboration, requiring approximately 12 months of work, in addition to the initial 3 months required to define the research proposal. This investigation is particularly relevant to considering the upgrade of the LHCb detector, particularly the introduction of a scintillating neutron imager in the forward acceptance of the detector, which is ideal for improving the accuracy of B^0_s lifetime measurements by minimizing systematic errors associated with beam condition monitoring. Although the feasibility of this upgrade has not been thoroughly assessed within this study, it is envisioned that further research will be necessary to thoroughly evaluate the physics potential and required technical advancements of this proposal. By leveraging the unique capabilities of the LHCb experiment, this research can lead to breakthroughs in our comprehension of exotic forces and the behavior of quarks and mesons. This research focuses on solving a stochastic optimal control problem where the underlying process is a diffusion with discontinuous drift and a highly irregular boundary condition. The main contribution is a proof that the discretized scheme converges accurately, with an error rate of $O(\sqrt{h})$, where $h$ represents the level of discretization. The method employs a crude approximation approach, involving a mesh size $H$ for the underlying process and a time step $h$ for the time domain. The scheme is then shown to converge rapidly towards the optimal control problem solution, even when the underlying data is very irregular. This achievement is significant because it surpasses the typical error rate associated with the $L^\infty$ norm, which is often linked to the smallest space and time steps rather than their product. The approach also yields meaningful conclusions about the convergence of the scheme when the relevant norms are different. The strategy used here involves a slight modification of the scheme and the introduction of a modified scheme that serves as a reference. The convergence proof relies on a numerical differentiation formula and the properties of the scheme's limits. The performance of the scheme is demonstrated through a numerical example. The research is an extension of the findings from the papers by Raouang ["A Stochastic Control Problem with Discontinuous Drift", arXiv:1905.01798] and Taksar ["On a Stochastic Control Problem", arXiv:1811.00334]. The error rate achieved in this study also surpasses the rate linked to the square root of the time step in the paper by Basham, Carter, and Ray ["Convergence of a discrete time, continuous state, Ito process control problem", Mathematics of Operations Research, 1998]. The research introduced here also addresses the convergence of a discrete time version of the problem. The relevant literature review includes the papers by Basham, Carter, and Ray, as well as the work by Cvitani\'c and Karatzas ["Equivalence result for stochastic differential games", Stochastics and Stochastic Reports, 1993], which established the equivalence between a stochastic control problem and a game against nature. The approach used here is an adaptation of the strategy employed in the paper by the same authors ["On a stochastic control formulation of a mathematical program with complementarity constraints", Mathematical Programming, 2011]. Our analysis is based on 84,471 cosmic ray events detected by the Telescope Array and their anisotropic distribution is described using a dipole pattern. As we examine the most energetic particles, which have energies above 4 EeV, we discover a surprising decrease in anisotropy sensitivity and a shift in directionality that could be linked to misdirection towards the North. This finding remains significant after accounting for fluctuations caused by the limited number of detected particles. We estimate the anisotropy amplitude to be less than 2.8 x 10^-3 for an isotropic distribution and suspect the true value could be higher due to potential errors in our assumptions. We consider possible explanations for this anomaly including an exclusive focus on the most energetic particles, limited detection capabilities, and inaccuracies in our analytical methods. Although we find that anisotropy studies are more complex at higher energies, our research holds significant value as it paves the way for further investigation into the physical phenomena underlying these energetic cosmic events. We propose enhancing the anisotropy detection capability by increasing the minimum required energy. We estimate this would allow us to detect anisotropies corresponding to a 3.5 EeV energy threshold and expect that more sensitive detectors will be essential for uncovering the underlying causes of the anomalies observed in our research. We also propose testing for anisotropy in specific directional patterns that could be linked to particular energetic particle sources. We propose two test strategies: conducting a comprehensive search for the most likely direction of the anisotropy by reconstructing the anisotropy pattern from individual event energies, and conducting a comparative analysis of anisotropy in different directional patterns that could be associated with particular energetic particle sources such as the Galactic Center. We also propose testing for anisotropy in specific directional patterns that could be associated with particular energetic particle sources including the Galactic Center. We estimate that detecting an anisotropy corresponding to a 3.5 EeV energy threshold will require a 20 times increase in the number of detected particles via next-generation cosmic ray experiments with the same effective collection area as the Telescope Array. We also outline the scientific value of such an experiment which we propose could be realized through a collaborative effort between researchers around the world. We propose naming it the Cosmic Ray Spectrum and Anisotropy Experiment or CRASE. We outline the technical capabilities and potential detection capabilities of the CRASE for a range of effective collection areas from 10,000 to 300,000 square meters.

This paper provides characterizations for the finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras that are nilpotent and solvable, categorizing them based on their dimension. It also examines the properties of these algebras in relation to their dimension and rank. A notable finding reveals that a nilpotent Zinbiel algebra with a solvable Malcev sequence has a specific structure, indicating it can be classified as a special type of nilpotent algebra that has a cascade nilpotent characteristic. This discovery leads to an inventory of all finite-dimensional nilpotent Zinbiel algebras over any given field, completing a prior classification that stopped short of considering nilpotent algebras in the nilpotent characteristic of that field. The research also uncovers instances of non-solvable and nilpotent Zinbiel algebras, demonstrating that neither solvability nor nilpotency are equivalent to each other, nor are they equivalent to being of the nilpotent characteristic of the field in question. The study's findings expand upon a classification of finite-dimensional associative algebras that are nilpotent, building on the work of Skrabber and Zelazko, while the results regarding solvability and nilpotency characteristics were independently obtained with different methods, leading to a simultaneous publication of these findings. The research mentioned above was conducted by the authors without knowledge of the prior work mentioned above, being an independent exploration of the same mathematical theories and concepts. The theorems developed in this paper are also applicable to the classification of finite-dimensional associative algebras that are nilpotent, offering a broader context to the results about Zinbiel algebras. A comprehensive analysis of fluid dynamics fluctuations has been developed to better understand the properties of the quark-gluon plasma in heavy-ion collisions. Building on previous work, additional insights are gained by incorporating momentum-dependent correlations of flow harmonics, and the approach is refined to accommodate ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. The proposed method leverages recent ELISA parameterization of viscosity to its consistency, and the resulting predictions of charged particle distributions and flow coefficients are obtained with the inclusion of fluctuation dynamics. These predictions align with data from the Large Hadron Collider, and the approach shows that fluid dynamics fluctuations efficiently capture essential quark-gluon plasma properties, thereby justifying the necessity for thorough investigation of flow fluctuations in heavy-ion collisions. Furthermore, necessary improvements for future research are identified, and important factors affecting initial conditions and quark-gluon plasma properties are uncovered. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that fluid dynamics fluctuations embody a vital component of quark-gluon plasma behavior and serve as a crucial bridge between theoretical models and experimental observations. This method excels over traditional approaches to handling null values by providing accurate results for questions that would otherwise yield undetermined outcomes. This paper introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model to analyze nonlinear tendencies and significant transformations in discrete time series data. Different from static specifications, the TV-PARX model allows for dynamic interactions between variables and includes parameters that change over time, thereby better capturing complex patterns and shifts within data. We develop an iterative generalized method of moments estimation approach to estimate the TV-PARX model's parameters and provide the details of the algorithm used. To assess the performance and reliability of the TV-PARX model, we conduct Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we apply the TV-PARX model to real-world data sets, including a financial indicator and a biological measurement, and compare its performance with competing models. By incorporating explanations and graphical representations, we facilitate a deeper understanding of the TV-PARX model's capabilities and its potential applications in analyzing complex time series data. To undertake intricate grasping and manipulation tasks with multiple objects and uncertain environments, our proposed framework, Neural Descriptor Fields, carries out object identification and scenario understanding using deep neural networks. Initially, we utilized a dataset with numerous demonstrations, labeled objects, and 3D scene descriptions to fine-tune these networks. Later, with only a small set of demonstration data, our framework successfully mastered various tasks such as grasping, manipulation, and problem-solving by exploring the physical environment. The efficacy of NDF was demonstrated in simulated scanning scenarios with changing lighting conditions and real-world experiments using a robotic arm, by accomplishing tasks in novel scenes learned from just five demonstrations. Moreover, our framework was found to excel in comparison to alternative methods based on reinforcement learning and teaching by showing a substantial decrease in demonstration requirements and training time. Moreover, with the introduction of a novel learning rule, our framework was able to overcome the limitations of representation in its descriptors by continuously updating them during the learning process. The code and models of our proposed framework are available at this link https://github.com/qzhang84/NDF Grasping.

The linear scaling of the gap is supported by a more general argument that is independent of the specific details of the code and the message passing algorithm. We used wide-field photometry data from the TESIS scanner to determine vertical aerosol optical depth (AOD) at several locations. A novel method was developed to calculate AOD without relying on absolutely calibrated images, by comparing them to calibrated data from two all-sky scanners at the same location. This comparison involved fitting polynomial functions to the differences between pairs of images, taken at the same time but with different calibration levels. The validity of this approach was tested with simulated data and shown to be effective, even in cases with varying solar zenith angles and cloud conditions. A network of ground-based stations with wide-field photometers can provide continuous, long-term aerosol data, but requires regular visits from technicians to calibrate the instruments, which can be costly and logistically challenging. This new method eliminates the need for absolute calibration, enabling real-time calculation of AOD from raw data, and has significant implications for future aerosol monitoring systems. The study also highlights the importance of properly characterizing the spatial distribution of light sources within images to ensure accurate results. The effectiveness of this approach was demonstrated using data from two locations in Russia: the Repyehovka observatory and the Yekaterinburg urban area. The resulting AOD values showed good agreement with traditional methods, based on comparisons with data from co-located two-all-sky scanners. This breakthrough in wide-field photometry processing has substantial implications for future aerosol monitoring systems that can provide continuous, long-term data with minimal maintenance costs. The approach has been made publicly available as a software tool, known as AEROSCAN, which can be used by other researchers working with similar instrumentation. Accurate object pose estimation in complex real-world scenarios is a difficult task, largely because it involves projecting multiple objects that are linked together. Current approaches typically treat each projected shadow separately, making it challenging to achieve a high success rate. We address this challenge by introducing a novel method called Projected Shadow Connection Network, which connects projected shadows of multiple objects with different poses by learning their internal structures. This mechanism enables our approach to estimate the poses of all projected shadows simultaneously, resulting in a significant improvement in success rate compared to existing methods. We evaluated our method on two challenging datasets, Indoor Scene Layout and 3D Reconstruction with Conventional Camera, and achieved success rates of 67.2% and 85.7% on these datasets respectively, surpassing the current state-of-the-art performance. We also conducted an extensive experiment by combining our approach with a state-of-the-art indoor scene reconstruction method, which led to a notable increase in reconstructed indoor space area. We have made our code and models publicly available at https://github.com/zwang84/PSCN.

We propose a novel extension to the Graphical Lasso framework, which enables the estimation of sparse precision matrices while accounting for hidden factors. This approach, called the Graphical Lasso with latent variables, leverages a hierarchical modeling structure to connect the precision matrices of observed and latent data. We then derive the optimization algorithm to estimate these connected precision matrices, adding to the existing literature on Bayesian structural learning. Additionally, we introduce a method to construct conditional regulatory networks from the estimated precision matrices. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this new extension through comprehensive simulations and a real-world application involving gene regulatory networks. This method is particularly useful for analyzing multilayered data networks and has implications for various fields, including genetics, neuroscience, and finance. This study investigates how the pressure within a cavity beneath an impacting solid surface affects surface seal dynamics, specifically the formation of ribbons or spots that occur when the impacting object bounces off, causing a wave of pressure to build and then release inside the cavity. To simplify the situation, we focus on a single-dimensional cavity and conduct physical modeling to analyze how pressure dynamics influence surface seal dynamics. According to our findings, when the impacting object moves quickly, the pressure within the cavity rises rapidly, leading to the formation of a ribbon-shaped surface seal, whereas slower impacts result in higher pressure peaks at the edges of the cavity and thus produce spot-shaped surface seals. Furthermore, our research indicates that the distance over which the impacting object travels before it bounces off plays a crucial role in controlling the formation of ribbons or spots by influencing the pressure wave frequency and amplitude within the cavity. In addition, our data align with previous research on the dynamics of impacting solid surfaces, which found that the relationship between the distance the object travels before bouncing and the formation of surface seals follows the same pattern, whether the object is impacting a solid surface with a cavity or a flat surface. To address this limitation, we used X-ray photoemission spectroscopy to analyze the electronic structure of cubanite, particularly focusing on its valence band composition. The results show that the valence band electrons can be explained using a superposition of cubic cuprate, delafossite, and magnetically ordered substances. By comparing these references, we were able to determine the relative proportions of electrons in cubanite and found that they are evenly distributed between copper and iron atoms, which may contribute to the stability of the rock-salt sublattices within the cubanite structure. This equality in electron distribution also provides insight into the strong ferromagnetic ordering we observed, as it suggests that strong exchange interactions prevail in cubanite. Additionally, we were able to identify an apparent hole deficit in the rock-salt sublattices, which may be linked to the charge stability of cubanite. Furthermore, our analysis allows for a comparison with other materials that share similarities with cubanite, which could be useful in the search for this mineral and in understanding its unusual properties. It also highlights the value of combining experimental and theoretical data in understanding the complex electronic structures and resulting phenomena observed in natural substances. Research involving quantum dots embedded in acoustic cavities has yielded significant findings, and by adjusting the driving laser frequency, we found that its effect on Rabi oscillations can be reversed simply by changing the direction of its propagation. In a coupled quantum dot and acoustic cavity system, driving the cavity directly results in coherent Rabi oscillations between the dot and cavity, while driving the dot indirectly leads to cavity Rabi oscillations, with the cavity serving as a waveguide. By modifying the driving frequency, the Rabi oscillations shift between the direct and indirect pathways, allowing for interconversion between them. This interconversion can be completed within milliseonds using laser powers in the order of tens of milliseconds, and its rate appears to be independent of the cavity's decay rate. Furthermore, this phenomenon maintains its integrity in both classical and quasi-conditional Rabi oscillation scenarios. The role of the cavity's decay rate, as well as the driving and detuning values, were examined through numerical simulations. This discovery paves the way for driving Rabi oscillations in quantum systems that are linked to cavities with lossy elements, and its potential applications are vast. It is further suggested that this phenomenon could be an indicator of non-classical behavior in the coupled system. Ultimately, this finding provides a new level of control over Rabi oscillations, allowing for the interchange between different pathways, and it is anticipated to significantly enhance the performance of quantum devices that incorporate coupled cavity systems. It is proposed that this phenomenon be referred to as the Bichromatic Effect. It is also proposed that the Bichromatic Effect be utilized as a diagnostic tool to determine the coupled system's quantum properties by examining the rate of its direction reversal. It is estimated that the direction reversal rate can distinguish between a purely classical and a truly quantum coupled system, with the latter exhibiting a significantly greater rate of about two orders of magnitude. It is also discovered that the Bichromatic Effect maintains its integrity in both coherent and incoherent Rabi oscillation scenarios. We investigate a herringbone lattice, a non-trivial extension of the Shraiman-Anderson model, as it is implicated in the structural characteristics of certain biological membranes. This lattice can be controlling through quantum fluctuations, leading to a mysterious phenomenon known as the "quantum classically transition". We studied this phenomenon by applying various perturbations to the Hamiltonian, replacing the ideal herringbone configuration with an array of coupled dimer systems. These modifications allowed us to adjust the lattice's dimensions, altering its behavior from classical to quantum phenomena. Notably, we discovered conditions under which the original configuration can be recovered, either partially or completely, through classical fluctuations alone. Furthermore, we found that the coupled dimer system shares key characteristics with the discrete quantum Yang-Mills theory, potentially providing a realistic scenario for the theory's quantization. Additionally, we observed the emergence of a discrete gauge symmetry in the coupled dimer system, which can be distinguished from its broken phase. These findings reveal the versatile nature of the herringbone lattice, offering a framework for understanding intricate phenomena in complex systems. Given its biological membrane origins, we propose the cytoskeleton-membrane hybrid model as a realistic representation of these systems. This model incorporates a herringbone lattice membrane interacting with an actin-like cytoskeleton, demonstrating the robustness of the herringbone lattice's unique characteristics even in the presence of this interaction. Given its intricate architecture and dynamic nature, we suggest that the herringbone lattice, and by extension the cytoskeleton-membrane hybrid model, holds significant scientific value, awaiting further theoretical and experimental exploration. This research paves the way for applying the coupled dimer system to the discrete quantum Yang-Mills theory, offering a realistic, explicitly broken symmetry scenario for the theory's quantization. This development could, in turn, contribute to a deeper understanding of the quantum classically transition in its original context. This study also sheds light on the coupled dimer system's relationship with topological order and its connection to the broken symmetry that gives rise to it. This knowledge can be utilized to explore the intertwined issues of the quantum classically transition, topological order, and its underlying causes. This research demonstrates the coupled dimer system's versatility, extending beyond the herringbone lattice to potential implications for complex biological membranes and other systems featuring coupled dimer arrangements. Notably, our calculations reveal contrasting outcomes for the success probabilities of these states when produced via beam splitters and parametric amplifiers. When using a beam splitter, we find that the chances of successfully creating a SPCCS are significantly lower, specifically $1/e^2$, in comparison to $e^{-2}$ for the parametric amplifier. Our study also compares their quadrature amplitude distributions with those of coherent states, revealing distinct differences. We introduce a novel generative model, called the polymer sequence deepstack generator, that produces complex polymers composed of multiple types of monomers. This model treats each polymer as a hierarchical stack of monomers, emulating the same structural pattern observed in actual macromolecules. By representing each monomer as a sample from a categorical distribution, the model captures the diverse range of polymer structures, including those with multiple subunits and branching configurations. Unlike previous methods that either focus on entire sequences or divide them into non-overlapping parts, our model splits each monomer into its own sequence of stack operations, allowing it to learn both the structure and chemical identity of each monomer. Through the evaluation of four different datasets, our model demonstrates improved performance compared to existing techniques, particularly in predicting the structures of proteins and other biopolymers. Additionally, it is shown that this model can generate specific features of biopolymers, such as the position of particular chemical groups, with a high degree of accuracy. Furthermore, it is possible to modify the model so that it can create new biopolymer structures that have the same general form as those in the training data. This enhanced model maintains the capabilities of the original model while producing more realistic and diverse biopolymer structures, incorporating long-range interactions and multiple subunits in its design. It is called the extended polymer sequence deepstack generator. This technique provides a valuable framework for generating biopolymer structures that are accurate and realistic, and has the potential for wide application in fields such as drug discovery and design. It is particularly useful for developing virtual biopolymers that can be used in place of real ones in these fields, where it has been shown to be more cost-effective and more environmentally friendly. This model can also be used to analyze the complex structures of biopolymers by automatically identifying different components of these structures, making it a valuable tool for biologists and chemists. It is necessary to note that while this model is capable of incorporating long-range interactions into its design, it does have some difficulty with certain types of structures that have very long chains of monomers, such as DNA molecules that are composed of chains of up to millions of monomers. It is possible to address this limitation by dividing such large structures into smaller, more manageable parts, but this can make it more difficult to preserve the relationships between different components of these structures. In recent years, attention mechanisms and convolutional neural networks have significantly improved image segmentation, specifically in medical imaging, including esophageal tumors. The challenges posed by large memory requirements and slow computation led researchers to use structured attention and efficient convolution methods in a specific unet variation, which significantly improved both computing speed and memory efficiency while maintaining high segmentation accuracy. Building upon this work, a new unet variant was developed, labeled Dilated Dense Attention Unet, which incorporates multiple convolution operations, density attention, and dilated convolution in both encoding and decoding stages of the network. The proposed method successfully balances computation efficiency and accuracy by utilizing 12 convolution layers, which enables it to handle high-resolution images and segment tumors with precise boundary detection with a modified loss function. The feasibility and effectiveness of this model were validated through experimental data with varying resolution and modality, yielding outstanding results with an overall Esoph-CA dataset score of 85.4%. The code for this research has been made publicly available on GitHub, which includes an automatic hyperparameter optimization process utilizing the Ray Tune toolkit, a real-time tumor segmentation module, and a 3D extension of the model. The current variation is suited for two-dimensional image segmentation tasks. The code also includes guidelines for installing required packages, preprocessing data, and evaluating the model. The code has been tested using Ubuntu 20.04 LTS and Python 3.8. The future direction of this research involves incorporating spatial information from neighboring pixels, which the authors believe will further improve the accuracy of the model. The project has the potential to be applied in real-world scenarios, such as providing personalized treatment plans for cancer patients with tumors in the esophagus. The code has been viewed over 50,000 times on GitHub and the related research paper has been cited over 200 times. These demands drive the need for advanced NLP techniques that can effectively manage multiple languages. To this end, we present a mixed-language generative model called MIGT3 or the Multilingual Integrated Graphical Theorem-based Text-to-Text transformer, which surpasses previous benchmarks in cross-language text generation and enhances understanding of graph-based theoretical foundations of transformer architecture. Moreover, our model delivers comparable results to state-of-the-art models in shorter text generation tasks, thereby establishing a new benchmark for future integrated graph-based transformer research. Calculating energy loss functions for complex materials like tantalum oxides requires a detailed computation that takes into account both local field effects and spin-orbit coupling, which can be significant for these systems. Based on the linear response formalism, we've developed an approach that accurately determines energy loss functions using the polarizability of the material, which is further derived from a one-loop calculation of the dielectric function. This approach has been tested with a simplified model of a solid, and has also been applied to several tantalum oxide compounds with different ligands, which have shown a noticeable impact of spin-orbit coupling on the energy loss function, particularly evident in compounds with heavier atoms like oxygen, Ta, and Cl. These results demonstrate that neglecting spin-orbit coupling can lead to an incomplete description of electron interaction and, by extension, may result in an inaccurate interpretation of photoelectron energy shifts in archaeological interfaces. Ultimately, our study underlines the necessity of considering spin-orbit coupling in the computation of energy loss functions for tantalum oxides, which is a crucial aspect for understanding photoelectron energy shifts in these compounds, particularly in regards to oxidation states of heavy atoms. Additionally, our approach provides a means to predict energy loss functions from the polarizability of materials, which can be measured experimentally, and suggests the potential for reverse engineering of energy loss functions from known compounds, which would facilitate a deeper understanding of the chemistry behind electron energy shifts. Finally, our approach has implications for the comprehension of archaeological interfaces by probing photoelectron energy shifts in tantalum oxides, which offer a unique combination of robustness, spin-orbit coupling, and a varied range of compounds and reactions, making them an ideal model for testing and developing new photoelectron theory. This is particularly important for understanding oxidation states of heavy atoms, which are notoriously difficult to determine with other methods, and has the potential to greatly enhance our understanding of the chemistry behind electron energy shifts, not just in tantalum oxides but in other systems with heavy atoms as well. The growing physical and social segregation of communities, as described by Bill Bishop in "The Big Sort," has significant implications for the dissemination of false information online. Our research suggests that, due to geographical isolation, individuals are more likely to be connected to a limited pool of information sources within their local community, making it easier for them to spread misinformation to a confined audience. We quantify the effect of "The Big Sort" on the spread of misinformation by examining changes in the size and diversity of local information networks. Our results indicate that the reduction in diversity of these networks has led to a significant increase in the spread of false information, with the largest impact being on elections and political events. Furthermore, we find that initiatives promoting social diversity and increasing access to broader information sources can effectively mitigate the spread of misinformation in isolated communities. Our study provides a theoretical framework and empirical evidence highlighting the crucial role of social segregation and local information networks in the online dissemination of false information and associated consequences. Our findings have practical implications for strategies aimed at combating the spread of false information in closed social systems. Our study uses a unique combination of theoretical analysis, online experiments, and empirical data from over 1 million Wikipedia users to support our results. Our data include reliable indicators of user segregation, as well as relevant real-world events that can be used to track the effectiveness of interventions promoting network diversity and reducing the spread of false information. Our research demonstrates the critical link between social segregation, local information networks, and the online dissemination of false information, and shows that targeted interventions aimed at increasing network diversity can lead to significant reductions in the spread of false information, with the largest impact being on elections and political events. Our results remain relevant in the current political climate, marked by increasing social segregation and the widespread dissemination of false information online. To understand the underlying principles behind speech instructions in teaching tasks, whether they're aimed at assisting others or animal training, it's necessary to analyze how demonstrations, audio guidance, broken tasks, and errors influence the related semantic concepts. With this goal in mind, we've developed a multimodal teaching model that generates speech based on visual demonstrations and considers the intended listener's knowledge. To evaluate this model and similar semantic models, we've created a dataset of teaching scenes with multiple demonstration types, audio guidance for tasks like object manipulation, and accompanying semantic speech files. Our dataset, which we've named TeachSpeech, is an original contribution with 500 diverse teaching instances, spanning 20 concepts and 5 object categories, and is available for public use. We've conducted experiments using TeachSpeech to demonstrate how variations in demonstration types, audio instructions, subtasks, and errors affect the related semantic concepts, and have found that incorporating listener knowledge and avoiding explicit audio instructions reduces the semantic distance between demonstrations and the desired concept. Conversely, demonstrations with errors increase the semantic distance. Furthermore, our results show that our proposed model produces more semantically similar speech in comparison to a baseline model, and we've observed the importance of considering listener knowledge in teaching tasks, particularly when the goal is to point out specific objects. Our model and baseline experiments are reproducible using our publicly available TeachSpeech dataset. It is hoped that this dataset and associated experiments will facilitate future research on the underlying principles of speech instructions in teaching tasks. To ensure transparency and facilitate reproducibility, our experiments are being made available through dedicated APIs that are publicly accessible. It is worth noting that to ensure fairness in experimentation, we have not used any models or algorithms that were developed in-house as baseline models, rather we have used publicly available models such as the multimodal embedding learning model mentioned in section 2. It is also noteworthy that our proposed model and baseline models are simple and do not employ any complex techniques such as memory-augmented architectures, recurrent architectures, or reinforcement learning, in order to ensure that any future improvements are truly indicative of the proposed approach and not the result of complex architectures. It is also worth mentioning that our model and baseline models are designed to utilize the learned embeddings of the objects involved in the teaching scenes, rather than direct visual features, in order to focus solely on the semantic aspects of the teaching scenes. It is also important to highlight that our model experiments are feasible due to the relatively small size of our TeachSpeech dataset, which makes the dataset suitable for fair and reproducible experimentation. Conversational systems, found in various automated agents, require rigorous quality assurance due to their complex nature. Despite the importance of testing these systems, a significant roadblock exists in the form of automated testing frameworks. Current frameworks are often inflexible and difficult to adapt for different applications, posing a challenge for developers who need to create customized tests. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach called "Selective Relevance Ranking" that leverages machine learning to prioritize information relevant to a specific conversation task. By simplifying the input data, our approach enhances the performance of automatic evaluation metrics and improves the effectiveness of natural language processing models. Furthermore, we introduce a new metric called "Conversational F-score" that assesses the accuracy of automatic evaluators in comparing different models and frameworks for conversational systems. Our approach and proposed metric are validated through extensive experiments involving multiple models and evaluation methods. We introduce Incompatibility MDP (I-MDP), a framework that incorporates incompatibility as a state variable in a Markov Decision Process. This framework enables us to formally model decisions that result in incompatibilities, which can lead to new states and ultimately affect future decisions, by drawing upon concepts from Dynamic User Equilibrium and Pairwise Incompatibility. The resulting model facilitates an understanding of how incompatibility, defined as incompatible outcomes resulting from previous decisions, affects current and future acceptance opportunities in kidney transplantation by accounting for donor-incompatibility preferences. We then establish the conditions under which the optimal policy with respect to future incompatibility-free days can be considered as reaching a state of pairwise incompatibility user equilibrium. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between the I-MDP model and the existing literature on the problem of maximizing incompatibility-free days, thereby facilitating an understanding of how waiting time strategies are affected by incompatibility preferences. Finally, we outline the steps for constructing policy-relevant simulations from real-world kidney transplantation datasets. The resulting I-MDP model provides a valuable framework for analyzing complex decision-making in kidney transplantation by incorporating incompatibility as a state variable, and demonstrates the utility of incorporating prior knowledge about incompatibility preferences into simulation models. The approach presented in this research can be applied to other transplant scenarios involving multiple incompatible donors, as well as other decision-making contexts characterized by time-dependent, uncertain, and complex incompatibility relationships. The underlying methodological framework of incorporating incompatibility as a dynamic state variable is similarly applicable to other critical transplantation issues, such as liver transplantation. Despite their success in many applications, word embeddings struggle with the nuances of financial language, causing problems for machines that rely on these embeddings. Our analysis suggests that the limitations of current embedding techniques result from the frequent co-occurrence of opposite words in financial contexts, which induces a form of semantic drift affecting the embeddings. In wideband communication systems, optimizing multiple objectives is common due to limited resources. Fair-throughput and sum-throughput are two such objectives that often require compromise with each other. We developed an optimization framework to achieve both high fair-throughput and sum-throughput rates. This was made possible by formulating the problem as a multi-objective optimization problem and solving it using the $\epsilon$-constraint method. We also established the structure of optimal solutions to aid in solving the problem. Despite the problem's complexity, we found solutions for it in two specific scenarios: with only two users and in a scenario that has no user limit. In both cases, we found the optimal solution strategy. Our results demonstrate the fairness rates and corresponding sum-throughput rates for both the two-user and unlimited-user cases. This knowledge can be utilized in other non-trivial cases, such as communication systems with changing user limits. We validated our analytical findings with numerical results from simulated data. This involved comparing the performance of our optimal solution with that of a random solution. Our findings showed that our solution resulted in significantly higher fair-throughput and sum-throughput rates compared to the random solution. This margin increased with higher values of $\epsilon$. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to various communication systems, including those with changing user limits, as long as the condition of varying user limits is met with time constants that are much longer than the system's time constant. This ensures that the user limits can be considered constant during each optimization cycle. Our approach also considers prior knowledge and real-time data as input to aid in the optimization process. This is particularly important in dynamic systems where accurate prediction is crucial for achieving optimal performance. Our approach was tested in a simulation of a communication system with changing user limits and varying channel conditions. This involved up to 50 users with time constants that ranged from several seconds to minutes. Our approach was found to achieve optimal solutions in the majority of cases. However, in cases where the user limits changed too quickly, it did not achieve the optimal solution. Our approach is suitable for various applications, including cellular networks, satellite communication systems, and cognitive radio systems. Conveying complex dynamics from visual observations through generative models is a fascinating yet challenging task. A notable example is the statistical model proposed by Dukes et al., which uses a deep neural network to generate turbulent flow patterns consistent with Rayleigh--Bénard instability based solely on temperature difference variations at the surface. Existing research relies on either direct access to dynamical equations or external knowledge to model such complexities. In contrast, Abhishek et al. introduce a novel approach to generate Rayleigh--Bénard turbulence by training a deep learning model that relies solely on boundary conditions and produces snapshots of temperature variations at different heights. Unlike previous solutions, this model solves the problem without premising knowledge of instability mechanisms or using dynamical equations, and it is significantly more efficient, reducing the number of required data points from 750,000 to 15,000 over three dimensions. The proposed model achieves this performance improvement by using a unique generator structure that mimics the characteristics of convection rolls, an essential feature that is rigorously mathematically proven to be essential for accurately modeling the roll pattern without losing generalization ability. The resulting model demonstrates improved performance, a larger range of applicable Rayleigh numbers, and higher precision in predicting temperature variations when compared to existing solutions, outperforming them in all aspects tested. The proposed model has the potential to serve as a foundation for more complex fluid dynamics simulations. The underlying generator structure, which reflects the specific characteristics of convection rolls through learning the correct eigenfunctions of the Stokes operator, represents a novel and intriguing application of deep learning in the context of partial differential equations. In this method, known as FastFit, DGLAP evolution plays a significant role, and the results show that FastFit can accurately reproduce the original data with minimal deviation, supporting the validity of current PDF fitting methods. Furthermore, the study reveals that fitting PDFs to deeper jet scales becomes increasingly challenging due to dominant hard scattering contributions, but FastFit excels at capturing these dominant components, allowing for a scale-dependent fit that accurately represents the evolution of PDFs. The investigation also delves into alternative scenarios where the jets are produced at a deeper 14 TeV scale within the same LHC dataset, and the results demonstrate that these deeper scales are largely inaccessible to PDF fits on their own, but FastFit successfully uncovers this hidden information about PDF evolution. The research demonstrates the robustness of FastFit to extend beyond current PDF fits, offering a promising means to unlock deeper scales that are currently unaccessible, thereby significantly increasing the range of available PDF scales for matrix element calculations. The endeavor also entails a significant advancement in the integration of DGLAP evolution within a PDF fitting framework, and the findings are already applied in recent successful fits of underlying PDFs, complete with detailed validation against multiple datasets. The approach has been successfully employed in fitting PDFs to jet data at higher scales, as well as in fitting other hadron colliders, and the research paves the way for an infinite range of possible deeper scales that can be explored with Future Hadron Colliders. The associated code is publicly available as part of the PDF fitting toolkit, and the results from the study are already incorporated into established PDF sets. We introduce a variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) framework that enhances policy gradient estimation by leveraging importance sampling and counterfactual policy estimation. The framework counteracts the negative effects of unequal importance weights resulting from selective experience replay, enabling us to develop efficient reinforcement learning algorithms in various settings. In particular, we develop a straightforward and efficient algorithm that uses uniformly sampled experience replay, counterfactual policy estimation, and importance sampling to calculate policy gradients. We establish the convergence rate of $O(1/\sqrt{K})$ for the average cumulative reward under i.i.d. data samples, improving upon existing results for uniform experience replay. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed algorithm. Moreover, we provide an alternative batch policy gradient estimation method using the empirical importance ratio, its theoretical analysis, and a counterfactual policy estimation procedure that is potentially useful on its own. We also discuss multiple possible extensions of our work, including generalizing to non-uniform sampled experience replay, counterfactual policy estimation in complex evaluation environments, and policy gradient estimation using end-to-end counterfactual policy architectures. We publicly share our code and research data in accordance with our findings' potential value for future research efforts. We hope that our results, code, and data will facilitate future advancements in reinforcement learning methods involving experience replay. A key aspect of conversational AI that lacks thorough research involves understanding the relationship between theory of mind and dialog generation capabilities. This uncertainty extends to both simple mental state-based dialog tasks and more complex, real-world applications like customer service chatbots. Our proposed project aims to explore the significance of theory of mind in a specific dialog task – engaging in empathy-based conversation – and in a more general case – generating relevant dialog responses. Our empirical study involves creating generative models using transformer-based dialect applications, with the goal of improving them using theory of mind. Our results show that incorporating mental state-based dialog scenarios improves the efficacy of these models, providing evidence for the value of theory of mind in dialog generation capabilities. This discovery holds true across various assessments, indicating that the integration of theory of mind is beneficial for the model's performance. Our findings also reveal distinct advantages of using empathy-based dialog tasks and provide valuable insights into the relationship between theory of mind and dialog generation capabilities that are not task-specific. Our project code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/Dialogue-Lab/TofM-Dialog-Generation. A highly efficient numerical method called Hierarchical Gravity-Lattice Algorithm Modified (MG-GLAM) is developed to speed up cosmological N-body simulations. By reconstructing the gravitational potential using a grid of successive sub-lattices and modifying the code to employ multi-GPU architecture, MG-GLAM significantly outperforms existing codes in terms of computational efficiency. In a simulation of a flat, expanding universe with an isolated massive particle, MG-GLAM achieves a speedup of one order of magnitude over its single-GPU counterpart when using 256 GPUs in a cluster. Furthermore, MG-GLAM demonstrates the ability to accurately replicate the same simulation results as slower codes, including the location of matter overdensities and deficits at different points in time, even when using a small fraction of the original number of particles typically employed in similar simulations. In particular, MG-GLAM is able to achieve the same level of precision as slower codes when using 10 times fewer particles. In addition, MG-GLAM complies with standard outputs employed in similar research, including the power spectrum of matter density fluctuations and the scalar power spectrum of comoving curvature, and successfully replicates previously obtained research data. Ultimately, the development of MG-GLAM lays the groundwork for a new code that can efficiently incorporate additional physical phenomena, such as the effects of dark matter particles via direct detection or phase space filling. This code has the particular advantage of being relatively simple compared to other complex simulations. The MG-GLAM code is publicly available and tailored for use on large-scale supercomputers. The code's underlying methodology is also theoretically sound and physically intuitive, making it an attractive numerical solution for a broad range of N-body simulations. The code's specific speedup achievements and the broader implications of the MG-GLAM model are significant contributions to the field of cosmological simulations. The code is particularly well-suited for simulating isolated massive particles in an expanding universe, but it can be easily adapted to model more complex configurations, including the distribution of matter in galaxies and galaxy clusters. The subsequent analysis of these simulations can provide valuable insights into the behavior of various self-interacting dark matter scenarios. The full potential of the MG-GLAM model is yet to be realized, but it has the potential to significantly advance our current understanding of dark matter dynamics. The code is available online at https://github.com/ChrisGwillem/MGGLAM. This development is analogous to single-complex-plane SLE, where a growing branch cuts the complex plane along an infinite length. We also establish the connection between growing polygons in the upper half-plane and growing polynomials in the Riemann sphere, which in turn are driven by the evolving boundary within the plane. This relationship allows us to recharacterize the plane's evolving boundary as the image of a random process of transforming monic polynomials with distinct roots on the Riemann sphere. The ALICE experiment observed significant increases in strange quarks, known as strangeness enhancement, particularly in central pp collisions at 7 and 13 TeV. To better understand these phenomena, a new analysis was conducted of prompt charm production in these collisions, also accounting for charm quarks that have undergone beauty decay. This research established a minimum angle between the directions of charm and beauty particles, calculated charm production rates more precisely, and confirmed previous findings of increased strangeness in central pp collisions. Furthermore, measurements of charm and beauty production rates in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV are consistent with inelastic pp scattering processes for the first time. To facilitate further study, detailed data on charm and beauty particle properties have been made public. Charm production cross-section calculations from various models were compared to the experimental results, revealing discrepancies, while theoretical predictions for beauty production at higher energies have been obtained from existing studies. Overall, this research has expanded the understanding of heavy-flavor quark production in pp collisions and protons and heavy-ion collisions, with implications for future experiments at the LHC. To ensure the durability of this research, essential information has been made openly available on the ALICE repository, allowing for ongoing development and future experiments to build upon it within the spirit of FAIR and OA practices. A survey of the Galactic plane conducted using the e-MERLIN radio telescope has yielded a significant discovery of 60 radio pulsars, including 16 that exhibit low speeds, suggesting they are connected to Low Mass X-ray Binaries (LMXBs). The findings are consistent with previous observations in the solar neighborhood, revealing a relationship between neutron star LMXBs and millisecond radio pulsars. It's estimated that approximately one-fifth of these binaries produce X-rays and are classified as narrow beam sources, while the remaining ones, with wider beam sources, were not identified in the survey. The current observation is insufficient to determine the total population of these binaries in the Galaxy, but it does provide a preliminary estimate of 13 to 60 narrow beam LMXBs existing within the Galactic bulge region. The discovery of these pulsars and the resulting insights into their evolution will be explored in greater detail. The full data set is exceptionally rich, offering potential for the detection of pulsar companions through spectroscopic analysis of X-ray spectra from LMXBs, which could also be used to confirm the binary nature of certain sources, including one that possesses a long orbital period. The survey's primary field is positioned on either side of the Local Bubble region, perhaps revealing a connection between the missing pulsars and the existing void. The comprehensive analysis of these pulsars and their surroundings will be a subject of future study. The survey's limitations are known, having suffered some interference from wide beam pulsars and not having detected the most distant or the most faint sources, which would require a more in-depth analysis, along with a comprehensive understanding of the Galactic population of these objects. The survey has additionally discovered six new gigahertz peaks line features, which are thought to be associated with certain pulsar populations, also uncovering a previously unknown relationship between these features and spin periods of pulsars. The survey has additional significant findings, including the discovery of three new pulsar candidates, one of which exhibits a modulation of X-ray emission, a large population of millisecond radio pulsars in the Galactic bulge, and a possible void connected to the Local Bubble region. The survey data have the potential to lead to further research, such as the analysis of the mass function of the pulsar companions, the investigation of the Gigahertz Peak Emission features and the population of pulsars in the Galactic bulge, and the possible pulsar associated with the Vela SNR. Quantum mechanics governs the behavior of molecules at their most fundamental level. As such, adjustments to a molecule's quantum state can influence its chemical reactivity, making it a potentially valuable tool for enhancing reactions or slowing down unwanted chemical changes, like combustion or polymerization. To effectively manage a molecule's chemical reactivity, it's crucial to understand how its vibrational components interact with its electronic state. Presently, our capability to control these interactions is limited by our current technological capabilities, specifically in regards to accurately directing optical pulses at frequencies that correspond to vibrational energies. This challenge can be overcome with the development of optical fibers capable of transmitting high-frequency signals with precise control, enabling us to manipulate a molecule's quantum interactions with greater precision. This advancement also presents an opportunity to explore novel approaches to chemical reactivity controlled by light, including the use of quantum wells and nanotubes. This report discusses the theoretical applications of such an approach to controlling chemical reactions with light, as well as the practical considerations of using optical fibers to deliver vibrational-mode-specific optical fields to molecules. This research demonstrates how the interaction of a molecule's vibrational components with its electronic state can be managed by an externally applied optical field, depending on the molecular environment, before declining as the distance between the molecule and the optical antenna increases. This knowledge can be refined to optimize chemical reactivity in novel systems, such as quantum dots and nanoscale metal-organic frameworks. Improving dialogue response diversity through diverse dialogue generation has several benefits, including better preparation for real-world conversations that frequently deviate from expected topics.  Yet, current approaches face challenges due to the heavy cost of varied data.  This study introduces a novel technique, top-k controlled conditional generation, which produces more diverse responses at a lower data cost by selecting generated samples based on perceived semantic differences.  Leveraging a simple yet effective similarity metric, we evaluate our method on three dialogue datasets (`Cambridge`, `DialRG`, and `EMLT`) and observe notable improvements in the diversity of generated responses, measured by the increased frequency of unique topics and shorter overlap with initial prompts.  Our approach has a data-efficient design, requiring 1% of the original quantity to achieve comparable performance, making it a promising solution for generating diverse conversations with limited data. A novel approach to estimating hadron decay densities into two particles systemizing the use of artificial neural networks has been devised. This method assigns a probability to each possible two-particle invariant mass based on various relevant variables, such as four decay products properties. A significant advantage of this approach lies in its capability to effectively handle complex density functions, especially in situations where multiple hadron decay paths exist, as it does not require prior assumptions about the underlying processes. A key aspect of this method involves developing training algorithms to correctly assign probabilities to incorrect two-particle systems, which can be considered redundant combinations of the original decay products. A suitable solution has been found using a neural network composed of multiple artificial neural networks, which has been tested on real-world data from the LHC, specifically ALICE experiment data, and has shown an order of magnitude improvement in the accuracy of hadron decay density estimates compared to traditional approaches. Furthermore, this method has the potential to enhance the accuracy of other hadron decay density estimations, such as those involving three or more particles, although such an extension would require additional developments. This hadron decay density estimation method has been made publicly available as part of the THNN package, which can be obtained from the CERN GitHub page. This innovation has the potential to enhance the accuracy of other hadron decay density estimations, such as those involving three or more particles, although such an extension would require additional developments. This approach has been made publicly available as part of the THNN package, which can be obtained from the CERN GitHub page. Further developments are also being considered for addressing three or four particle hadron decay densities. Memory-resident attacks like Flush+Reload primarily rely on the consistent behavior of memory eviction and refilling processes, which vary across systems.  To enhance the efficacy of these attacks, we propose HyperDegrade, a technique that modulates the frequency and intensity of memory operations to accommodate different target memory blocks, ultimately enabling the efficacy of these attacks on timewise diverse and memory-hierarchical systems.  Our technique, implemented using assembly language instructions, successfully compromises sensitive information from various platforms, including Linux-based embedded devices, real-world web servers, and virtualized cloud infrastructure, by reducing the required time and number of attack traces needed.  Our findings highlight the vulnerability of memory-based security protocols, specifically OpenSSL's SSLv2 protocol, which often uses insecure random number generation, and our proposed approach could be crucial for the development of more effective and adaptable memory-based attacks.  Our attack data and implementation details are available for secure memory attack researchers.  Additionally, we provide a statistical analysis of observed memory behavior to guide potential memory-based attacks, highlighting the widespread susceptibility of systems to such attacks.  Our proposed approach has been made public to facilitate secure memory protocol development and to provide actionable data for the memory attack research community.  Our approach builds upon existing research, notably the work of Le Bossan, Basso, and Evans, as well as the Flush+Reload attack described by Hermans, Schmidt, and Poppelier.  Our statistical analysis is an initial step towards creating a memory behavior dictionary, which could significantly enhance the effectiveness of memory-based attacks, informing future memory attack research, and guiding secure memory protocol development, by illuminating the widespread vulnerabilities of systems to such attacks, and highlighting the crucial factors that influence memory block accessibility, with the aim of developing more efficient memory-based attacks, and more secure memory-based protocols. The study of these cocycles, integrated up to a coherent choice of gauge, forms a Lie algebra whose representation determines the invariants. The paper demonstrates the equivalence between this Lie algebra and the classical Lie algebra of loop vectors, thereby establishing that each loop vector cocycle is equivalent to a set of integrated cocycles and thus represents a specific knot invariant. The resulting framework enables an intuitive understanding of the fundamental properties of these invariants, which include simplification properties along the Reidemeister moves. In collaborative scenarios between agents with varying levels of capability, effective decision-making is crucial for achieving common goals. A new stochastic cooperative game framework, called Cooperative Semi-Markov Decision Process (CSDP), is established to model decision-making challenges for agents with different abilities and differing levels of difficulty in completing tasks. The CSDP framework incorporates an opportunity cost approach to address distribution imbalances and provides computationally feasible algorithms for obtaining optimal cooperative policies and distributing tasks fairly among agents. Through theoretical and numerical studies, the benefits of cooperative decision-making and the effectiveness of proposed algorithms are demonstrated. A software framework has been created to test and validate the CSDP framework, and potential applications in related fields are also illustrated. The CSDP framework can be used to model and solve decision-making problems in various real-world scenarios, such as power grid management, transportation systems, and social networks. This paper conducts an investigation of privacy vulnerabilities in vertical federated learning. We develop and execute two sensitive-data leakage attacks, a Generative Adversarial Network-based attack and a support vector machine-based attack, against two vertical FL protocols widely adopted in practice. The results show that our GAN-based attack successfully reconstructs sensitive data with reasonably high accuracy, while the svm-based attack only succeeds to a limited extent. Furthermore, we propose an enhanced protocol combining both data encryption and differential privacy, and compare it to the existing protocols by analyzing protocol security and efficiency. Our findings highlight the privacy risks associated with vertical FL and highlight the need for enhanced security measures, also providing a utility-efficient solution to support large-scale implementations. Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF) have been introduced to speed up kernel methods by reducing the number of features needed while maintaining accuracy. Improving upon Random Fourier Features (RFF), PRFF selects specific random frequencies that are more likely to be effective, thus requiring fewer features. However, the optimal frequency set to use varies with the data and target function. We address this limitation by modifying the PRFF algorithm to create a method that automatically chooses the most suitable frequencies, which we call Adaptive PRFF (APRFF). Experimental results across various datasets and kernel types show that APRFF consistently outperforms RFF and PRFF in both feature dimension and prediction accuracy. Furthermore, APRFF demonstrates superior performance compared to traditional methods such as SVM and GMM, achieving a 3.5% higher accuracy on average when using a significantly reduced number of features. We also provide mathematical analysis of the algorithm and prove that APRFF maintains the same expected value as the original kernel, thus preserving its original properties. To facilitate broad dissemination, we have made the APRFF code publicly available on GitHub, ready for use in the machine learning community.

The purpose of this letter is to provide further details about the origin of BigApple and to clarify any misconceptions associated with the notation previously used to identify it. The functional in question was derived from a Gogny-type interaction, and it yields a saturation point for nuclear matter at an energy density of 16.75 MeV per particle, with pressure and bulk modulus values of 16.94 MeV per particle and 175.66 MeV, respectively. We have also developed a gradient correction to the density gradient expansion of the surface energy density. Notably, the predicted neutron skin thickness of $^{208}$Pb is 0.193 cm, with a value of 0.084 cm derived from the neutron density distribution. The relationship between isovector nuclear matter and the isospin-dependent Coulomb energy, as well as the connection between the density gradient surface term and the density gradient of the nuclear density, were both investigated. The resulting BigApple-Gogny density functional was utilized to calculate the energies of various nuclear states, yielding root-mean-square radii values in agreement with experimental data, with deviations of less than 0.2% for both proton and neutron radii. The calculated binding energies exhibited a discrepancy of 0.5 MeV per nucleon from experimental values, primarily due to the lack of a three-body force component in the energy density functional. The moment of inertia and pairing energy were found to be nearly unchanged with the new density functional. The BigApple-Gogny functional also demonstrated robustness under various parameter variations. A crucial aspect of the functional is its inability to reproduce the reference density matrix obtained through an inverse procedure, highlighting the complexity of uniquely determining the reference state of nuclear matter. The failure of the functional to reproduce the original Gogny force components also implies that the energy density functional approach is not suitable for reverse engineering the Gogny force. Notwithstanding these limitations, the BigApple-Gogny functional provides a valuable independent verification of previous research on nuclear matter properties. The absence of electronic scattering, indicated by the low value of the electronic specific heat capacity, supports the idea that this material could be "superconducting without damping". The interplay of Dirac electrons and strong coupling leads to an unusual behavior of the charge density, with certain orbital pockets remaining unsatisfied, contributing to an excess of negative charge that gives rise to alternate bond lengths and directions, and could be a necessary condition for the emergence of "bad metal" behavior in GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$. The material's complexity has been demonstrated through the disagreement between theoretical models of its electronic behavior using the perfect crystal approximation, and those obtained using the real crystal structure, highlighting the significance of considering the actual arrangement of atoms in theoretical analysis, rather than relying on simplified models. The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has thoroughly examined rare processes involving heavy neutral leptons. By examining data from 13-TeV proton-proton collisions, amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of integrated luminosity, restrictions are placed on the mass of heavy neutral leptons and their coupling to neutrinos in three scenarios: 2nd, 3rd generation specific and universal cases. In the universal case, where heavy neutral leptons freely exchange electrons, Newtonian physics limitations prevent masses above 79.5 GeV from being confirmed. In the 2nd and 3rd generation specific scenarios, where heavy neutral leptons primarily interact with tau or bottom quarks, masses up to 458 and 325 GeV are ruled out, respectively. These discoveries position future experiments for the possibility of discovering heavy neutral leptons in specific scenarios with optimized production methods, involving the collision of 100 TeV protons produced in the LHC's high-luminosity phase with heavy neutral leptons in the decay channel of bottom quarks and tau particles. In this scenario, where the elastic scattering process off atomic nuclei is considered, detection limits could be further refined to include masses as low as 325 GeV. Additionally, other rare processes involving heavy neutral leptons such as the production of top quarks and heavy neutral leptons, the decay of heavy neutral leptons into pairs of light quarks, and the decay of heavy neutral leptons into a photon and a gluon or a W and a bottom quark are also examined. 3D face reconstruction is a complex task that requires modeling various pose-dependent and pose-independent factors. Previous approaches divide pose-dependent and pose-independent factors into separate sub-networks, which can lead to inaccuracies due to the mixed nature of certain input data. This research introduces the Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet), a novel framework that separates pose-dependent and pose-independent factors within a single sub-network using two distinct faces that represent different viewing angles. By feeding the combination of two different viewing angle faces into the network, it accurately estimates both pose-dependent and pose-independent factors, employing face alignment to ensure integrity. Experimentation reveals the advantages of this method in predicting 3D faces from limited and noisy input data, outperforming competing techniques in the 3D face reconstruction and face transfer domains. Furthermore, it demonstrates the capability to reconstruct 3D faces from varying viewing angles from limited two-view setups, producing results of a higher quality compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Experimental code and models are available for use at https://github.com/zwang84/SADRNet.

We provide new formulas for the average number of deepest nodes in standard and marked ordered trees. Our formula for the former, which represents the number of nodes at the highest level, is given by a simple closed-form expression as $\frac{3a+1}{2(a-1)}$, where $a$ is the number of nodes. This formula can be further utilized to calculate the expected number of the highest level, which is given by $\frac{3a+1}{a-1}$. For the latter, we derive the average number of deepest nodes as $\frac{4a^2+2a+1}{a^2-a-2}$, along with the expected number of the highest level as $\frac{4a^2+2a+2}{a^2-a-2}$. These findings build upon the work of Schaefer, who initially derived closed-form expressions for the number of longest paths and the average number of deepest nodes in standard and marked ordered trees, with proofs based on recursive structures and generating functions. Our approach is distinct, relying on the standard and marked tree interpretation of the ballot chain election process. This approach allows us to leverage the uniform distribution of node levels, enabling the use of basic expectations and variances properties to derive average values. This alternative method also enables the exploration of additional questions, such as the distribution of the highest level node in standard and marked ordered trees. Furthermore, our results can be applied to a 'first-fit' storage problem, which parallels the longest path problem in the context of tree elections. By utilizing our average values, we can determine the expected number of nodes that cannot be assigned to the lowest levels in standard and marked ordered trees. This expectation can be further utilized to calculate the standard and marked tree versions of the 'first-fit' storage problem as discrete Conway constants. Accurate optical character recognition is fundamental to efficiently processing large quantities of written documents, such as historical vote tabulations.  A key challenge with optical character recognition is the presence of spelling errors in the predicted output, which can be particularly difficult to address when the correct context is limited, as is the case with many historical documents.  To enhance the effectiveness of optical character recognition, we developed a novel spell correction algorithm tailored for this type of data, leveraging the power of deep learning models.  This algorithm leverages the limited contextual information available to prioritize the most likely corrections, thereby minimizing unreliable guesses when the context is uncertain.  Our evaluation using a historical election dataset revealed significant improvements from the current state-of-the-art methods, with a significant increase in the accuracy of the optical character recognition output when combined with a standard spell correction model.  Furthermore, our algorithm demonstrated exceptional performance on a modern text corpus, showcasing its versatility beyond historical documents.  Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Trivadana/ContextualSpellCorrection.  This algorithm has been applied to the historical election dataset discussed in our associated research paper, which can be found at this link https://arXiv.org/abs/2207.02632.
