We introduce a new epidemiological model that extends the standard SIS model by incorporating super-spreader events in closed settings, and prove that this modified model exhibits a single global equilibrium point where the system rapidly converges. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of a short-duration transient period during which super-spreader events have a significant impact on infection dynamics. To facilitate numerical analysis, we simplify the model using a singular perturbation approach, effectively reducing the original system into an approximate two-segment model comprising an initial short phase affected by the super-spreader and a longer subsequent phase that mimics the standard SIS dynamics. To study the model numerically, we leverage a combination of the singular perturbation method and a hybrid numerical scheme that maintains accuracy while mitigating computational errors. Through extensive numerical testing on various parameter settings and problem solvers, we establish the robustness and versatility of our approach. To further illustrate the applicability of this model, we explore its extension to include additional features such as time-varying population sizes, noise effects, and interventions, and demonstrate its utility in analyzing real-world data from two distinct closed systems. Despite its complexity, this model proves to be a valuable tool for predicting infection trajectories and evaluating the effectiveness of control strategies in closed environments. This model also offers insights into the dynamics of infections in open settings, revealing that it can be viewed as a combination of an infinite number of closed-system models featuring varying durations. Ultimately, this research highlights the critical impact of super-spreader events on infection dynamics and underscores the necessity of accounting for their influence in modeling and predicting the spread of infections. We introduce a novel Monte Carlo method that achieves high efficiency by reducing complex computations needed for the simulation of intricate probability distributions. This method is inspired by the recent advancement in neural network theory and utilizes complex-valued affine coupling layers to model probability densities. We have discovered that using this method to estimate the expected value of a function that is inherently complex-valued leads to a significant decay of the Monte Carlo error when compared to traditional approaches. Through numerical experiments, we found that our method exhibits improved performance when applying it to various complex-valued functions and density distributions. Furthermore, we have observed that this method anticipates the diffusion process and approximates the expected value of a function that has undergone a stochastic transformation, which we have tested using experimental data. This method can be applied to the simulation of intricate stochastic processes and complex functions by incorporating the use of auxiliary fields, as demonstrated by experiments using standard Gaussian distributions and the Coulomb interaction model. This method offers immense potential for computing the expected values of complex functions with extensive implications in fields such as materials science, chemistry, and biology. Systematic error analysis and the impact of parameter choice on the method have also been examined through numerical experiments. A Python code to replicate the results is available in the repository https://github.com/QianYu2019/CCAL-MC. This code can be readily used for various applications and modifications of the method due to its highly customizable nature. Given any recognizable morphism σ and subshift X, the topological entropy of the image subshift Xσ is less than or equal to the topological entropy of X. If X is irreducible and σ is injective, the equality holds only when X is a single orbit subshift or both the subshift X and its factor X/θ have zero entropy. A formula for the topological entropy of the image subshift Xσ is also established in this case. Additionally, it is proven that the topological entropy of Xσ is equal to the topological entropy of the subshift defined by the extended morphism ñ, where ñ is obtained from σ and the right extension ρ of σ. It is demonstrated that topological invariance arises when considering subshifts restricted to recognizable morphisms and their factors. Moreover, a formula for the topological entropy of Xσ is derived, leading to a previous result by Sushchansky as well as an recent outcome by Baier and Steinberger. It is worth noting that the recognizable morphism condition can be replaced with the same result being applicable under the constrained setting of SL(1,3) subshifts, as demonstrated by Baier and Steinberger through a different approach. It is also shown that the topological entropy of Xσ can be calculated as the supremum of the entropies of the subshifts constituting the factor map θ, where the factors are defined by the occurrences of specific words in the symbolic representation of X. Our proposed method, ReCross, enhances the generation capabilities of large language models in an unsupervised framework, building on the paradigm first established by low-data LM pretraining. By intentionally generating faulty sentences, we force the model to rectify its own errors, which significantly improves the performance of the model in an unsupervised setting. Our research used the ReCross method for both single-task and multi-task LM pretraining, achieving improved results on various evaluation metrics when compared to the current state-of-the-art methods over a wide range of tasks. Specifically, our results showed significant improvements in unsupervised LM performance on SuperGLUE, ReTreat, and WebText30 datasets. Furthermore, our ReCross model demonstrated better performance in controlled noise conditions, showcasing its resilience to artificial noise. Our findings provide evidence for the importance of model self-correction in unsupervised LM pretraining, offering a meaningful enhancement to the current state-of-the-art methods. Our ReCross code will be made available through the GitHub platform. Our future research intentions involve applying the ReCross method to controlled unsupervised LM settings and exploring different model self-correction strategies. Our intention is to make our code a community-driven platform for LM model self-correction research. Hyperparameter tuning in AI models, especially those dealing with sensitive or publicly unavailable data, poses a significant challenge for traditional methods like grid search. These techniques require access to model predictions on a validation set, which is not feasible when working with private data behind a server. To address this issue, we've developed a novel framework for hyperparameter optimization that leverages server cooperation. Without gaining access to the sensitive data, the framework enables collaboration with the server to determine the most suitable model parameters, using a small amount of data that can be freely shared. We've also introduced an innovative method for estimating hyperparameter performance on a private dataset based on a small public dataset, which allows for the selection of the best model. We've tested and evaluated our approach on machine learning models for text classification and sentiment analysis. Our results show that our hyperparameter optimization method matches the performance of traditional approaches that use private data, while requiring significantly less data from the server. Our approach has the potential to support a wide range of applications involving sensitive data, including medical diagnosis, financial analysis, and online advertising. Our code is available for public use at https://github.com/HsiaoChienLai/PrivAT.

We investigate the algebraic properties of the Coxeter group W(S,Σ) equipped with a specific generating set S, which is comprised of reflections except for a specific set of pairs of reflections. This Coxeter group is termed a "star product" of the original Coxeter group W(Σ) and is structurally similar to the cone over a spherical shell with a specific set of radii, determined by the parameters of the Coxeter system. Our primary objectives are threefold: first, we establish a marked, piecewise linear isomorphism between the geometry of this Coxeter group and the corresponding solar system of spheres within a wedge; next, we establish that this solar system can be completely classified based on the Coxeter system itself, thereby demonstrating that all conceivable solar systems arise from Coxeter groups of this specific form; lastly, we discover that only a minimal number of spheres exist in this solar system, compared to the more general case of Coxeter groups known as Riesz groups, for which no theoretical upper limit exists when considering all possible combinations of parameters. Moreover, we prove that among all possible star products of Coxeter groups, only a small subset comprises those with a finite number of spheres, which we further subcategorize into three distinct types based on the values of specific roots and the structure of their generating sets. Finally, we establish a notable connection between these star products and the fundamental groups of certain geometrically interesting spaces, specifically the shell-shaped spaces known as Coxeter shells, for which we discover distinct classifications based on the underlying Coxeter system. These classifications, in turn, are closely related to the fundamental groups of corresponding torus knots and links. Our comprehensive investigation into these star products also involves an in-depth examination of their resultant fundamental groups, as well as the fundamental groups of the associated shell-shaped spaces, which are akin to variations of braid groups, specifically the group known as the Whitehead braid group. Our research further reveals that these fundamental groups can be viewed as certain modifications of both the braid groups and the Artin groups, which in turn are closely related to both the Coxeter groups and the associated solar systems of spheres within a wedge. Our study of these solar systems also involves an exploration of their resultant presentation formats, from the initial Coxeter presentation to both simplified variant presentations and finally to the more intricate presentations associated with the associated spaces, which in turn are a combination of both the solenoid groups and the associated Coxeter groups. We investigate the spread of rumors within a population by applying compartment model principles to network theory. This approach enables us to analyze the dynamics of rumors by applying the power law distribution, which has been observed in various societal contexts. We develop a mathematical model that incorporates multiple stages of information dissemination, taking into account both public communication networks and geographical proximity. By applying this model to a circular population with uniform information distribution, we derive fundamental coefficients that characterize the speed and decline of rumors through their initial propagation phase. Furthermore, we establish relationships between these coefficients and variables such as the population size, communication range, and movement rates between locations. These findings are demonstrated numerically through simulations of a stochastic model of rumor spread. Our analysis highlights the significance of both precursor information and geographical location in influencing the intensity and gradual fading of rumors. Our research contributes to a broader understanding of how information spreads through networks of individuals in physical spaces. Our model and associated results have implications for the management of misinformation and the effective dissemination of trustworthy information within communities. Our numerical simulations are capable of predicting various coefficients that govern the dynamics of rumors through network interactions and geographic mobility, offering valuable insights for policymakers and researchers seeking to prevent the spread of false information and promote trustworthy information within networks of individuals in spatial communities. We have determined the distance to the Fornax cluster by using the planetary nebulae luminosity function (PNLFF). This analysis is based on a comprehensive catalogue of 8,517 faint point sources within the cluster's central region, compiled from deep images taken with the VLT's VIMOS and the Hubble Space Telescope's WFC3. The resulting PNLFF indicates a central velocity dispersion of 102 km/s and a distance of 4.88+0.13-0.12 megaparsecs to the cluster, confirming our previous estimation of the distance based on the luminosity function of globular clusters. Additionally, we have examined the PNLFF for possible deviations from the expected form, finding that the mass of the most massive stellar progenitors has increased with time, consistent with theoretical predictions, and the cluster's central density is found to be characterized by a density jump of 3.5+0.5-0.4 megaparsecs-2. We have also calculated the megabasic density unit (MBDU) for the first time, which is equivalent to 2.5x10^3 solar masses/ megaparsec^2, and has used the PNLFF to constrain the mass of the most massive stellar progenitors as 7+2-1 solar masses, consistent with current understanding. Furthermore, we have used the PNLFF to model the mass function of single and binary stellar mergers, and have predicted the expected number of ultracompact X-ray binaries in the cluster, which could be investigated with future high-energy observations. Finally, we have used the PNLFF to investigate the mass function of white dwarfs, finding that it agrees with the mass function inferred from wide binary observations, and has a minimum mass of 0.45+0.05-0.05 solar masses, and a maximum mass of 1.15+0.15-0.15 solar masses. The detailed analysis of the PNLFF has also enabled the creation of a reliable metallicity estimate for the cluster, which is 1.5+0.5-0.5 times the solar metallicity, and has confirmed the presence of metallicity dispersion among the planetary nebulae, with a range of -1.5<[Fe/H]<0.5 dex. The study has also used stellar isochrone fitting to determine the age of the oldest stars in the cluster as 10.7+1.7-1.

Our proposed generative stream framework, called LifeStream, is a metadata-free method that generates high-quality numerical streams for classification tasks, using only input data and a performance metric such as accuracy. LifeStream creates compact streams with approximately 100x fewer numerical values than the original dataset, while demonstrating equivalent or superior performance in comparison to hand-optimized numerical libraries on various real-world datasets following standard classification protocols. These results are coupled with empirical findings that highlight the benefits of dimensionality reduction in numerical stream generation, as well as analytical insights into the theoretical advantages of using streams as opposed to traditional numerical representations. Furthermore, LifeStream is showcased in two significant applications: one utilizing sentiment analysis and the other focusing on embedded systems. Our findings demonstrate that streams generated by LifeStream maintain the integrity of original numerical data, resulting in improved predictive models when utilizing metadata-free approaches, and significantly reducing the memory requirements of models in embedded system scenarios. Our framework and research data are available at https://github.com/StreamMining/LifeStream. Our experiments comply with applicable ethical regulations, and the relevant information is detailed in the supplemental materials available at https://stream-mining.org/LifeStream-supplemental.html. LifeStream's performance has been compared to leading hand-optimized numerical libraries, including TensorFlow's Tensorflow, SciPy's scipy, NumPy's numpy, Matplotlib's matplotlib, pandas', pandas, and MKL's mkl, and the evaluation metrics and results are presented at https://stream-mining.org/LifeStream-baselines.html. Our proposed method demonstrates a strong foundation for metadata-free numerical stream generation and related applications, and areas for future improvement are discussed. Our approach and findings contribute significantly to the study of numerical stream generation and related topics, and the associated code and research data are available for public use. Our research showcases the advantages of using streams in classification tasks and provides a framework for overcoming the limitations of traditional numerical representations, and our results can be built upon in the study of embedded systems and sentiment analysis. Our approach enables the development of metadata-free approaches that preserve the integrity of original numerical data, and our findings demonstrate the benefits of dimensionality reduction in numerical stream generation. Our method facilitates the creation of compact streams with significant memory savings, and our experiments are fair and comply with ethical regulations. We investigate how loss function diversity impacts neural network performance.
Previous research implies that rare loss functions like KL Divergence could yield
better results than standard cross-entropy, despite being less common.
To explore this further, a simple multi-task architecture was developed to
simultaneously learn two tasks with contrasting loss functions, which exhibited
superior performance on both tasks when the loss functions were mismatched.
Notably, using KL Divergence as one of the loss functions enabled the network
to generalize better from large dataset, as it was less prone to overfitting
compared to using the network's own output as the target distribution.
Surprisingly, using rare loss functions like KL Divergence or the network's own
output as the target distribution enabled the network to successfully classify
both a difficult set of handwritten numbers and a simple numerical system, despite
never having seen these tasks during training.
In contrast, standard loss functions failed to achieve this level of generalization. 
The techniques developed in this research, such as using contrasting loss functions
to prevent overfitting and enabling network capacity for generalization, are simple
and easily applicable to a wide range of tasks involving neural networks. 
The associated code can be found at https://github.com/MaynardF/ContrastingLoss.

This study develops a computational approach to simulate the thermomechanical properties of polymers as they undergo crystallization resulting from stretching. By combining thermodynamic principles with material modeling techniques, a three-part framework is established to represent the interaction between polymer chains, crystals, and interfaces. Specifically, the material model incorporates the formation and breakdown of polymer-crystal bonds, as well as the evolution of polymer chain entanglements. By utilizing a computational method called the finite element method, the proposed model can be applied to solve problems involving large deformations and temperature changes. The validity of this model is demonstrated through simulations of experiments, such as stress relaxation and crystallization-induced hardening, with results shown in the accompanying figures. The proposed model also demonstrates the occurrence of crystallization at temperatures below the melting point in tension, but above the point in compression. Furthermore, the model successfully replicates the phenomenon of bond breakdown during stretching, as observed in experiments involving draw ratio curves. The impact of material parameters on the model's results is subsequently investigated through sensitivity analysis. The developed model exhibits promising performance and has inherent capabilities to represent additional physical phenomena, such as chain slippage and latent heat release during crystallization, by incorporating the energy balance equation into its structure. The approach presented in this study provides a foundation for future extensions aimed at incorporating additional material properties and experimental data. The resulting model demonstrates a high degree of realism when simulating microstructural changes within polymers and has significant potential for application in areas like material design and manufacturing processes. A video's novel view prediction can be challenging due to the infinite possible viewpoints, although some are plausible and relevant to others. Our proposed framework, titled 'Dual Video Understanding Network' (DVUN), tackles this challenge by dividing viewpoints into two categories: familiar and novel, and represents the understanding of a video through two distinct dual networks. These dual networks operate on novel and familiar viewsets, and map the underlying factors and content of a video to its inherent structure, respectively. By generating a video from the learned representation using a common decoder, DVUN enhances novel view prediction by exploring the relationship between various viewpoints of the same content. Experiments on the MVSOA and Charades datasets demonstrate DVUN's capability to predict novel views of a video with unobstructed line-of-sight, and show that it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in view change scenarios. Additionally, DVUN's ability to generate videos from partially observed scenes and build understanding of a video's underlying structure are also highlighted. The code for DVUN is available at https://github.com/zhengxiaoyi/DVUN.

However, in reality, Bismuth layers may scatter electrons and affect the Hall effect. A more realistic model is then proposed for the multilayer, focusing on the Bismuth layers' impact. It suggests that the Hall voltage is influenced by the Cobalt layers at the interface and an accumulation of electrons on the Bismuth side. This leads to an additional scattering mechanism, with the Hall voltage displaying a nonlinear relationship with the number of Bismuth layers. Experimental verification of this prediction is also proposed. Moreover, this model can be applied to other transition metal/Bismuth multilayers. It indicates that to minimize electron scattering, it's essential to consider the interface compatibility of materials rather than limiting the number of layer pairs during the fabrication process. This is especially true for X-ray amplifiers relying on these multilayers, as reducing scattering also increases the Hall voltage, thus improving the sensitivity of these devices. It is also possible to analyze the electron accumulation on interface Bismuth layers by varying the thickness of the Cobalt layers. Vector leptoquark searches at the LHC primarily focus on the dominant production pathways, which involve quarks and their corresponding lepton partners. To enhance the accuracy of these searches, we developed a method called NLO+PS, which incorporates a next-to-leading order (NLO) signal calculation to model dispersive effects, in addition to using the leading order (LO) signal for collective processes. Through theoretical studies and pseudo-experiment analyses, we found that NLO+PS can significantly improve the agreement between predicted and observed cone reconstruction efficiencies by up to a factor of 5, especially in vector leptoquark searches for masses above the top quark threshold. We also investigated additional sources of uncertainty in our results and found that they can be minimized by employing an optimal leptoquark field identification method. To facilitate widespread adoption, we have made our NLO+PS efficiency simulations publicly available for various cone reconstruction algorithms used in leptoquark searches. These simulations can be utilized for various leptoquark scenarios and other similar new physics searches at the LHC. To facilitate the dissemination of this efficiency information among different research groups, we propose a possible framework for sharing such data across institutions via collaborative platforms used by LHC researchers. Ultimately, we believe that the adoption of NLO+PS signals in leptoquark searches will provide a more precise understanding of the underlying physics and likely lead to the discovery of vector leptoquarks at the high-luminosity LHC. To that end, we have made the code and documentation for our NLO+PS simulations openly available on public repositories on GitHub. To facilitate further development and maintenance of this effort, we propose the creation of a leptoquark research working group at CERN that would serve as a platform for collaboration, data sharing, and future expansion of this initiative. Such a venture would not only enhance the vector leptoquark search program but also serve as a model for other LHC new physics searches in the future. To make this working group a reality, we suggest establishing a lightweight operating structure with the following key components: a contact person, a code repository, a documentation platform, a collaboration channel, and a set of operating principles that ensure openness, transparency, and fairness among participating research groups. By sharing our NLO+PS simulations and advocating for a broader leptoquark research working group, we hope to enhance the vector leptoquark search program at the LHC and explore possibilities for similar initiatives in the future. Our research fills this gap by applying contextualized BERT embeddings to various coreference resolution models and evaluates their performance against centering theory predictions. Re-estimating the accurate distance between WiFi signal fingerprints and their corresponding geographical locations is a problem that has impedments on various machine learning tasks, including classification, regression, and optimization. A common approach tries to predict the distance between neighboring fingerprints, yet this method has its limitations when dealing with significant geographical distances. Another strategy utilizes a nonlinear optimization method to determine the minimum cost associated with assigning each location to a specific fingerprint, but this process is computationally intensive and not distance estimations per se. Instead, a linear programming algorithm can be used to estimate a higher approximation of the minimum cost, which in turn can be used to calculate an approximate distance between fingerprints. Another approach uses a linear regression model to predict distance based on the similarity between fingerprints, but this method fails to account for any missing data effectively. In contrast, our proposed method suggests utilizing a multi-layer neural network to predict distance between neighboring fingerprints, but only considers an limited set of nearby data as input, thus reducing any computational costs and allowing it to handle missing data with ease. We put our algorithm to the test on a large real-world dataset consisting of 50,000 WiFi signal fingerprints gathered across three university campuses in Australia, and the results show our machine learning based approach outperforms the traditional method of estimating distance as being equal to the fixed interval between neighboring fingerprints. Furthermore, our algorithm's performance was found to be robust and scalable, given the minimal computational requirements needed to run the model. Ultimately, our method provides a convenient and accurate solution for assigning a precise distance between geospatial locations based on WiFi signal fingerprints, and has the added benefit of being easily implementable in real-time applications. In addition, our algorithm's performance was found to be directly proportional to the quality of the training data used, with the current dataset showing some limitations, namely the minimal consideration given to time-based information, which could, in theory, impact the effectiveness of the model in certain scenarios, given the static nature of WiFi signal fingerprints in between readings, and the absence of any temporal information being viewed as a missing value, thus requiring the algorithm to infer this information on its own. This aspect is further explored in the discussion section, along with potential applications and limitations of the proposed method. Our research develops several techniques for examining the PSF, including conventional methods such as data preprocessing and difference mapping, as well as more innovative approaches like analyzing the standard deviation of the PSF and detecting asymmetric patterns, which can indicate binary asteroids with highly eccentric orbits. We present an original approach to assess network effects resulting from interactions within a system of connections, taking into account both direct and indirect relationships. This methodology enables the estimation of influential factors, including those stemming from connections, by utilizing a randomization inference framework and a structural model of network formation. We apply our methodology to an analysis of military alliances formed during the Cold War period, incorporating geographical proximity and ideological differences as factors influencing these alliances. Our results show that the positive impact of forming an alliance is largely confined to the alliance's immediate members, while there is also a positive effect on groups that are not directly allied but have strong connections to those that are allied. We demonstrate that the effect of being connected to a group of allies is significant, especially for groups that are structurally likely to form connections with others. Our findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between direct and indirect connections when studying network effects. We also find that the influence of being connected to a group of allies doubles for groups that are structurally likely to form connections with others, indicating a non-negligible impact of network peer effects that persists even after factoring in geographical proximity and ideological differences. We validate our approach by conducting a robustness check using alternative specifications of the model, and show that our methodology can be applied to other datasets representing complex networks of connections. We conclude by highlighting the policy implications of our research, suggesting that targeted interventions aimed at strengthening key connections in a network could yield substantial benefits, while also highlighting the risk of disrupting existing connections that support network stability. Our approach to estimating network effects also offers a framework for assessing the impact of external interventions on complex networks of connections, providing a valuable tool for informing policy decisions in this domain. Our results are published in the academic paper "The Geography of Influence: Estimating Network Effects in Complex Systems of Connections" published in the Journal of Political Science. We further explore the methodology's applications to other networks of connections and present additional findings from our analysis of military alliances during the Cold War period. We also examine the methodology's performance using simulated datasets representing different types of network effects. We demonstrate that our approach accurately captures the influence of network peer effects, even in scenarios featuring non-linear relationships and varying levels of complexity, while also demonstrating the limitations of alternative approaches to estimating network effects resulting from connections. We conclude by highlighting the methodology's potential to contribute to the understanding of network effects in various real-world applications and in controlled laboratory settings. We also outline potential areas for future research, including the development of more efficient estimation procedures and the application of the methodology

A significant challenge in developing effective natural language processing models lies in acquiring large-scale data sets labeled at the individual word level. Single-to-multi-label (S2M) sampling offers a potential solution by producing annotated text with multiple labels for a given sentence, using existing single-labeled data, without increasing labor costs. Our research presents a complementary approach to S2M sampling: multi-to-single-label (M2S) sampling. Beginning with a set of multi-labeled data, M2S sampling generates separate labels for each word in a sentence by utilizing word-specific priority scores and uniform sampling. Our results show that both S2M and M2S sampling techniques can produce high-quality multi-label data without additional expenses and achieve comparable performance to models trained on individually labeled data. Interestingly, M2S sampling is found to be a more effective technique than S2S sampling in specific settings, demonstrating the versatility of sampling methods for annotating data at the word level. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zuoyu2016/single-to-multi.

The challenge of detecting cardiovascular abnormalities from noisy physiological data is a significant problem that affects machine learning models.  This paper introduces a new method, balanced cross-entropy loss, which is designed to enhance the robustness of these models.  Balanced cross-entropy loss tackles classification imbalances that occur when predicting conditions from multi-class patient data, such as echocardiogram images.  It achieves this by splitting the class probabilities and predicted classes into two separate components, which are then differentiated using two different networks.  This approach allows the model to focus on distinguishing between different conditions and make predictions based on features that characterize each condition, despite the presence of noisy data.  The results of experiments conducted on two publicly available datasets show that balanced cross-entropy loss leads to a significant improvement in the detection of cardiovascular abnormalities, such as mitral regurgitation and left ventricular ejection fraction, as identified by an expert clinician, when compared to the standard cross-entropy loss and other popular loss functions.  The code of the proposed method has been made available on a public repository.  The research presented in this paper has implications for the development of machine learning models that detect other cardiovascular abnormalities from noisy data.  The challenge of detecting these conditions is a critical problem that affects many patients worldwide, particularly in low-income countries with limited access to advanced medical technology, such as cardiac ultrasound machines.  As a result, developing more accurate and robust models that can detect these conditions from lower-quality data, such as echocardiogram images, is essential.  The proposed method demonstrates the challenges faced in detecting these conditions from such data and provides a solution that addresses these challenges by modifying the loss function used to train the model.  The result is a model that can detect these conditions more accurately, even when the data is of poor quality, such as in a low-income setting.  The code of the proposed method has been made available on a public repository at https://github.com/omaragrawes/balanced-cross-entropy-loss. Initially, we train universal models on raw data, which are then fine-tuned for specific activity recognition tasks on a mini-batch level. This improves performance by eliminating biases present in individual data sets and enables the discovery of universal patterns essential for accurate recognition. Furthermore, we enhance performance by employing an adaptive learning rate for gradient updates during transference to mini-batches. Our approach surpasses the original FedHealth framework and traditional methods in activity recognition accuracy. We provide comprehensive experimentation on public datasets, alongside empirical analysis of our approach's efficacy. We conclude that our approach, with adaptive learning, yields the highest accuracy achieved to date for activity recognition, demonstrating the versatility of this approach for other healthcare applications involving wearable technology. Portfolio management strategies for cloud computing resources are influenced by various optimizations, including utility and multi-objective optimizations. This study divides portfolio management strategies into four categories based on optimization type and resource pricing model. We examine the critical factors impacting portfolio effectiveness, specifically acquisition and sale efficiency, through mathematical modeling and simulation. Further, we propose two optimization methods, utility and multi-objective optimization, and demonstrate the seamless integration of these approaches with cloud computing resource pricing models. The results show that considering future resource demands when selecting a portfolio increases acquisition efficiency, while ensuring there are suitable portfolios available for sale in the future market enhances sale efficiency. The proposed utility and multi-objective optimizations are shown to be more effective in achieving balanced portfolios than traditional optimizations. Finally, we outline potential research directions for this domain. This study is an initial step towards addressing important issues affecting cloud portfolio efficiency with a view towards facilitating better optimization solutions. The methodologies and results provided offer actionable insights for cloud portfolio management in a variable market environment. The approach can be further developed to tackle more intricate problems and real-world applications, as evidenced by ongoing and potential future work highlighted in the study. The efficiency of an interview panel can be significantly enhanced by employing algorithms for task scheduling and combination, which enables the optimal creation of panels from a pool of applicants through interviews. To tackle the problem of an uneven number of N applicants being interviewed by a panel of M members, we develop two complementary solutions. Firstly, we introduce a computational approach, accompanied by a user-friendly application, that enables the automatic generation of panel schedules for up to 100 interviewees, ensuring the minimum number of required interviews is met while adhering to a first-in-first-out order. Secondly, we outline a more advanced algorithm suitable for processing larger sets of data. By leveraging these algorithms, recruiters can streamline the interview process, reducing the number of interviews needed by approximately 20-30%. Furthermore, these solutions yield consistent outcomes, thus making them reliable tools for professional recruitment settings. The code and application associated with this research are now openly accessible online. The study and its supplementary materials were recently successfully used in a real-world recruitment context involving 250 applicants. The underlying idea of panel scheduling can be applied to other similar problems involving hierarchical evaluation processes. The work presented has been tested on real-world data and compares favourably with existing optimal solutions obtained via conventional methods used as a baseline. This research focuses on solving a backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE) with two unknowns, subject to a diffusion-based underlying system that can be observed directly and an underlying drift component whose information is fragmented and must be reconstructed from historical data. To tackle this problem, we first establish the existence and uniqueness of a solution for this BSDE, then derive an optimal payoff that maximizes the expected utility of its future variations. Our proof involves utilizing the optimal payoff as a final value problem for a forward stochastic differential equation (FSE), which we then solve by first reversing the underlying diffusion system and then solving another FSE with a different drift component. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the optimal payoff can be achieved through a portfolio that consists of a risk-free asset, a credible defaultable bond, and a credible credit default swap, and that this portfolio minimizes the expected cost of its implementation. Ultimately, this research provides a theoretical foundation for understanding how the presence of an underlying diffusion affects the optimal payoff in the context of BSDEs, as well as empirical strategies for implementing this optimal portfolio in practice. This work is an extension of the results found in the PhD research presented in the thesis of the last author. We also provide an extended version of this research in the form of a thesis. We have tested the validity of the solutions obtained in this research by applying it to fragmentary information about the default times of two different companies. This testing has been conducted using two different methods: one based on simulated default times and another based on historical default times. Both of these methods have proven to be effective in validating the solutions obtained in this research. We have also tested the robustness of the solutions obtained in this research by conducting the same tests and validations using only a limited amount of fragmented information about the default times of these companies. The significant rise of lepton flavors at colliders can be attributed to new physics, specifically the production of leptoquarks. In an attempt to enhance sensitivity to rare processes, an asymmetric leptoquark pair production approach is proposed, where leptoquarks are produced in pairs and one leptoquark interacts with a specific lepton flavor, while the other interacts with a different lepton flavor, possibly more frequently. This process is most effective for certain lepton flavors that are produced in large numbers, such as electrons and muons. Furthermore, an analysis of the proposed method's effectiveness in various leptoquark models reveals that it excels in scenarios involving rare lepton flavors. In the context of the Standard Model, this approach can lead to the detection of leptoquarks with significant mass, specifically up to 600 GeV, using the 13 TeV LHC. Additionally, this method demonstrates its versatility in accommodating future colliders and leptoquark theories. In the realm of Beyond the Standard Model, this approach can also lead to the discovery of leptoquarks with unique properties, such as charge ${-2}$ leptoquarks, which are otherwise difficult to find. In summary, an asymmetric leptoquark pair production approach can significantly expand the capabilities of colliders to detect new physics involving rare lepton flavors. Our analysis focuses on approximate analytic expressions for signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) in PTA experiments involving the combination of individual data sets. We evaluated various approaches, including an often-quoted expression, and found them to be inferior to others, leading to inaccurate conclusions about the optimal data combination method. Furthermore, we observed that the most precise results match those obtained via optimal weighted combination, thus offering a suitable alternative in scenarios where the underlying distributions are unclear. Our study utilizes a straightforward template, but its implications are more broad, given the many analogous problems involving the combination of distinct signals in data. Our results are specifically relevant to PTA experiments featuring the same astrophysical source, but the methods we investigated are generally more versatile, having been tested with scenarios featuring different sources and signal periods. Our findings are valuable for future PTA experiments that likely will incorporate new sensitive detectors, such as NANOGrail, that combine different sensitive frequency bands, and may also be relevant for other low-frequency sensitive PTA experiments that combine different sensitive frequency bands, such as the one envisioned by the AstroSat gravitationally sensitive interferometer. Our research demonstrates the importance of carefully validating the performance of sensitive detectors before combining individual data sets, and we strongly advise against relying on commonly quoted approximate SNR expressions, given their inaccuracies, but rather to use more precise alternatives, if available, or to consider more general methods that automatically account for the optimal weighted combination of signals in the data. Our evaluation code is available upon request, and we encourage other research groups to test the performance of their own code with our benchmark tests. This project focuses on developing a method for fitting differential equations to complex datasets, specifically those from epidemiological studies, using a robust algorithm called the Strong Stability Exponential Solver (SSES). The main consideration in fitting differential models to data is biological feasibility, meaning the parameters of the model must make sense in the context of the underlying system. The existing approach to achieve this, based on the theory of robust stability, comes with significant computational costs that limit its use for large-scale and real-world data applications. In contrast, the SSES algorithm offers a faster and more practical solution, thereby enabling the fitting of differential models to complex epidemiological data with large numbers of parameters and samples. The performance of the SSES algorithm is demonstrated through experiments on real-world datasets from the COVID-19 pandemic study, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods, including both traditional optimization algorithms and machine learning models, in terms of both computational cost and biological feasibility. Our research involves studying open $n$-fold pendulums to represent an atomic condensate subjected to a blue-detuned laser, specifically around the point where an atomic mode loses stability and an atomic molecular mode gains stability. This paper introduces a novel application of a centuries-old problem - the knights and horses problem - to efficiently organize data storage. By reframing the challenge as a binary tree construction problem, we develop an optimized solution using trait-based coding. This approach leads to a significant reduction in required DNA storage space. Furthermore, it offers a flexible framework for managing storage partitions that can be adapted to various applications, including those that require multiple, diverse information types. A notable feature of this design is the use of non-overlapping binary codes to prevent data confusion during decoding. To illustrate the practical utility of this approach, we demonstrate how it can be modified to efficiently retrieve specific types of data from stored genetic information. This is achieved by maintaining distinct primer pairs that can be used to locate desired stored data. A major benefit of this approach is the minimal additional storage required to support data retrieval operations. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, we provide experimental results showing the outcomes of applying it to various primer pair designs and storage schemes with different levels of fragmentation. These experiments demonstrate a significant reduction in required storage space and the presence of an optimal zone for applying this approach to existing DNA data storage systems. A notable finding from these experiments is the presence of an optimal interval for applying this approach, below which larger primer pair sizes lead to increased storage needs. This phenomenon is attributed to the conflicting demands of keeping primer pair sizes small enough to prevent storage fragmentation while ensuring they are large enough to encode meaningful information. To facilitate widespread adoption of DNA data storage, we emphasize the importance of developing efficient coding solutions that effectively balance these competing requirements. A coding scheme that efficiently balances these demands is anticipated to play a crucial role in the successful deployment of DNA data storage technology. We also propose a possible extension to this approach that could support more complex encoding challenges, such as those requiring multiple, distinct codes, by utilizing a novel application of a centuries-old problem - the knights and horses problem. This extension could provide a coding solution that meets the needs of future DNA data storage systems, which are expected to become increasingly complex in the future. We anticipate that the development of efficient coding schemes will be crucial for the widespread adoption of DNA data storage technology. Accurate riverbed bathymetry estimation is crucial for understanding and managing rivers, particularly in turbulent flows. Although geostatistical methods are highly effective for interpolating flow velocities in smooth flows, they face significant challenges when applied to turbulent flows with complex geometries. A novel approach called Principal Component Geostatistical Analysis (PCGA) has been developed to address these challenges by utilizing flow velocity data and bathymetry information. PCGA introduces a new matrix decomposition approach, incorporating spatial correlations and varying point process intensities to account for riverbed features, such as scour pools. By incorporating a non-parametric approach to model these intensities, PCGA enhances previous research by facilitating the estimation of bathymetry without pre-existing knowledge of point process parameters. The PCGA method demonstrates significant improvements in estimating flow velocities and bathymetry compared to existing techniques, with the advantage of being a single, integrated model that estimates multiple variables simultaneously. Furthermore, PCGA offers substantial computational efficiency gains, achieving a 30 times speedup on high-performance computing systems. The effectiveness and efficiency of PCGA make it a valuable tool for modeling unguarded river flows with complex geometries, and the method has the potential to be applied to other unguarded flow scenarios with limited measurements. The PCGA algorithm is publicly available as part of the R riverPCGA package on GitHub, alongside the associated data and documentation. Future developments aim to enhance the method by incorporating additional geophysical information, such as water levels and temperature data. The current implementation of PCGA can be utilized for modeling flow velocities and bathymetry in rivers with the following characteristics: average flow depths ranging from 0.5 to 2.5 meters, and river lengths of up to 100 meters, with the capability to handle scour pools with depths up to 1 meter and widths up to 2 meters. The PCGA algorithm has been evaluated using data from realistic laboratory experiments and real-world river applications, prior to its use in modeling real-world rivers with the assistance of researchers from the U.S. Geological Survey. The code and data associated with this research are available at the following URL: https://github.com/jhurn/riverPCGA. The Madsen-Weiss theorem, a significant result in topology, was originally proven by the duo Andrew Madsen and Shmuel Weiss. This theorem found a fascinating connection between moduli spaces of surfaces and topological constructs known as Bauldfl fibres. Firstly proven in 2007, the Madsen-Weiss theorem embodying this connection raised intriguing questions about its inherent properties. Notably, whether the theorem holds true at the level of homotopy types, without considering the topological structure, has been a subject of debate. The theoretical framework known as the Madsen-Weiss theorem, serves as an integrating force for multiple independent results, which individually showed that the components of the moduli spaces of surfaces can be broken down into more manageable parts, with each part maintaining a certain level of stability, a property topologists refer to as the b-principle. The desire to understand the original Madsen-Weiss theorem within the context of the b-principle led researchers to reexamine the underlying mathematical theories and prove several key results that make up the core of the Madsen-Weiss theorem, before finally connecting these components to the moduli spaces of surfaces. The end result is a more unified and comprehensive explanation of the original Madsen-Weiss theorem, the moduli spaces of surfaces being just one instance of this broader theoretical framework known as the Madsen-Weiss theorem. The scientific discoveries made during this research endeavor have the potential to give back to the wider mathematical community by providing a more streamlined and generalized version of the Madsen-Weiss theorem that can be used to educate future generations of topologists. The research discussed in this article also relies on the collective efforts of various other scientists, including the influential mathematician Tim Perutz, who made a critical contribution to the field. Key findings show that when using equal weight coefficients and a coarse space associated with a specific norm, the condition number of the preconditioned operator is closely related to the subdomain-level algebraic norm and a term representing the Asymptotic Convergence Rate (ACR). However, this assumption may not always hold, especially when analyzing complex systems with multiple interacting components, such as cultural evolution and neural networks. Furthermore, we apply our model to explain the rapid spread and the slowing down of cultural ideas within a theoretical population, and to describe the distribution of neural connection delays in a simulated model of the brain. Additionally, our approach can be incorporated into existing machine learning algorithms to improve their accuracy. Our study demonstrates that considering correlations and heterogeneity is crucial for accurately predicting the tempo of cultural evolution and neural connectivity, and our results show that our approach enhances the performance of current machine learning models. Our model can be refined to address a wide range of diffusion processes, including those seen in genetic, economic, and environmental systems. We studied the interplay between self-phase and cross-phase modulation in identical counterpropagating light modes within a loop resonator. Our analysis, supported by numerical simulations, reveals that cross-phase modulation exceeds self-phase modulation by a factor of twenty-five, leading to nonlinear effects that are much more pronounced than expected. This distinction makes phase modulation in loop resonators an appropriate model for realizing discrete soliton compression and identity-preserving transformations. Furthermore, we discovered that the interplay between the two phase modulation effects results in the creation of a unidirectional wave that maintains the identity of the original signal, potentially finding applications in identity-preserving signal processing. Moreover, we found that a ring resonator configured to exhibit cross-phase modulation in identical counterpropagating modes offers significant advantages over other implementations, including those utilizing fiber Bragg gratings, than can realize discrete soliton compression and identity-preserving transformations with minimal loss. This advantage holds true when utilizing a single resonator to realize both cross-phase and self-phase modulation, or when utilizing a coupled resonator system to realize cross-phase modulation in identical counterpropagating modes, with a ring resonator offering a twenty-five times stronger nonlinear effect at the same input power than a fiber ring resonator. This advantage can be attributed to the difference in photon distribution across the resonator material, rather than the resonator loss or nonlinear index change. Consequently, we propose utilizing a ring resonator configured to exhibit cross-phase modulation in identical counterpropagating modes for realizing discrete soliton compression and identity-preserving transformations with minimal loss, in addition to supporting the recent experimental demonstration of a ring resonator-based soliton compressor that enables identity-preserving signal transmission over thousands of kilometers. This proposal is relevant to the development of future high-capacity, long-haul optical communication systems. The distinctive feature of this method is that it examines how effectively the reinforcement learning algorithm adapts to successive tasks within the same curriculum, rather than relying on traditional benchmark transfers between distinct tasks. Our research involves testing multiple high-performing reinforcement learning methods across three different curriculum trajectories, and the results reveal interesting patterns that reflect the algorithms' ability to excel in specific scenarios. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that controlled changes in curriculum design can be utilized to develop a concise benchmark that mimics the complexities of real-world environments and tasks, allowing for more precise and efficient evaluations of reinforcement learning algorithms. Our approach and results can be applied to various applications, such as testing artificial agents in simulated environments and evaluating reinforcement learning methods for real-world settings. Process behavior evolves significantly in response to changes in its operational environment, necessitating techniques for detecting these changes using observational data. A key challenge in this field is representing relationships between process events, which have been addressed using Decorrelated Convoy Routes (DCR) graphs. Here we enhance previous work by providing an algorithm to identify the source of changes in process behavior, which can be represented as a difference between two DCR graphs. This difference representation, which we call the Deviation Convoy Route (DCR), enables distinction between transient and persistent changes in process behavior. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, we present experimental results using simulated data models. Additionally, we illustrate the application of this approach to a real-world example involving a manufacturing process. A natural extension to this work involves exploring ways to intervene in the process to reverse undesirable changes in behavior. A possible starting point for this purpose involves identifying the most critical events contributing to the deviation from desired process behavior. We have made the code and data for this research publicly available on GitHub, which can be accessed using the following link: https://github.com/wise-nus/process-learning. We explore the relationship between distinct compactifications of the moduli space $M_g^n$ for smooth complex projective varieties of degree $d$ with a given geometric property, examining how these compactifications relate to each other through natural maps. Our investigation focuses on two main types of compactifications: (1) the compactification proposed by Heiermann, resulting from a process of specialization, and (2) a Hodge-theoretic compactification developed by Funaro and Moretti. By analyzing the inclusions of irreducible components in both compactifications, we establish statistical evidence to indicate that the geometric and Hodge-theoretic compactifications have the same number of irreducible components. Moreover, we establish that the map from the Hodge-theoretic compactification to the geometric compactification is an isomorphism of component inclusions, with the added feature of being an equivariant map under the action of the braid group. Our findings also reveal a notable distinction between these compactifications, as the former contains components that are not part of the latter, specifically those consisting of varieties with certain rational singularities, thereby shedding light on the structure of these missing components. Our research is an expansion upon previous work by myself, focusing on the case where the projective varieties have a fixed dimension $n=4$ and degree $d=1$. In this revised study, we remove this constraint, enabling a broader generalization. Our approach and key results can be applied to a broader context of algebraic varieties defined within projective spaces of any given dimension, with the option to include additional conditions. We observed a significant discrepancy in NUV-r colors for the two most massive elliptical galaxies without any systematic errors. Both galaxies, Vuldus and M84, exhibit unusually dark NUV-r colors, more so than expected based on their stellar masses. When considering the color gap, it's essential to note that NUV-r values become uniformly darker with increasing mass for galaxies weighing up to 1.5 times the most massive group, consisting of elliptical galaxies like Nucleus of NGC 5128 and M87. Although both Vuldus and M84 lie within the typical mass range, their NUV-r values remain 0.29 colors deeper than predicted, suggesting a peculiar characteristic unique to the most massive galaxies that self-consistently explain their blue UV-upturn components and previous color measurements. It's also noteworthy that the UV spectral slope in the far UV band, observed with the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph, is significantly bluer for Vuldus and M84 than for other massive galaxies, further highlighting this distinctive behavior. The unique characteristics of Vuldus and M84, revealed through photometric and spectroscopic analysis, offer valuable insights into the physics governing extremely massive galaxies, revealing a possible direct connection between their unusual NUV-r colors and their exceptionally large cores, likely resulting from massive mergers similar to Vuldus itself. As a result, we propose a new classification for the most massive galaxies, characterized by their darker NUV-r colors, blue UV components, and large cores, and suggest they represent a distinct evolutionary path, formed through major mergers that result in the suppression of star formation and sustained core growth. The observed characteristics in Vuldus and M84 are consistent with this model, presenting a framework for understanding the intricate relationships between binary supermassive black holes, galaxy mergers, core growth, and the unique appearance of the most massive galaxies. The necessary ingredients for this specific evolution, including initial mass function, stellar feedback, and core merger efficiency, are yet to be fully understood and require further research. The distinctive nature of Vuldus and M84, reinforced by their simultaneous hot and cool stellar populations, poses challenges for previous studies and highlights the risk of oversimplification in classifying galaxy populations. As a result of      limited data availability and variation in patient behavior, traditional machine      learning methods have proven ineffective.  We propose an innovative framework      based on a novel feature extraction technique that leverages diffusion maps to      analyze admission data from intensive care units.  This approach enables the      derivation of distinct features related to patient recovery, which can be used      in classification and regression models to facilitate precise predictions and      resource allocation decisions.  Through extensive simulations and real-data      applications, our research demonstrates a significant improvement in prediction      accuracy compared to traditional methods, thereby presenting a promising      solution for addressing the challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic.  We      also provide an open-source code for replication purposes. As the      pandemic continues to evolve, this research paves the way for developing      scalable and dynamic models that account for changing global patterns of      patient behavior.  To ensure transparency and reproducibility, we have      thoroughly documented our code and data procedures in a detailed appendix.  This research has several real-world applications, including but not limited to, optimizing distribution of ventilators, allocating limited beds in ICUs, and predicting mortality rates. To facilitate broad dissemination, we have made all code and data necessary for replication openly available on reputable public platforms. Fake news has been a rising concern on social media platforms, spreading rapidly and causing real-world damage, and thus detecting it is crucial. Despite significant progress in the task with traditional approaches, deep fake detection remains challenging, likely due to the ever-evolving nature of fake content. To effectively address this issue, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework, MetaFEND, which enhances the effectiveness of the current deep fake detection models by accounting for the following key factors: 1) the variability of labeling information, 2) the differences between distribution streams, and 3) the need for robustness transfer across domains. MetaFEND successfully integrates multi-label information learning, adapts to new domains with rapid generalization, and incorporates domain knowledge for improved performance. We conduct extensive experiments using real-world datasets, and the results indicate significant improvements over existing deep fake detection methods and conventional approaches, including accuracy rates of 84.67% for Confound and 83.33% for NewsTrust21 in multi-label settings. Moreover, MetaFEND demonstrates its versatility by achieving top performance in various robustness transfer scenarios and scenarios with intense label noise. We make the proposed framework and experimental datasets available for public use. Moreover, we provide a user-friendly, web-based interface for predicting the authenticity of individual pieces of content at this link: https://metafend.iscas.vip/. We also introduce a method for identifying individual pieces of false information, which is available at this link: https://fakefinder.iscas.vip/. We plan to expand on our work by using these models and methods to enhance the performance of general machine learning models when faced with new domains and complex labeling information. We believe that our research has significant implications for the detection of false information and look forward to collaborating with others in this area. We have made the code and datasets for our experiments available online for the benefit of the research community. We have also developed two web-based applications that can be used to predict the authenticity of individual pieces of content and to help annotate new pieces of false information that can be used to train machine learning models. A region of interest (ROI) in medical imaging can be efficiently broken down into a sub-problem of imaging decomposition, where the goal is to identify and extract specific areas of the original image by using a trained convolutional neural network (CNN). In our investigation, we focused on using a trained MRI acquisition contrast change detector, known as the contrast learner, to accurately locate areas of high signal within T2-weighted images. Through theoretical and practical insights, our research revealed that the contrast learner can effectively pinpoint signal intensities above a certain threshold, thereby simplifying the ROI segmentation task into simply setting this threshold. In addition, we formulated an optimized problem to determine the ideal threshold, which directly reflects the ROIs, and further established that this problem is computationally undecidable and belongs to the NP-Hard category. To overcome these challenges, we developed a gradient-descent based learning algorithm that successfully trains the contrast learner using a simplified cost function, and the resulting framework was successfully applied to actual MRI data with a significant reduction in computational time required for comparison with the existing state-of-the-art methods. In particular, our results showed a 10-fold decrease in computing time necessary for the evaluation of a novel MRI contrast change detection method known as LSTMs4CCD. In another application, we used a multi-CNN framework to efficiently identify and extract specific hip bone features from knee MRI scans, thereby accurately diagnosing certain hip bone abnormalities such as femoral acetabular impingement. Through visual demonstrations and quantitative metrics, our results demonstrated the effectiveness of using a trained CNNs to pre-process high-dimensional imaging data, and we further made the raw MRI code package publicly available for reproducibility purposes. This paper introduces a novel algorithm that refines line joins in vector graphics, specifically line joins along curved paths that have been approximated by large fan-shaped segments. Our approach builds upon Karman's method, which produces high-quality line joins for straight segments, by extending its capabilities to include curved segments. Unlike existing approximation techniques that concentrate solely on creating smooth connections between adjacent line joins, our algorithm considers multiple joins simultaneously, ensuring a consistent, detailed representation, particularly in areas with intricate features. Our algorithm achieves this by employing a specialized technique called point bundling, which ensures that points representing line joins can be accurately represented, even in areas with complex, overlapping features. Our approach modulates the size of line joins based on local density information, thereby maintaining a balanced representation across both densely packed and isolated regions. Furthermore, our algorithm leverages Karman's method by using it to enhance line joins along straight segments that make up the boundary of each fan shape. Our approach has been implemented as part of the Tega vector graphics renderer, and the resulting line joins can be viewed in interactive visualizations available online. Experimental evaluations of our algorithm demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency, showcasing its applicability to a broad spectrum of real-world datasets. Our algorithm's advantages are further highlighted through a comparative analysis of different approximation techniques, along with renderings of sample datasets that demonstrate the varying levels of fan-shaped line joins representation achieved by each method. We investigate the formation of multipartite entanglement among atoms in a cavity field, where one unentangled atom is present. This scenario can arise in a setup with a single cavity where multiple atoms interact one after the other. Using a suitable parameterization, we derive an essential condition for creating tripartite entanglement among the atoms. This condition cannot be met if the cavity field is initially set to a non-zero state that is symmetric under a certain unitary transformation. Consequently, such initial conditions will result in bell-like states among the atoms, potentially enabling testing of quantum non-locality with an increased number of parties. Furthermore, we demonstrate that reducing the number of non-interacting atoms can indeed facilitate the creation of multipartite entanglement among the remaining atoms. Additionally, we analyze the evolution of entanglement generated in a cavity with two non-interacting qubits, uncovering distinct dynamics governed by the characteristics of the initial cavity field state, specifically its entanglement, ergasmerity, and orthogonality. In the general case of multiple non-interacting qubits, we establish that the distribution of entanglement among the qubits depends solely on the number of interacting qubits and the duration of interaction. Ultimately, our study highlights the challenges and potential opportunities associated with generating multipartite entanglement in cavity QED. Additionally, we introduce a novel class of Bell-state makers, utilizing single-photon sources, threshold detectors, and a lossy cavity, and possessing an inherent anti-jitter property that can minimize errors during testing of quantum non-locality in the presence of a gradient time sequence. This class of devices can be an essential component in testing quantum non-locality over extended periods, particularly in space-based environments. The associated research opportunities are vast, ranging from developing more efficient methods for creating Bell states in cavity QED to exploring novel applications for existing infrastructure, and from optimizing detector arrangements to investigating novel cavity designs, all of which are crucial for addressing the fundamental questions being investigated. The potential of cavity QED systems also extends to the generation of metapartite entanglement in solid-state systems, presenting an appealing combination of reliability, flexibility, and scalability, which could be a significant breakthrough given the current challenges associated with practical realization of reliable solid-state systems for universal quantum computation, and the potential of cavity QED to efficiently create entanglement among multiple solid-state devices, potentially enabling the development of large-scale reliable solid-state systems for universal quantum computation. This study introduces a novel method to analyze the evolution of optical tomograms, focusing on the effects of non-classical behavior such as entanglement dynamics and concavity changes in optical Bell and Wigner functions. To demonstrate our approach, we examine both theoretical and experimental scenarios of single-mode optical parametric amplification. The results show that our proposed indicator accurately identifies the onset of non-classical behavior, even when other indicators, such as entanglement entropy and the difference of two concave functions, fail to detect changes in the optical tomograms. Furthermore, our method successfully reveals the structure of entangled states after repeated parametric amplification, offering valuable insights into the dynamics of entanglement generation and loss. Additionally, we demonstrate the practical application of this approach using experimental data from a fiber optical parametric amplifier, and show that entanglement can be revived through phase modulation of one input field while keeping the other input field constant. This research provides a useful framework for studying the evolution of non-classical behavior in continuous-variable entanglement dynamics. The role of renormalization effects, specifically infrared renormalons, is being examined in the context of parton distribution functions. A detailed study of the impact of these effects on the gluon distribution, particularly in the large-x region, has been conducted. The contribution of infrared renormalons to the gluon distribution's uncertainty is significant, with an estimated impact of at least 1% on the gluon density at $x \approx 0.01$ and a mean energy scale of $\Lambda_{\rm QCD} \approx 300$ MeV. Furthermore, the relation between these uncertainties and the development of hadron structure functions in the large-x region is established. The findings also reveal that the effects of infrared renormalons become more pronounced with increasing x and are expected to influence not only gluon distributions but also other quark distributions. The study highlights the importance of considering these renormalization effects in the evolution of parton distributions, particularly in regions dominated by conformal field theories. The scope of the study is broadened to include the uncertainty associated with the development of hadron structure functions in the large-x region, represented by data from deep inelastic scattering experiments featuring light quarks. The relation between these uncertainties and the contributions of higher-twist interactions, power-law corrections to linear confining potentials, and the impact of infrared renormalons on hadron structure functions in the large-x region is explored. The study demonstrates that the effects of infrared renormalons are more pronounced in the coldest hadron states, as identified by the position of the first temperature-like momentum scale, $\hbar k_{\rm B}$, in relation to $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}$. The relation between these uncertainties and the development of power-law corrections to linear confining potentials in the large-x region is examined. The influence of infrared renormalons on hadron structure functions in the large-x region is demonstrated to be directly related to the stability of hadron states against temperature-like fluctuations in confining hadron systems. The study proposes a modified approach to estimating the uncertainty associated with the evolution of parton distributions, incorporating the effects of infrared renormalons and taking into account the limitations of current knowledge regarding hadron structure functions in the large-x region. This approach is applied to the gluon distribution, and the findings are compared with existing estimates obtained using the direct approach. Knowledge distillation is a significant technique for expediting neural network training by substituting a compact model for a complex, pre-trained network. Black-box knowledge distillation allows the compact model to learn from a complex network without accessing its internal information. However, current black-box knowledge distillation methods require decision-making processes for the compact model, necessitating additional computational resources. In response, we introduce decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, which enables a model without decision-making capabilities to efficiently learn from a pre-trained network by simply matching their output distributions. Unlike previous methods, DB3 does not involve deciding between data samples or constructing fake data sets. Instead, it directly compares output distributions between the model and the pre-trained network, representing a more straightforward and efficient approach to black-box knowledge distillation. We put DB3 to use in various scenarios, including retinal image classification and MRI-based disease diagnosis, and find it to be a highly effective method with notable improvements over current knowledge distillation techniques. Additionally, DB3 demonstrates its versatility by being applicable to both compressed and uncompressed models. A compact model trained using DB3 was found to possess performance on par with an uncompressed model, using nearly the same amount of computational resources. In summary, our research on DB3 knowledge distillation yields a notable breakthrough in efficient neural network training, presenting a minimal computational requirement while maintaining exemplary performance. All code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/linghong-wang/DB3_KD. In addition, we have released our DB3-based model retrievals on the following websites: Retinal Ischemic Change Detection Model and White Matter Disease Severity Assessment Model. Both models have been hosted on the Model Ingestion Platform developed by the company First Leaf.
