An analysis of $B$ meson decays into two neutral $K$ mesons is performed using 349 inverse femtobarns of LHCb data. The study evaluates the probabilities of specific decay sequences occurring, such as the conversion of a $K_e$ into two gamma rays that then convert into electron and positron pairs, or the direct decay of a $K_e$ into an electron and a neutral pion. These processes occur with uncertainties ranging from 10 to 20% for the larger branching fractions and exceed 50% for the rarer ones. This study yields updated estimates for several $B$ meson decay probabilities, including those involving neutral kaon conversions or neutral pions that then convert into electron-positron pairs. The findings also lead to a more precise calculation of the CKM matrix element $|V_{ts}|$ with an associated error of ± 0.016. This discrepancy arises from the uncertainties associated with the strong interaction effects that influence the behavior of the $B$ meson system. The study's results will be utilized in future searches for exotic physics interpretations and are already applicable to existing data sets of particle collisions. Given a solvable group G and a multiplicity-free module M, we establish the compatibility of the composition factor lattice of M with the subgroup lattice of G, thereby extending a result by Hsu and Shemueli concerning the reconstruction of the submodule lattice of M. This involves demonstrating that the composition factor lattice of M can be recovered from its associated imprimitive system, which in turn is determined by the original module M. As a key component of this proof, we develop an algorithm that identifies the composition factors of M from its submodule lattice and associated imprimitive system. This computational process is importantly seen to have polynomial complexity with respect to the number of subgroups in G. As additional contributions, we derive both the composition factor lattice and the associated imprimitive system of M from its module over the Cartan system, which provides a more general framework than the algorithm itself. It is also worth noting that in the case of abelian groups, we are able to simplify the requirements for the module M, eliminating the necessity for the absence of multiple submodules, which is a necessary condition arising from the presence of nilpotent composition factors. As an important byproduct of our research, we make notable advancements in the theoretical understanding of the composition factor lattice of a module, which we believe are equally significant to our primary findings. It is also noteworthy that our research results heavily draw from the fundamental work of Bannai and Ito on the composition factor lattices of group representations. It is also equally necessary to acknowledge the significant influence exerted by the paper of Hsu and Shemueli on our research conclusions. It is noteworthy that the term'multiplicity-free module' is used interchangeably with the term 'faithful module' in this context, which refers to a module M where the action of any non-trivial subgroup of G results in a non-trivial transformation of M. We introduce Co-Imitation Learning, a novel framework that enables agents to acquire skilled behavior in Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) by collaborating with less capable partners. Unlike conventional imitation learning methods, Co-Imitation Learning enables agents to effectively learn from others with similar levels of expertise, without requiring access to expert demonstrations. Theoretical convergence proofs demonstrate that Co-Imitation Learning converges globally, provided the action space is discrete, and there are sufficient exploratory opportunities. To facilitate practical application, we develop a sample-efficient algorithm based on policy optimization, paired with a feasible exploration strategy, and validate the effectiveness of our approach through comprehensive experiments across various assessment criteria, including efficient policy discovery, generalization, and robust performance. Existing imitation learning methods are surpassed by Co-Imitation Learning in multiple evaluations, highlighting the significant benefits of imitating comparable agents over conventional methods that rely on expert demonstrations. The code and associated data are available at https://github.com/ChenyuDong/CoImitationLearning. This research investigates how different methods of introducing a biased, polarized decoding scheme affect its error probability. Building on a concept by Kudele and Vardy, we develop a sequential decoder that applies varying thresholds during the process. This approach creates a decoded word that is increasingly difficult to distinguish from the original, as more frozen bits are identified. We establish an upper bound on the error probability of this decoder, taking into account its specific parameters and properties. Additionally, we demonstrate its reduced error probability in comparison to a uniformly polarized decoder. Furthermore, we establish a threshold value below which the decoder's performance consistently improves. This threshold value proves to be a minimum required bias intensity necessary for the decoder to succeed. We also analyze the consequences of using different bias distributions on data sets of varying composition. This leads to a new, more efficient decoder, requiring significantly fewer frozen bits (i.e., more decoded words) than prior alternatives. As a result, this decoder yields a lower error probability than both its uniform polarized and frozen bit count based counterparts. We investigate the potential performance gain of reinforcement learning models by optimizing the set of actions rather than individual data points. Our approach modifies the reinforcement learning objective to prioritize the quality of the generated text, considering both short-term and long-term improvements. We optimize the action space using a policy network and a critic network, and show that this approach outperforms traditional reinforcement learning methods on both WMT2014 English-to-German and WMT2015 English-to-French translation tasks, achieving comparable performance to strong supervised baseline models. We analyze the performance of our model by evaluating the importance of long-term optimization and the trade-off between its components. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of optimizing the action space for machine translation, and we make our code publicly available for future development. We also observe that our model is more resistant to negative rewards, making it a valuable solution for large-scale translation tasks with limited positive reward data. Our model's performance can be further improved by combining it with strong supervised baseline models, and we showcase the feasibility of this approach on WMT2014 English-to-French at an elevated difficulty level. Our model also exhibits a significant gain in robustness when evaluated on the Turking dataset, which simulates real-world translation environments with biased reference texts. Our paper further introduces two novel evaluation metrics that prioritize the importance of retaining the original text's semantic meaning and sentence structure, and we make our evaluation code publicly available for future use. Our approach has the added benefit of allowing seamless integration into existing sequence-to-sequence models, and we provide practical guidelines for optimizing the action space based on different reward schemes and learning rates. Our paper also addresses potential challenges and limitations of optimizing the action space, and we propose potential future development paths, such as incorporating external knowledge and handling extremely long horizon biases. Our model's code and evaluation metrics are available at https://github.com/TextGenerationGroup/ReinforceSequence2Sequence. Quantum information flow between an open system and its surroundings can move in both directions, as demonstrated utilizing a superconducting three-qubit system as a unitary operator. This system exhibits two-way information transfer for a duration of 12 qubit-gate interactions, as inferred from the degradation of quantum correlations within the system over time. The resulting data models bidirectional information dynamics, comprising both the degradation of quantum entanglement and the emergence of classical correlations within the system. These findings showcase the feasibility of dual-direction information flow in an open quantum system and highlight its potential applications in quantum technology. Furthermore, a newly proposed figure of merit, the quantum information cartan approach, is applied to demonstrate the diversity of information dynamics within multiple qubit configurations. This includes variations in entanglement distribution, as well as the interplay between quantum and classical correlations, all for the three-qubit architecture. This research paves the way for utilizing small-scale open quantum systems as models of complex, driven dissipative phenomena. We investigated the dynamic behavior of Ising spins arranged in a specific geometric configuration - each spin is connected to three neighbors - using a random regular graph with three edges per node, a model that exhibits unique thermal properties when subjected to temperature cycles. To better understand these properties, we simulated both quenching and cycling scenarios. During quenching, the hysteresis loop's shape remains consistent across various temperature differences, but cycling revealed more complex results. For low temperatures, the hysteresis loop flattens, while higher temperatures show a sharper loop with shifted onset points, influencing the loop's shape as it rotates with changing temperature. The discrete nature of the loop dissolves as the temperature increases, and we found that the loop's rotation speed accelerates with higher temperature differences. Notably, the loop's shape remains unaltered when the temperature varies in both directions from the same starting point, until it reaches a point where the magnetization suddenly switches more quickly. The spin network's unique properties also show a bias towards positive magnetization. The analysis of the results is straightforward and reveals how the loop changes with temperature. The complex dynamics of the Ising spins in a triangular network result from a balance between the heat released during the quenching process and the energy retained by the spins between cycles. The correlation between the spin interactions and the network's geometry influences the results, making them distinct from those seen in regular lattices. The unusual shape of the hysteresis loop in this specific network has not been observed in other random models, making it a fascinating example of how the interplay of disorder and geometry can drive complex dynamics, especially when subjected to external stress cycles, and may be relevant to other nonlinear systems exhibiting hysteresis. The regular random graph model also offers a simple framework to study the effects of changing temperature on nonlinear systems with discrete solutions and multiple stable states, providing a promising area for future research. The study of these dynamics using the regular random graph model can be extended to other nonlinear systems, such as the three-state Potts model, which shares the same thermal properties, giving insights into the broader class of junction-driven dynamics in complex networks. The study of these dynamics using the regular random graph model can also be used to investigate the energy storage capacity of nonlinear systems with hysteresis, a crucial aspect for practical applications, such as energy harvesting from vibrating structures, where the hysteresis loop's area represents the stored energy. The research demonstrates the importance of considering the non-equilibrium dynamics of spin interactions

Recent studies near the Sun have revealed the energetic requirements for solar particles to reach close to the solar surface, and how these energies compare to those needed at a distance of 1 AU.  Based on data collected by the Solar Wind Charge Energy Spectrometer on board the Solar and Helios Observatory, we found that the distribution of lower-bound energies needed to reach within 0.48 AU of the Sun can be described by a power law with a peak energy around 10-20 times stronger than observed at 1 AU, and varying little with direction.  However, above about 10 times the average energy required to reach that close to the Sun, the distribution becomes Rayleigh-like, with the most probable energy becoming significantly smaller at lower heliocentric distances, and varying more greatly with direction.  One possible explanation for these findings is a significant presence of extremely rapid solar particles that can reach within 0.48 AU of the Sun with relatively low energy, and another possibility is particles originating from the solar wind itself, able to reach the inner solar system without requiring as much energy.  Either way, these findings suggest there may be multiple sources of solar particles active in the inner solar system, and highlight the importance of continued research in this area.  The energy distributions we observed also compare interestingly to model simulations predicting much higher energies required to reach that close to the Sun, and the need for a more sophisticated understanding of solar particle distributions.  The knowledge gained from this study is particularly significant for planning future missions observing the inner solar system, and could greatly impact our ability to protect both people and electronic equipment from harmful solar particles.  The data underlying this research is available upon request, and the code used to analyze it can be found in the relevant GitHub repository.  Future work should also consider how the conditions we found vary over time, and how they relate to solar flares and other events that drive the release of solar particles into space.  Ultimately, a better comprehension of the energetic processes giving rise to solar particles in the inner solar system will be crucial for improving our ability to forecast solar particle storms, and the potential damage they could cause to both people and electronic equipment in space and on Earth.  The knowledge gained from this research will be valuable for planning both current and future space missions, and could also be applied to protecting people working in areas near the Earth's surface, such as construction workers, aircraft passengers, and people living in areas with high altitude. Thanks to extensive research in affective computing, systems can effectively recognize emotions from various sources, including written text, speech, and video. Despite significant progress, many challenges remain, particularly in achieving cross-lingual and domain adaptability. A significant obstacle hindering systems from achieving versatile emotion recognition capabilities is the widespread use of language-specific and domain-specific models. To tackle this limitation, we present a pioneering multilingual and multi-domain sentiment analysis framework called MosaicNet, comprising an adaptive reservoir PC and a layer-based header PC. By integrating an efficient attention mechanism and layer-based header PC design, MosaicNet exhibits enhanced performance and adaptability when operating with new data. Our model demonstrates superior performance in comparison to current state-of-the-art approaches on widely used emotion recognition datasets, including the Multilingual Emotion Corpus, the Emotional Intensity Corpus, and the Standard English Emotion Corpus. Notably, MosaicNet shows significant performance gains in recognizing emotions expressed in Portuguese, particularly when evaluated on data it hasn't been trained on. This achievement indicates a significant advancement towards creating a versatile system capable of accurately identifying emotions expressed in languages that the system hasn't been exposed to during training. Our proposed model also exhibits robust performance in challenging real-world applications, such as recognizing emotions expressed in customer feedback text. This framework's versatility, combined with its efficient memory requirements, make MosaicNet a pioneering solution for a wide range of emotion recognition tasks and scenarios. Our code is available at: https://github.com/sonu-sejel/MosaicNet. Our datasets are available at: https://github.com/RaysonTan/Multilingual-Emotion-Corpora. Our model's limitations and potential areas of improvement are discussed in the conclusion section of this paper. Our proposed model has the potential to create more adaptable systems that can accurately recognize emotions expressed in various languages and across different data sets, without the need for highly specialized models. This development can significantly broaden the range of applications for systems that recognize emotions expressed in text, including feedback from customers, social media posts, and vast amounts of multilingual online content. Our model exhibits superior performance in comparison to current state-of-the-art approaches on widely used emotion recognition datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in recognizing emotions expressed in languages that the system hasn't been exposed to during training. Furthermore, our model shows robust performance in challenging real-world applications, such as recognizing emotions expressed in customer feedback text. Our proposed model's memory efficiency, combined with its versatility, make it a pioneering solution for a wide range of emotion recognition tasks and scenarios

A novel approach is presented to create one-dimensional supersymmetric quantum mechanics potentials with quantum non-singularities. These potentials, which satisfy the conditions of superymmetry, are found to be directly related to the harmonic oscillator when utilizing a specific algebra known as the polynomial Heisenberg algebra. This algebra consists of the usual ladder operators, an extra operator that acts as a scalar operator, as well as a parameter that is found to be linked to the non-singular regime of the potential. As an example, the energy levels of the harmonic oscillator are derived utilizing this algebraic approach. The proposed method can be applied to create potentials with non-singularities for any number of supersymmetry levels. The relationship between these potentials and their corresponding parent potentials is explicitly defined. The proposed algebra also leads to an intuitive explanation for the shift in parameter that occurs in the non-singular regime. The energy levels obtained utilizing this algebraic approach match the results obtained utilizing the method of quantum inverse scattering. A key characteristic of chaotic systems is their exponentially increasing sensitivity to initial conditions, a property that can be quantified through the calculation of their growth rates - specifically, the computation of their Liapounov exponent. A newly developed algorithm simplifies this calculation by eliminating the need to operate directly on the system's equations, instead leveraging a dual form to determine the exponent from a stationary correlation function. This approach is particularly efficient for large numbers of variables and has been successfully applied to demonstrate the chaotic nature of two complex systems: a randomly selected subset of a genetic regulation network and an animal food web. Furthermore, this method's versatility is demonstrated by applying it to an existing mathematical model. The developed algorithm is part of a larger toolbox of dynamical system analysis algorithms, which are versatile, efficient, and easily modifiable, making them ideal for integrating into machine learning models. These algorithms have been specifically designed to operate within a neural network architecture that can be trained on sample data to predict various key properties of different dynamical systems, including their Liapounov exponents, period, correlation dimensions, and the occurrence of oscillations. This architecture and associated algorithms have been tested on multiple models of different complexities and have been found to accurately predict their associated properties. The developed algorithms are available as an open-source package called DynaNet. The relationship between a system's complexity and its number of variables follows a non-linear logarithmic pattern, which can be captured through the application of a specific curve-fitting algorithm. The validity of this model has been validated through the use of various metrics, including the mean squared error, R-squared value, and the standard error, on multiple subsets of data. The impact of adding new variables to a system on its predicted properties is found to exhibit a non-linear pattern, which can be characterized by a degradation phase followed by a stabilization phase, as measured by the standard error, R-squared value, and the mean squared error. The potential benefits of using DynaNet in comparative studies of different models that simulate the same real-world system are demonstrated through an example based on a brain network model. Finally, the limitations of the current approach and potential areas for future improvement are discussed. The implications of using machine learning to predict the properties of complex systems are far-reaching, with potential applications in the simulation, comparison, and understanding of real-world systems that cannot be fully comprehended through traditional analytical methods alone. A generational equity framework is proposed to evaluate the distribution of chances in society, enabling assessment of how societal opportunities affect different age groups, including future generations. Within this framework, a statistical measure is developed to allocate opportunities based on societal indicators, such as education and employment rates. Using this measure, differences in allocated opportunities are then analyzed to determine their impact on the socioeconomic status of current and future populations. A case study examining data from Canada reveals notable disparities in allocated opportunities across different age groups and ethnicities, with negative consequences for these groups' future socioeconomic status. Furthermore, by simulated scenarios, it is demonstrated that addressing opportunity disparities through fair allocation could significantly benefit marginalized populations and, in turn, benefit the entire society in the long run. Moreover, it is shown that fair allocation leads to a more equitable distribution of opportunities that align with the needs of future generations, with the added bonus of benefiting the current population to a certain extent. Ultimately, this research highlights the value of considering the effects of policy decisions on future generations and highlights a potential pathway to achieving intergenerational equity through fair allocation of opportunities. It is also demonstrated that fair allocation is feasible with existing data resources, as illustrated by the analysis of Canadian data, and it is proposed as a valuable tool for informed decision-making that takes into account the long-term consequences of policies and wealth distribution schemes. It is observed that the proposed measure correlates strongly with established social mobility indicators, suggesting it as a practical and effective alternative for assessing social mobility. It is also shown that fair allocation can be applied to assess intergenerational equity within the context of public policy by examining examples of US and Canadian government policies, and it is demonstrated that these policies either widen the gap between current and future populations or help reduce this disparity, depending on the policy in question. It is also noted that fair allocation can be used to evaluate the validity of certain policy assumptions and scenarios can be simulated to determine the potential effects of policies on future generations. It is also proposed that fair allocation be utilized as part of a broader assessment of public policy that considers both its short-term and long-term consequences on different age groups within a society. It is also demonstrated that fair allocation yields comparable results to traditional analytical methods used in economics, and it is also shown to be a valuable tool for informing business decisions and managing corporate social responsibility initiatives, by enabling the evaluation of opportunities for different age groups within an organization and its supply chain, and it is also proposed as a mechanism for assessing the intergenerational equity of financial products and services. Initially considered too small to be significant, recent research reveals that these measurements can reveal phenomena such as matter-wave soliton formation, weak CP violation in heavy neutrinos, and interactions with dark matter, all of which would have distinctive patterns of distribution across different locations in the accelerator. Given the accuracy of modern particle accelerators, which can measure beam orbits to a precision of several nanometers, the potential for discovering new phenomena, particularly those related to low-energy particle physics, is considerable. Although initially aimed primarily at testing fundamental physics theories, the scope of such experiments has expanded to also to provide a sensitive tool for testing the particle accelerator itself, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of the accelerator and its components, particularly the effects of radiofrequency electric fields and magnetic gradients on the beam motion. The various implementations and theoretical formulations of beam-beam interactions offer a comprehensive resource for experimental design, allowing for the prediction of orbit differences across different accelerator configurations, and thereby facilitating the discovery of new phenomena in a way that is accessible to particle accelerators around the world. We develop a distributed optimization algorithm for a cooperative system consisting of multiple agents, some of which may intentionally disrupt communication by sending false information. To compensate for this interference, we introduce a degree measure to assess an agent's communication efficiency and implement a reporting strategy that adapts to efficient agents and restricts exchange of information with less efficient agents. As a result, the efficient agents must now communicate more precise, aggregated data about their optimization parameters. Despite this limitation, we prove that the algorithm converges towards the global minimum. To illustrate the effectiveness of this approach, we apply it to a scenario involving multiple robots optimizing a joint mission plan in a complex environment. Experimentation with a real robot network reveals that the proposed technique can successfully resist disruption caused by delayed data from certain agents. Additionally, simulations demonstrate the algorithm's robustness in various environments and against different types of malicious behavior. We also analyze the trade-off between communication efficiency and convergence speed. Finally, we emphasize the potential wider implications of this research for other distributed learning tasks. The related theory and algorithm are outlined in detail in the supplemental materials. The decentralized learning framework we developed is highly versatile and adaptable, with potential extensions to other topologies, different types of malicious behavior, and various optimization problems. We introduce a new linearization task called word ordering, where the goal is to arrange unmarked words into a specific order based on their grammatical function. Building upon this, we establish a framework for evaluating linearization performance that is free from the limitations of existing approaches that rely on marked dependencies. Within our framework, word ordering is viewed as a sequence of operations that sorts unmarked words according to their semantic relationships. A straightforward model to achieve this is proposed, and our results on three different datasets reveal substantial performance gains achieved by both a baseline generative model like BART and a state-of-the-art T5 model through cross-domain training, despite both models struggling with the fundamental challenge of learning unmarked representations. Ultimately, our assessment shows that learning unmarked representations proves significantly more challenging than their marked counterparts, with both models exhibiting lower performance in word ordering compared to partial tree linearization, despite having easier data availability. Our findings also highlight significant performance improvements achievable through the application of cross-domain training, with the most notable gains observed in the Stanford Word Ordering dataset. Our proposed evaluation framework, model proposals, and resulting values all contribute to the advancement of word ordering as a well-defined linearization task that is both theoretically and practically relevant. Our research, model comparisons, and empirical studies are all part of our overall endeavor to reexplore the fundamentals of word ordering in the context of modern deep learning techniques. Deepfake images are progressively difficult to distinguish from authentic ones, prompting the need for a new approach that considers a broader context, including the underlying production methodology. A significant obstacle in addressing this challenge is the limited availability of high-quality deepfake data, prompting researchers to utilize synthetic datasets for training and testing purposes. In response to these difficulties, we develop a novel deepfake detection network, termed CSDNet, tailored for multi-domain applications. This network integrates cross-stitch connections to facilitate seamless information sharing across different domains, enhancing its performance and serving as a significant contribution in its own right. In order to gather more reliable training and testing data, we generate two synthetic datasets, designated Deepfake-Studio and Deepfake-Mobile, reflecting real-world scenarios. These datasets comprise 10,000 high-quality deepfake images each, surpassing existing benchmarks in terms of image clarity and diversity. Our evaluation utilised these datasets reveals that our CSDNet model achieves superior performance compared to current leaders, including a significant improvement of 13% in the case of the FSDC dataset. Additionally, our research showcases the shortcomings of existing deepfake detection models when processing low-quality, domestically generated images, highlighting the pressing need for more robust training data, along with our proposed solutions. Our research and datasets are available at https://yilab.org/projects/Deepfake-Studio/. Our detection network and associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/chaoslife101/CSDNet. Our best model has been made available on Microsoft Deepfake Detection Challenge Platform under the name CS-DNet_Studio_Mobile. It ranks among the top-performing submissions in the challenge leaderboard. The environmental impact of our research was minimized by conducting experiments on NVIDIA V100 GPU models in a sustainable data centre powered by renewable energy sources. Our analysis reveals that participants in Forsage, a decentralized scheme built into the NFT marketplace, suffer significant financial losses. On average, users end up losing nearly 70% of their initial investments, with 3 out of 5 users incurring losses above 50%. This substantial decline can be attributed to the inbuilt referral structure that favors early adopters, resulting in significant investments being concentrated in the hands of a few key participants. This concentration leads to numerous opportunities for fraud, including scams like "ghost accounts" used to siphon funds from other users. Furthermore, the Forsage network exhibits a small-world pattern, with isolated clusters that rarely interact with each other, presenting a barrier to free flow of NFTs and cash between them, thus limiting potential gains. This has resulted in many users being trapped in Forsage with large debts, further exacerbating the widespread losses observed. This research provides an initial glimpse into the intricate dynamics of Forsage, with potential for future investigation into its implications on a sustainable, decentralized community of users. This discovery was made following a review of 15,000 user transactions involving over 30 million dollars, spanning nearly two years. This finding is expected to spark further analysis of the ethical considerations underlying Forsage's design, as well as its potential classification as a pyramid scheme. This approach to reviewing Forsage transactions may also be applied to evaluation of other decentralized schemes built into marketplaces, with a potential for revealing underlying patterns of fraud among users. This approach can be made available for general use by providing the associated Python code publicly. This research was inspired by a discussion about Forsage governance presented at the 2021 ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems. We have discovered two likely globular cluster candidates in scan data from the VST, which covers areas of the Milky Way not previously explored for such clusters. Located in the third quadrant of the sky, these clusters are designated VSTC00 and VSTC01 and are estimated to be very old, existing for over 13 billion years. With an estimated distance of about 20,000 light-years, these clusters are on the edge of the galaxy and are part of the galactic bulge's outer region. Although they are distant, we were still able to identify their characteristics, such as the small size of their main sequence stars and the presence of blue and red giant stars at their centers. These features will need further verification, but if confirmed, these clusters could help us better understand the formation of the galaxy. Currently, there are about 160 known globular clusters in the Milky Way, but many more are believed to exist on the outskirts of the galaxy. If the newly discovered clusters are confirmed, they will provide us with more information about the galaxy's early life, especially how it formed its central bulge. Additionally, these clusters could give us a clearer picture of the movement of stars in the outer galaxy. To confirm their status as globular clusters, more in-depth observations are needed, but they show great potential and we are planning to observe them further with the VLT and the Hubble Space Telescope. We also found another possible cluster, VSTC02, which is likely a foreground open cluster rather than a globular one, but it does show some interesting characteristics, such as a large group of blue and red giant stars, which we will continue to study in the future. We have made images of these clusters available for download from the VST archive and the European Southern Observatory (ESO). If the newly discovered clusters are confirmed, they will be added to the official list of globular clusters in the Milky Way, which is maintained by the Centre de Données astronomiques de Strasbourg. If not, they will still contribute to our understanding of the galaxy's open clusters and its movement. We are planning to continue searching for more clusters on the edge of the galaxy using future scan data from the VST and the Advanced Wide Field Imager for the VLT. Researchers analyzed three solar flares with prominent hydrogen emissions using spectroscopic observations from the Solar Dynamics Observatory. A detailed examination of these flares revealed significant differences in both optical and far-ultraviolet continuum properties. The corresponding line broadening of the hydrogen emission also varied substantially, with one flare showing particularly wide lines. This exceptional line broadening was observed in a flare with particularly hot and dense plasma in an umbra, which the team found to be uncommon during flares. By comparing this umbra flare to the other two flares, with similar energies but cooler plasma, they found that the line broadening was significantly greater and the continuum spectrum was hotter. This contrast enabled them to test a theoretical prediction made by a recent paper, which suggested that the line broadening should be greater in flares with particularly hot atmospheres, even after accounting for temperature contributions from other processes. The team found this prediction to be true in this specific case, which they believe could be an indicator of a rare type of flare that quickly reaches high temperatures and may influence mass loss from cool stars. The team was also able to estimate the optical depth of the photosphere during this flare, which they found to be much smaller than expected, indicating that flares can produce intense light and may influence the mass loss from cool stars over time. The team found that the line broadening was directly related to the optical depth of the photosphere, which they believe is driven by a balance between expansion and absorption in the atmosphere. This balance can vary between different flares, which the team propose could be an important factor in mass loss from cool stars, particularly those with outer atmospheres like alpha Proxima, where flares can create temporary holes that may allow mass escape through radiation pressure feedback, rather than being trapped in the outer atmosphere. The team propose that these rare flares with particularly hot atmospheres could be essential in regulating mass loss from cool stars, which could be investigated further by analyzing past and future solar flare observations with spectroscopic capabilities. The current understanding of solar flares, particularly the relationship between hydrogen line broadening and continuum properties in different flares, can be applied to other stars with flare activity, such as flare stars in the Milky Way and extragalactic satellites like Kepler-10b's host star, which the team propose could help clarify the processes governing mass loss from these stars. The methods used to analyze the solar flares can also be applied to other solar flares with suitable spectroscopic observations, which the team found are plentiful in past and future solar data sets

Our novel Point Cloud Framework (PCF) addresses accuracy issues against rotations and mirrorings in supervised learning models for 3D point clouds. Our framework enhances data robustness by utilizing low-frequency Fourier coefficients, thus providing a more in-depth representation of point clouds. Utilizing PCF led to PointCloudNet, a convolutional neural network that achieves enhanced performance on various 3D classification and segmentation tasks by employing spatial and directional point-wise convolution layers. Our experiments show significant improvements in metrics for Model Agnostic Robustness (MAR) and certified accuracy under twisting transformations and reflections. PointCloudNet demonstrates superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art point cloud models on various 3D classification and segmentation tasks, showcasing the versatility of PCF. Our code has been openly shared for public use.

The RPA method has been successfully applied to evaluate the poles associated with the electric dipole giant resonance in $^{16}$O. To further develop this approach, a contact interaction was introduced in a 4-fold degenerate harmonic oscillator shell to simulate interactions between two pairs of Nilsson levels, specifically between the 2p and 0p shells. This interaction caused significant effects on the poles, particularly on the lowest energy pole, which is indicative of a direct reaction-like behavior. In contrast, a significant portion of the RPA amplitude remained unaffected by the interaction. To interpret these results, the use of a perturbative approach was considered, along with a comparison to the harmonic oscillator case, which is a direct reaction-like configuration. In the case of the harmonic oscillator, the RPA poles can be accurately determined using a perturbative approach up to the third order. The evaluation of the RPA poles also involved the application of the second order perturbation theory to the 0p shell, as well as the evaluation of the RPA amplitude to the second order with respect to the perturbation. These calculations allowed for an comparison with previous studies on the harmonic oscillator case. Additionally, the use of a perturbative approach was extended to the 2p shell, which involved the evaluation of the RPA amplitude to the first order with respect to the perturbation. The results from these calculations demonstrated the accuracy of the RPA description of the poles associated with the electric dipole giant resonance in $^{16}$O, specifically for the 2p shell. However, the RPA also predicted the existence of additional poles associated with the 0p shell, which could not be accounted for within the harmonic oscillator model. The duration of this research project was approximately one year. The data used for the calculations was obtained from an experimental measurement conducted in the 1970s. The goal of this research project was to thoroughly investigate the RPA poles associated with the electric dipole giant resonance in $^{16}$O, specifically within the harmonic oscillator model, as well as to consider higher order corrections. The outcomes of this project have been published in six research papers. The first paper explored the outcomes of adding a contact interaction to a pair of Nilsson levels, while the second paper investigated the outcomes of introducing an interaction between two pairs of Nilsson levels. The third paper involved the application of a perturbative approach to evaluate the RPA poles up to the third order, as well as to evaluate the RPA amplitude up to the second order

The idea that new stars could be seeded with cometary particles originating from previous generations of stars, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, inspires interest in identifying environments conducive to this phenomenon. Certain circumstances, such as binary or multiple star interactions, giant shock waves from supernovae, and the gravitational influence of passing stars, can disrupt the orbits of long-period comets and eject them from their parental systems. These comet ejections, now interstellar comets, carry a potential for biological diversity and pose a risk to nearby planets. We propose that regions surrounding dead binary and multiple star systems could be ideal places to search for these interstellar comets and considerations for identifying and isolating these regions are presented. These regions, characterized by extensive nebular remnants, offer opportunities for detecting ISCs through high-sensitivity UV and X-ray surveys and could also harbor habitable exoplanets that might be affected by incoming cometary particles. The study's focus is on single and double linear star configurations, but the principles it involves are applicable to more complex configurations. The necessary observations and necessary parameters for searching these regions are also outlined. Accurate population density evaluations are crucial in wildlife research, yet traditional methods often fail to account for animals that have not been detected, leading to biased estimates.  A promising alternative involves spatial capture-recapture (SCR) methods that can handle movement patterns and non-detections, yet these models are often too computationally intensive for large-scale studies with multiple detectors, resulting in density estimates with wide confidence intervals and limited site-specific information. To address this challenge, we developed a novel Bayesian Bayesian multi-resolution Gaussian regression (MRGR) model that provides more precise density predictions by operating on a coarser geographical scale and then switching to a more precise scale near areas with high species activity.  Through simulations and a real-world example featuring black bear movements across a large forest area, our MRGR model was shown to offer more accurate population density estimates with narrower confidence intervals than the standard SCR model, and the performance of both models was found to be sensitive to detector placement layout.  We have made the MRGR model publicly available through an R package called'scregr' for easy application by wildlife researchers.  By leveraging the capacity to incorporate external information and remove the need for a capture history model, the MRGR model can be a valuable tool for a wide range of animal population density assessments across varied landscapes. is presented to facilitate the creation of tests by providing a sequence of

We introduce a novel randomized distributed algorithm tailored for estimating the size of disk-based networks where node connections are unknown. This algorithm is suitable for networks consisting of non-interacting components and focuses on finding the total network size. Our contribution also includes a revised estimate of ${O}(n^{3/2})$ for the expected number of computations required to determine a network of $n$ nodes, surpassing previous standards. This performance is achieved without the need for counting the number of network components or knowing the number of connections between nodes. Our solution builds upon a random visitation order that enables nodes to make independent estimates of the network size by calculating the square root of the sum of weighted unique discoveries made during the visitation process. This approach takes advantage of a previously proposed recursive relationship identifying the weighted sum of discoveries as the product of the current node's degree and the visitation weight when encountering a node, and doubles the node's weight when encountering a node for the second time. This algorithm's performance is compared to an ideal counting-based approach, and its computational efficiency is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and numerical results. A generalized version of the algorithm is explored for networks consisting of non-communicating components, along with an discussion on various implementation variants. Our results show that the proposed algorithm excels in scenarios with large networks and extensive connectivity, and provides a compelling solution for estimating the size of complex, unknown networks. We analyze the performance of a novel nonparametric approach to estimating queue lengths at intersections based on traffic flow data. In contrast to existing parametric methods, this nonparametric method is more versatile and doesn't require specific intersection types. Our study utilizes real-world data from an urban environment to evaluate the accuracy of this nonparametric method, which outperformed both traditional parametric models and baseline estimates in terms of mean absolute error. Specifically, the mean absolute error when estimating short-term queues ranged from 12.5 to 17.5 seconds, and the estimated long-term queue length mean absolute percentage error ranged from 12.4 to 14.6%. Furthermore, by analyzing trip purposes and examining the relationship between estimated and actual queue lengths, our study reveals that this nonparametric method accurately estimates longer queues, demonstrating its effectiveness even in challenging traffic conditions. The methodology and findings presented can serve as a framework for other cities seeking to estimate queue lengths using traffic flow data. The code and data used in this study are available for public use. The proposed nonparametric method shows the potential to enhance existing traffic signal control algorithms and other applications benefiting from accurate queue length estimation. The practice of estimating queue lengths without a priori assumptions about intersection dynamics can also be applied to other transportation-related problems and research tasks. The employed data architecture and the method itself can serve as a foundation for further research into nonparametric applications related to traffic flow. The built-in robustness of this method implies that it could be successfully used in areas with limited infrastructure, such as certain rural areas, and it has the potential to be used in real-time settings with suitable algorithm adjustments. The built-in simplicity of this method also makes it suitable for other non-traffic flow nonparametric applications, such as those involving acoustic data, that require similar dynamics analysis. We introduce a novel numerical approach to solving the Hamiltonian constraint in the context of 3+1 dimensional general relativity, specifically designed to efficiently handle complex geometric configurations with varied conformal factors. Unlike traditional methods, this scheme bypasses the intricate process of accurately resolving these factors, instead utilizing a hybrid approach that directly manipulates a simplified representation of the inverse conformally transformed quantity. This strategy, which leverages an iterative algorithm inspired by the Gauss--Newton method, enables the solution of the Hamiltonian constraint to be found without the need for sophisticated grid resolution settings. Furthermore, this approach can be used in conjunction with existing solvers, and its benefits are demonstrated through successful applications in two different scenarios. These results showcase the effectiveness and versatility of this new scheme, which can be an valuable tool for ongoing research projects involving the solution of the Hamiltonian constraint. This approach has been tested as part of the higher-order BSSN (HOBBES) project, an extensive numerical campaign aimed at understanding collision solutions in the context of general relativity, but it is presented here independently of that project. This new scheme has been successfully applied in simulations of black hole collisions in vacuum, as well as in scenarios involving matter and radiation, and it is a valuable contribution to the existing body of work on these topics. This approach has the potential to significantly enhance the efficiency of future simulations of the same type, and it is particularly well-suited to the high-performance computing environment of the HOBBES simulation framework. Anomalous Nernst effects in solids are generally observed in ferromagnetic materials with strong spin-orbit interaction. Researchers have found that antiferromagnetic antiperovskites can exhibit unusual Nernst effects due to significant spin-orbit interaction and robust non-magnetic channels. Studies have demonstrated that the anomalous Nernst coefficient in EuGa2 can be modulated by temperature and magnetic field. Furthermore, theoretical calculations suggest that the anomalous Nernst effect in NiTa1.75V0.25 can be explained by considering short-range magnetic interactions and spin-orbit interaction. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic materials and may lead to new applications. The complexity of these materials also raises challenges in theoretical modeling. The study of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskites can be further explored by conducting theoretical calculations of the anomalous Nernst coefficient using multiple scattering electronic structure methods. The interpretation of these results will necessitate the development of new theories that take into account the complex magnetic configurations of these materials. The anomalous Nernst effect in EuGa2 can be tuned by changing the sample orientation during measurement, suggesting potential for use in spin-based thermoelectric technology, but the search for suitable substitutes for rare earth elements like Eu will be essential for large-scale production. The study of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskites like NiTaV can be expanded upon by conducting comprehensive experimental studies of various elements and compounds to establish design principles for optimizing the effect, and by conducting theoretical calculations of the anomalous Nernst coefficient in multiple scenarios to inform these experiments. Specifically, under the assumption that the gradient of the obstacle obstacle possesses a certain level of regularity, denoted by $W^{1,p}$, we demonstrate that its corresponding solution also satisfies a certain Sobolev norm criterion, notably without relying on the inclusion of a second order term in the energy functional. The initial proof, which was validated for a particular instance of the obstacle problem involving a moving boundary, relied on the application of a regularity-lifting result that was specifically tailored to that instance. By contrast, the extended result is obtained through the utilization of different methods. In particular, the time-dependent case is demonstrated by using the time-independent result as well as a trick involving the introduction of a fixed obstacle. On the other hand, the time-independent case with a moving boundary is established by utilizing the time-dependent result in addition to the mentioned time-independent result of the time-dependent case with a moving boundary. We define a new concept called mesoscale flatness for a surface in hyperspace and use it to characterize surfaces with constant mean curvature within a specific bounded range. This characterization involves an explicit formula that showcases the relationship between the surface's position, its curvature, and the distance from a given plane. This result can be viewed as a variation of the classical Bernstein problem, initially explored by Yau in 1975, although our approach is distinct. Specifically, we are examining surfaces in R^4 with mean curvature bounded above and below, whereas Yau considered surfaces in R^3 with a similar condition. Our primary goal in introducing mesoscale flatness becomes apparent when we analyze an interesting type of solution to a specific nonlinear Schrödinger system, known as the Lui Hui system. This system includes a term that represents a measure of the square of the modulus of the derivative of the function, which, when considered in the context of the R^4 hyperspace, can be interpreted as the mean curvature of a surface. By applying this interpretation, we are able to reuse the surface's characteristics to obtain an explicit formula that facilitates the solution of the system. Additionally, this formula serves as the foundation for establishing an inequality that can be used to prove the solution to the system exists and is unique. Moreover, this solution exhibits certain properties, such as being defined for an infinite timeframe, possessing specific growth characteristics, and maintaining a specific fixed ratio with its derivative. Furthermore, this solution can be viewed as a result of the interaction between two distinct components, each corresponding to a specific sign, with the absolute value of the derivative of the function being confined within a specific range that is directly proportional to the distance from a given plane. We examine the Lotka-Volterra model, a fundamental predator-prey system, to explore the consequences of intelligence among species with different characteristics. In our analysis, we consider two types of intelligence measurements: one represented by a nonlinear response to population sizes and the other embodied in a memory-based dynamic feedback mechanism. Our studies on these intelligent systems, carried out through numerical simulations and bounded rationality methods, reveal a wide range of possible dynamics, from unstable to coexisting or cyclic dynamics. Notably, we find that the presence of intelligence can lead to a notable delay in the extinction time of the species, thereby illustrating the adaptive benefits it confers in challenging environments. Moreover, we establish the existence of a critical intelligence intensity threshold below which the species will eventually go extinct. Our findings are also demonstrated to be applicable to the Mackey-Glass model, another well-known dynamic system. Our research highlights the significant impact of intelligence on the coexistence of species and offers a theoretical framework for understanding the effects of different intelligence intensities and types on dynamic ecosystems. Ultimately, our results provide a practical illustration of the benefits of intelligence in the face of environmental changes, thereby emphasizing its crucial importance for species survival. Our research outcomes are further validated by means of the Hilbert transform and the degree map method. Our work also reveals intriguing dynamics, including periodic and chaotic oscillations in the population sizes, as well as the notable effects of intelligence on the corresponding dimension estimates. Our research outcomes can be applied to a wide range of natural and social dynamic systems featuring predators and preys. Our work demonstrates the substantial adverse impact of low intelligence on species coexistence, thereby emphasizing the necessity of developing intelligent conservation management strategies that take into account the complex interactions within dynamic ecosystems. Our research outcomes can be visually represented through phase diagrams, illustrating the relationships between different dynamic behaviors and various system parameters, thereby providing actionable insights for the sustainable protection of species with high intelligence levels. Our research outcomes also offer practical applications for the effective management of dynamic systems featuring complex interactions among multiple components, thereby highlighting the significant benefits of introducing intelligence into these systems. Our research outcomes can be utilized in multiple real-world scenarios, including the regulation of stock markets, the control of epidemics, and the maintenance of ecological balance in natural environments. Our research outcomes demonstrate the substantial advantages of integrating intelligence into dynamic systems, thereby highlighting the potential for improving the coexistence of species, enhancing economic productivity, and reducing the risk of catastrophic failures. Our research outcomes also emphasize the necessity for developing quantitative indicators that can effectively capture the complex aspects of intelligence

We introduce a novel approach to proving a broad class of integral identities, specifically those known as $q$-polynomial identities, by utilizing geometric vectors. This method, which leverages the properties of harmonic algebra, provides a vectorized formulation of identities that are then applied to configure suitable weighting functions to derive the desired $q$-identities. This technique, which we call the "vectorized approach," enables the derivation of a range of $q$-identities by varying parameters, even in instances where the conventional derivation method is quite complicated. In this paper, we demonstrate the vectorized method's effectiveness by applying it to a variety of identities, including those with variable parameters, by utilizing the property of harmonic algebra to prove a general theorem that facilitates the configuration of weighting functions, thus obtaining the $q$-identities. In addition, we also introduce the concept of "mirror identities" and demonstrate that a significant class of $q$-identities can be expressed in a form that is considered "self-inverse." This particular form, which results from applying the vectorized method to a specific parameter setting, yields a set of identities that is encompassing enough to include all known examples in the literature, offering an organized and streamlined presentation of these specific instances of identities. This vectorized approach also presents a straightforward algorithm for deriving the weighting functions required for $q$-identities, even in instances where the conventional derivation method is very complicated, as well as providing a vectorized formulation that can be utilized to configure the weighting functions for a wide range of $q$-identities, thereby facilitating a deeper understanding of these particular identities. The muon g-2 experiment at J-PARC has the potential to verify the anomalous measurement reported in particle physics and provide a comprehensive understanding of the electroweak sector. The proposed study allows for the exploration of an unusual phenomenon known as the "electroweak precision puzzle," which entails an examination of beyond the Standard Model theories in the context of the weak interaction. Present and future experiments already constrain certain parameters that explain the muon g-2 anomaly and the W boson mass anomaly with great precision. However, many possible explanations of the "precision puzzle" remain unexplored due to future experimental limitations on probing certain beyond the Standard Model physics scales and particle energies. To fully address this puzzle, future experiments such as the muon colliders, top quark precision measurements at future hadron colliders, neutrino experiments with beyond the Standard Model sensitivity, and lepton-flavour violating processes in rare decays will need to be conducted with enhanced capabilities. This article outlines the scope of the "precision puzzle" and the relevant beyond the Standard Model physics, before detailing the parameters of future experiments required to resolve the issue. It is demonstrated that through optimized experiments, a significant portion of the parameter space related to the muon g-2 anomaly and the W boson mass anomaly can be made accessible for investigation. The proposed study is valuable for guiding the design of future experiments and could facilitate a deeper comprehension of the electroweak precision puzzle. The research mentioned here is part of a larger project aimed at understanding the physics driving the muon g-2 anomaly and the W boson mass anomaly, and informing the necessary future experiments required to solve this "precision puzzle." The project also involves examining the interconnections between the two anomalies, as well as their connections to other rare processes in particle physics. The feasible future experiments identified in this study could simultaneously explain both the muon g-2 anomaly and the W boson mass anomaly, in addition to exploring the underlying beyond the Standard Model physics that gives rise to both anomalies. The proposed study is an initial step towards addressing the possible causes of both the muon g-2 anomaly and the W boson mass anomaly, and could lead to a deeper understanding of the underlying physics if both anomalies are confirmed in future experiments. The research on the muon g-2 anomaly and the W boson mass anomaly presents a unique opportunity to explore the consistent explanation of both anomalies by probing the parameter space of beyond the Standard Model theories through future experiments in particle physics. By employing the OPE, the two-loop correction to the anomalous dimension of the spin-three conformal primary, represented by the operator $T^3$, can be calculated and is found to be zero. These OPE relations, in turn, lead to the identification of the spin-three conformal orbifolds within the $sl(3)$ Toda conformal field theory. Accurate brain-computer interface (BCI) decoding relies on precise electrical mapping between neural signals and intended actions. Recent studies using high-resolution electrocortical recordings during walking demonstrate significant discrepancies between actual and predicted step timing. To enhance the efficacy of such BCIs, it is essential to explore more accurate decoding methods, especially in comparison to conventional electroencephalography (EEG) techniques. In this research, a novel approach involving A-train depth-electrocortical potentials was developed and tested on a dedicated animal model of walking motor control. By utilizing a generalized linear model, researchers successfully decoded potetial patterns associated with specific phases of the gait cycle, with decoding accuracy exceeding 90% in both ECoG and EEG signal replicas. Furthermore, the current study reveals that the accuracy of ECoG signal replication surpasses EEG replication accuracy of 80% in comparison to the 20% difference observed between actual and predicted gait cycle phases based on ECoG versus EEG signals. Additionally, the findings demonstrate the distinct informational content of different cortical frequency bands, with notable contributions from high-frequency bands in ECoG signals and low-frequency bands in EEG signals. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the feasibility of precise gait cycle phase decoding using A-train depth-electrocortical potentials and highlights the potential applications of such BCIs in predicting walking functions for patients with specific neurological disorders. In particular, with the current study's advancements, it is now possible to envision the utilization of ECoG-based BCIs in predicting walking capacities in patients with particular neurological conditions, such as spinal cord injuries or multiple system atrophy, for whom precise gait cycle phase decoding is crucial. In such cases, the difference between actual and predicted gait cycle phases based on ECoG versus EEG signals is quite significant, at 20%. Therefore, the development of more accurate BCI systems, such as the novel approach presented in this research, is urgently needed. Many real-world systems, including cultural networks and mobile communication connections, evolve over time and require a different kind of representation than static graphs.  Our novel deep learning framework, DECENNT, is the first dynamic graph convolutional network designed to capture long-term patterns in time sequences of graphs.  Unlike conventional methods that use hand-crafted techniques to account for changing graph structures, DECENNT utilizes a continuous time series approach, mapping both node and edge representations through continuous equations that resemble dynamic system models.  This unique design allows our model to capture long-term patterns in time sequences of graphs, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods on various tasks, including node classification, group prediction, and link prediction, by significant margins.  Specifically, DECENNT achieves the highest accuracy on three public dynamic graph datasets, surpassing the current top performance by a 13.43% margin on the Taucylic dataset, a 12.58% margin on the Cora dataset, and a 10.43% margin on the Pubmed dataset. Analyzing the movements of various entities within images is a challenge that arises in multiple applications including biology, security, and sports analysis. Movement detection becomes particularly difficult when evaluating fast, complex, and superimposed movements, especially in video data. Existing techniques are largely confined to examining slow, separate movements found in static images. To address the limitations of current approaches, we present a novel algorithm called the Movement Operator Tree (MOT). This tree-based model leverages a unique operator designed to detect directions of pixel movements at multiple scales, allowing it to efficiently identify areas of changing intensity within an image. By minimizing the number of operators required, MOT achieves both reduced computational costs and improved performance when detecting movement across both static and video images. Evaluations conducted on multiple datasets demonstrate MOT's superior performance compared to existing methods, showcasing its effectiveness in accurately identifying movements of both biological and non-biological objects and scenes. Furthermore, the simplicity and efficiency of MOT make it a suitable solution for real-world applications involving high-resolution image and video data. We introduce the Nested Neumann algorithm, an efficient method for computing the inception complex of a polynomial map, which includes determining the inception depth, a measure that indicates how quickly the algorithm converges.  Our approach is distinct from other methods that utilize numerical complex analysis and the Neumann series of a operator.  Our algorithm is comprised of two main components: an approximation process that utilizes the Neumann series of an operator and a comparison method that ensures the inception depth's correct classification.  We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness by applying it to several polynomial maps with known inception properties and show how it efficiently calculates the inception depth of these maps.  Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's performance, which includes an examination of the relationship between its numerical accuracy and the inception depth of the polynomial map.  This analysis enables us to derive specific conditions that ensure the algorithm's convergence.  Our results show that the algorithm achieves a linear convergence rate, which is the fastest possible convergence rate it can attain, when the algorithm is applied to polynomial maps with a certain specific structure, known as the monic linear map, which includes the well-known linear map DNE.  Our research also includes an examination of the relationship between the inception depth and the algorithm's convergence rate, which provides additional insights into the properties of the Neumann series of an operator and the algorithm's convergence behavior.  Finally, we conclude our research by highlighting the algorithm's versatility and the various research opportunities it presents in relation to polynomial maps and the Neumann series of operators.  Our research paper is divided into five sections.  In the first section, we introduce the inception complex and the Nested Neumann algorithm, which is an efficient method for computing the inception complex of a polynomial map.  In the second section, we explain the algorithm's components and provide a brief examination of its convergence behavior.  In the third section, we apply the algorithm to several polynomial maps with known inception properties.  In the fourth section, we examine the algorithm's convergence rate from a numerical analysis perspective.  In the fifth section, we conclude our research and present future research opportunities.  Our research paper is a revised version of a previous paper we published in the journal Applied Mathematics and Computation. Recent theories have suggested that topological characteristics in physical systems can be used to classify their energy spectra. Nonetheless, implementing such calculations is complex and not practical for large-scale systems. Alternatively, researchers have proposed novel methods to detect the topological nature of physical systems based on their local properties. A newly proposed technique measures the disorder-induced changes in a physical system's energy levels and employs these changes to determine its topological classification. Although this method successfully classifies the topological nature of one-dimensional physical systems, it has not been applied to recognize two-dimensional physical systems that are spatially layered. In this study, researchers demonstrate how to extend the technique to a specific class of two-dimensional physical systems and layer-by-layer combinations of physical systems. Moreover, they develop a practical approach to detect the topological nature of these physical systems by analyzing the fluctuations of their energy levels. Finally, in an experimental context, this method could be used to determine the topological nature of chemical compounds based solely on the energy levels of their atomic constituents. This approach has been tested on theoretical models and realistic calculations of chemical compounds. It has also been validated by comparing its results with established methods of predicting topological nature. We investigate the performance of binary power control in large networks with many transmitters and receivers. Assuming a general optimization criterion, we show that a simple, low-complexity policy involving just two power levels can compete favorably with optimal power control. In particular, for a specific criterion that minimizes the longest waiting time for reliable data transmission, we find a policy with an even simpler structure--alternating between two power levels--which performs essentially as well as optimal power control. This result holds not only for large networks but also in scenarios with limited bandwidth and multiple interferers. In such cases, the reduction in the waiting time or required bandwidth can be substantial, offering practical advantages with minimal complexity overhead. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the best power levels for binary power control are inversely proportional to the variance of the channel quality estimation, consistent with previous simulations. Nonetheless, our study suggests a more precise relationship, highlighting the value of further research into binary power control, a crucial problem with significant practical implications. Despite the benefits of binary power control, with its minimal complexity and reliable performance, relatively few networks have implemented it due in part to the generally small gains it achieves in smaller networks. Our analysis is based on mathematical models which can be interpreted as reflecting the performance in various real-world scenarios, including those with multiple access interference, where the performance represents a combination of the performance of multiple receivers in the same network. Our research provides a framework for extending existing theories about power control in networks with the goal of improving performance through targeted optimization, by first considering simple policies that can serve as approximations. Unlike conventional integrated methods that employ a single time step for both fluid and particle simulations, MTSA utilizes independent time steps for each component. The algorithm ensures the consistency and stability of the solution by maintaining the accuracy of the fluid and particle models within their respective time frames. The development of the method is illustrated through the integration of the one-dimensional Lagrangian particle method with the one-dimensional boundary layer equation, and the resulting code achieves a 10 times improvement in computational efficiency for a given problem when compared to a traditional approach using the same level of numerical accuracy. The effectiveness of MTSA is also demonstrated across two-dimensional junction flow and bubble dynamics scenarios, exhibiting a 5 times gain in computational speed for the same numerical accuracy. Quantum annealing's effectiveness relies on a sufficient "annealing gap," the difference between the energies required to complete a task efficiently with quantum versus classical methods. However, determining the annealing gap from just outcome data is challenging due in part to the need to accurately estimate the classical energy required, especially when the number of generated classical samples is limited. This research develops an optimization framework for quantum annealing protocols that considers the classical energy's uncertainty, enabling the development of robust and efficient protocols, thus making the annealing gap's influence on the outcome more clear. By applying this framework to a specific problem - finding the ground state of a random Ising model - it is demonstrated that the annealing gap can be viewed as the difference between two classical energy barriers, with the larger one representing the classical energy required for a random Ising model and the smaller one representing the energy required when the algorithm is properly optimized. Furthermore, it is shown that the optimal quantum annealing time is inversely proportional to the annealing gap, thus implying that the optimal time depends on the classical energy barrier. This research also introduces two new quantities - the quantum speed advantage and the annealing time advantage - which provide additional insights into the performance of quantum annealing. It is demonstrated that the optimal quantum annealing time is exponentially sensitive to the number of random Ising model's disorder parameters, whereas the annealing time advantage is only power-law sensitive, with the difference reflecting the annealing time advantage's more rapid growth with increasing random Ising model's barrier depth. Consequently, this research underscores the significance of considering the annealing time advantage in assessments of quantum annealing's performance. A comprehensive theoretical investigation of the electronic structure and subsequent magnetic and electronic phases in 4e-band nickelates is presented. A consistent method to calculate band structures using a suitable atomic arrangement was developed, yielding consistent results across various oxidation states of these compounds, from NiO to Sr3Ni2O5. Notably, the absence of a fundamental inversion symmetry in these non-symmetric atomic arrangements was found to influence the energy levels, with the resulting band structures being a crucial factor contributing to their unique magnetic properties and unconventional superconductivity. Furthermore, the predicted effect of non-stoichiometric oxygen on the band structure, potentially leading to a topological phase transition in Sr3Ni2O5, was determined to require further experimental verification. Nonetheless, this study provides a unifying framework for the diverse electronic properties observed in nickelates, attributing their complexity to a combination of fundamental crystal symmetry properties, electron lattice interactions, and marginal electron hole doping. Schematic phase diagrams obtained theoretically are also presented, outlining possible paths to realizing novel magnetic and possibly unconventional electronic phases in these compounds. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the intricate band structures of nickelates are the primary driving force behind their complex electronic phases and offers a theoretical basis for understanding and predicting their diverse material properties. Given their rich physics and unconventional behavior, this study encourages further experimental investigation of these compounds, potentially uncovering novel mechanisms of magnetism and superconductivity. Ultimately, the universal physical principles governing the band structures of these compounds will also make this research relevant to a wider range of materials exhibiting 4e-band electronic configurations.
