Teaching a student model to make accurate decisions by combining existing knowledge bases without access to teacher models is known as knowledge amalgamation. A significant challenge in this process is ensuring the student model acquires relevant knowledge by observing the correct examples. We propose a novel approach, known as the saliency-based method, which leverages example-specific sensitivity information to guide the student model during training. In contrast to conventional approaches, this method facilitates the student model in identifying the most crucial data for its development by assigning it high importance. By doing so, the model is prevented from overreliance on noisy or less meaningful data. We test the saliency-based method on three different tasks and demonstrate its superiority over existing knowledge amalgamation methods by achieving significant improvements in model performance. Specifically, the model shows a 6.3% greater accuracy in predicting sentiment, a 4.8% greater F1 score in identifying text polarity, and a 13.3% greater accuracy in classifying medical codes. Furthermore, the proposed approach is valuable for tasks where large amounts of data are available, as it enables the model to reject unimportant examples and focus on the most crucial ones with ease. The code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/hantsail/saliency-based-knowledge-amalgamation.

We analyze the rational rank of elliptic curves defined over the field of rational numbers, within a specific class of quartic number fields that satisfy certain Galois group properties. Our investigation focuses on a category of Galois extensions known as S4, featuring non-trivial kernels in reductions of certain congruences. We establish limitations on the rational rank of these elliptic curves, demonstrating that there are infinitely many combinations of weights and characteristic polynomials for which the rational rank remains zero. Specifically, we demonstrate the inexistence of elliptic curves meeting specific criteria from the S4 family, resulting in a rank of zero for curves like y^2 = x^3 + ax + b, where a, b are rational numbers. Our proof involves constructing modular forms using Hecke operators, which enables us to apply properties of the Stokes operator. Ultimately, our findings build upon recent works of Diaz and Lozano, as well as Guvender, by expanding on their results for cases of trivial kernels. We also outline possible future directions for exploring similar problems within other Galois groups. Additionally, we establish connections between the rational rank of these elliptic curves and modular forms related to the E4, E6, and Delta examples. Our research was initially presented at the RISC Diophantine Geometry Workshop held in Linz, Austria. It has since undergone revisions based on feedback from participants. Our approach to achieving zero rank can be accomplished within 2-day workshops, whereas longer durations may allow for additional outcomes. For example, working within the A4, S3, and D4 groups settings could potentially yield more extensive lists of weights with zero rank. Furthermore, our methods have the potential to be adapted for discovering weights with rank one, which would necessitate an in-depth examination of 20,000 possible combinations. Given the constraints of our approach, our research is only applicable to weights with rank zero. It is essential to note that the majority of our results can be achieved through more direct approaches, revealing that the application of modular forms provides a versatile tool for achieving our desired outcome. By linking the nonequilibrium dynamics to an adiabatic expansion scenario, the relevant expressions can be made comparable to established nonequilibrium adiabatic theories. In the case where the initial and final equilibrium situations exhibit distinct temperatures and densities, we successfully derive an explicit formula for irreversible entropy, showing it to be a difference of cross-entropy terms. This nonequilibrium perspective is then utilized to analyze both abrupt changes in temperature and the quench between two different chemical potentials. The investigation reveals that the rate of irreversible entropy generation reaches a steady-state value, with its rate being proportional to the temperature difference and the square of the system size. Furthermore, we identify an effective temperature, associated with an entropy gradient, and demonstrate that it differs from the equilibrium temperature, thereby illustrating the complexities of its interpretation. The effective temperature is found to be proportional to the difference between the equilibrium temperatures and the system temperature, with the proportionality constant depending on the system's density and the quantum system's properties. The research provides a microscopic understanding of the concept of an effective temperature during quench processes. The study reveals that the relation between the effective temperature and the density gradient can be nonmonotonic, depending solely on the quench parameters, and may give rise to an inverse effective temperature, i.e., a decrease in effective temperature with increasing density, in contrast to its usual increase in classical systems. The research demonstrates that the effective temperature can serve as a nonequilibrium benchmark, with systems having an inverse effective temperature potentially exhibiting novel behaviors, such as novel phase transitions or emergent symmetries, which would be missed in conventional nonequilibrium descriptions. We investigate a non-unitary quantum dynamical system that incorporates both unitary and non-unitary processes, specifically a quasiclassical scenario with continuous measurement. By applying a time-averaging technique, we derive a simplified model that exhibits dynamics analogous to those of a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. Subsequent analysis of this reduced model involves calculating its eigenvalues, eigenstates, and the associated Wigner function. Notably, we establish an relationship between the time required to discern the initial state from the time-averaged state and the time-translation operator's standard deviation. This investigation also encompasses a comparison with a related Hermitian dynamics model, revealing distinct outcomes due to the presence of loss processes. Our study demonstrates that continuous measurement can effectively mask the effects of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians on a quasiclassical system. Furthermore, we identify conditions under which the Hermitian and non-Hermitian dynamics yield identical results, and in this case, we demonstrate that the time-translation operator becomes a constant, resulting in an undetermined set of initial states that continue to look the same after measurement for an infinite duration. This work has implications for our understanding of the distinguishability time in both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. Additionally, it sheds light on the adiabaticity condition in a quasiclassical scenario with continuous measurement, revealing that the time scale associated with the drift part of the dynamics dictates the time required to smooth out the initial condition, whereas the time scale linked to the fluctuation part of the dynamics, which arises from continuous measurement, determines the accuracy of this approximation. Lastly, the research demonstrates that the time-averaged state corresponds to the ground state of an effective Hamiltonian that incorporates both the initial system state and the time-translation operator, with the associated energy spectrum being a function of the time scale and the time-translation operator's standard deviation. Consequently, the discernibility time can be expressed in terms of the effective mass of the time-translation operator, with implications for our understanding of the interplay between the Hermitian and non-Hermitian components of the effective Hamiltonian in a quasiclassical scenario with continuous measurement. In this context, a nondegenerate simplex is one whose vertices are linearly independent. Our primary goal is to establish criteria for such a simplex to exist in $Q_n$ by examining configurations of nodes. For our main result, we demonstrate that there is a nondegenerate simplex in the unit cube $Q_n$ with $n^2$ nodes, arranged in a specific pattern, and centered at the origin. This achievement allows us to settle two problems posed by Malouf. Additionally, our analysis provides an alternative proof for an earlier result by Jorgensen and Kuwshoff. Furthermore, our analysis enables us to extend the parameters for which there are nondegenerate simplexes in $Q_n$ with certain specified properties, including those with a specific minimum distance between nodes and those with a certain maximal depth. Our research also explores the relationship between nondegenerate simplexes and a specific type of ID-systems. In doing so, we introduce a new concept called a deep set, providing an example of such a set as the set of nonnegative integers with the standard addition operation. By examining this example, we can determine the maximum possible depth of a nondegenerate simplex in the unit cube $Q_n$, showing it increases exponentially with respect to the number of nodes. Our study of the relationship between nondegenerate simplexes and ID-systems also enables us to establish a bound on the number of nodes in a nondegenerate simplex within the unit cube $Q_n$, finding it to be $4^n - 2$ for the case where the simplex is centered at the origin. A planetary atmosphere's long-term evolution could be influenced significantly by a cycle in which a planet's interior loses heat, causing its atmosphere to expand and potentially lead to interior-external mass transfer through planetary interior erosion. This process, simulated using computational models, resulted in the formation of a global atmospheric circulation pattern driven by a temperature gradient of approximately 10 degrees Kelvin per Earth radius. This temperature difference powered the migration of the planet's interior mass towards the surface and the subsequent mass loss from the atmosphere into space. As a result, the planet's atmospheric composition evolved over time, with heavier elements like silicon becoming locked within the planet, while lighter elements like oxygen remained in the atmosphere. Ultimately, this process led to the formation of a rocky core surrounded by an oxygen-rich atmospheric shell, with temperatures hot enough to prevent the condensation of heavier elements. This research demonstrates how a planet's initial conditions can shape its eventual fate, influencing whether it ends up as a rocky planet similar to Earth, a gas giant, or a planet with a massive atmospheric reservoir known as a super-Venus. This interior-external cycling of mass also provides a potential mechanism for the formation of a type of planet with a massive atmospheric reservoir, known as a super-Venus, which could explain the discovery of large atmospheric shells surrounding certain low-mass stars. This process is more significant for smaller planets with initial rotation rates similar to those of Earth, and it could be an important consideration in understanding the long-term evolution of exoplanets, particularly those with densities indicative of substantial atmospheric reserves. This research demonstrates the significance of considering the interactions between a planet's interior and atmosphere in computational models of long-term evolution, and it highlights the potential for investigating this complex relationship further using laboratory experiments and numerical simulations. This process could be an important factor in shaping the evolution of gasless giant planets like Saturn, and it may also influence the formation and eventual fate of giant planets known as sub-Jovians. This research also raises questions about the possible applications of this mass transfer cycle to understanding other astronomical phenomena, such as the formation of gas reservoirs surrounding certain binary stars and the composition of certain types of white dwarfs. This research introduces a multivariate point process model called nonlinear Hawkes networks to analyze complex systems featuring interconnected events. Based on a general Hawkes process framework, the nonlinear Hawkes network model incorporates adjustable trigger functions that allow it to capture the effects of specific events on the occurrence of other events, enabling the representation of diverse interactions, such as both short-lived responses to events and long-lasting influences. In addition to its applicability to broad interactions, the model also ensures positive specific branch rates, avoiding the degradation common in other Hawkes-based models. We have derived the conditional intensity function of the nonlinear Hawkes network, applying it to examine a paradigmatic example of a small-world Hawkes network with persistent interactions, and demonstrated its capabilities by recreating patterns of interactions found in real data, including the relationship between earthquakes and aftershocks. Furthermore, the nonlinear Hawkes network model has shown the ability to generate reliable signal reconstruction from noisy data and accurately identify crucial links between events. This model provides a versatile tool for analyzing complex interactions within multi-dimensional event processes, offering significant potential for its expansion into more intricate networks. Research involving laser-plasma interaction at a high frequency is often hindered by the requirement to slowly modulate the properties of plasma over several orders of magnitude, which can be challenging to achieve with conventional methods. A key component in controlling plasma behavior is the plasma waveplate, whose optimal thickness is determined by competing factors, notably plasma electron density, magnetic field strength, and the speed of the passing laser, and must be precisely controlled to avoid unnecessary distortion of plasma properties and to prevent the waveplate from becoming excessively thick. In an experiment conducted with a 10.53 GHz laser and a magnetic field of 1.5 T, plasma electron density was within a range that allowed for precise control, and as a result, a waveplate thickness of 1.1 mm was successfully achieved, thereby expanding the range of applicable frequencies for waveplate-based experiments by at least an order of magnitude. In addition, an attempt to employ a magnetic field to modulate plasma properties more rapidly was made, but was unsuccessful due to the need for an even stronger magnetic field to achieve significant modification of plasma electron density. An analysis of the necessary waveplate thickness was also theoretically examined via particle-in-cell simulations, and the results showed that even smaller waveplates could be achieved with more powerful lasers, and that the required thickness is highly sensitive to the properties of the passing particles, whether they are high-energy electrons or ions. Furthermore, possible applications of the waveplate technique were explored, including the modification of plasma electron distribution, the creation of plasma density gradients, and the improvement of plasma-based particle accelerators, and it was found that even a relatively simple modification of plasma electron distribution could result in significant improvement of plasma-based accelerators, with a hypothetical example suggesting that a plasma waveplate could increase the energy of electrons accelerated to 1 GeV from 1 MHz to 10 GHz, by reducing the necessary plasma length from 80 meters to 0.8 meters. Additionally, possible limitations of the waveplate technique were also identified, including the required precise control of plasma properties and the necessary thick waveplates, which could compromise the speed of experiments, but it was noted that the speed of experiments can be adjusted to match the available plasma and the necessary waveplate thickness can be minimized by adjusting the required particle properties. Moreover, it was pointed out that the required precise control of plasma properties could be achieved through the use of a magnetic field, which was found to be necessary for particle modulation in any case, and that the waveplate technique could be an effective approach for modifying plasma properties

A thorough examination of the parameter space reveals that a very small, non-negligible portion of the type-II two-Higgs doublet scenario could potentially accommodate a significant tau dipole moment, potentially within the reach of upcoming experiments. A general analysis of the most significant contribution yields a direct relationship with the tau Compton scale, which has far-reaching implications for the potential discovery of a significant tau dipole moment. A comprehensive examination of low-rate rank-metric codes' ability to correct errors is presented in this paper. Our main finding reveals that for code rates greater than 1/2, no universal, high-performance code can exist that is capable of accurately detecting and correcting all possible error patterns. To support our conclusion, we developed a highly efficient, generic decoding algorithm for rank-metric codes and established the maximum rate at which codes with a specific distance property can succeed in correcting random binary noise. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the optimal encoding strategy for rank-metric codes involves a linear feedback shift register with a particular structure, which we used to analyze the code rates achievable with increasing levels of error correction capability. Our results also compare with previous limits on codes with specific security properties, providing additional insights into their capabilities. Our research primarily focuses on code errors, but our methods and findings are relevant to a broader context of decoding problems that involve rank-minimization subject to a given margin. Our contributions are relevant to a wide range of applications, including coding theory, learning, game theory, and data analysis, all of which involve solving rank-minimization problems with various constraints, including a maximum allowed rank and a margin that ensures distinctness, as seen in the example of the Grassmanian matrix completion problem. Our coding framework and associated insights can be used in the efficient decoding of a wide range of learning and data problems that involve resolving the rank-minimization problem with a given margin, by treating these problems as instances of our coding framework. We investigate the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation of conserved current OPE blocks in CFT$_2$, drawing a distinction from the representation in CFT$_3$ with AdS$_3$ geodesic operators. The AdS$_2$ representation reveals a previously unobserved cross-term contribution, leading to a difference in operator expressions when compared to the AdS$_3$ representation. This difference results in a change in the operator's U(1) charge under the conserved current, with implications for its subsequent application in computing correlation functions. Furthermore, this novel cross-term term contribution presents an obstacle to directly using the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation for determining the U(1) charge of the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator. Nonetheless, we establish an explicit relationship between the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator and its associated Weyl vector in the U(1) gauge theory, enabling us to extend previous results on the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator's properties to the associated U(1) gauge theory. Ultimately, our investigation finds that the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation retains the same primary and descendant characteristics when compared to the AdS$_3$ representation, with both representing conserved current OPE blocks. By utilizing the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation, we also derive an explicit formula for the U(1) charge of the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator, in addition to confirming the equivalence of the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator with the Liouville theory's descendant operators in CFT$_2$. Moreover, our formula for the U(1) charge can be applied to compute the expectation value of the conserved current in the energy landscape of the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator, thereby extending the earlier work of Maldacena and Nagasaki on this specific topic. Our research paves the way for further exploration of the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator in both its standalone form and as a part of Liouville theory. Our investigation demonstrates that the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation resists the screening that the AdS$_3$ geodesic operator representation undergoes when considering multiple U(1) currents, allowing us to compute the expectation value of the conserved current in the energy landscape of the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator, with implications for its application in computing correlation functions

In 1976, Gelfand and MacPherson introduced an idea of combinatorial differential manifolds as a way to translate smooth equations into a language compatible with finite fields.  Their innovation laid the groundwork for an alternative interpretation of the theory of singularities.  Specifically, it enabled the creation of a framework that could handle and resolve singularities within the context of combinatorial differential manifolds.  Furthermore, it allowed them to prove the implication that a set of equations has only a finite number of solutions in any field if the combinatorial structure behind those equations meets a specific condition.  Building upon Gelfand and MacPherson's work, we have made significant advancements in the field of combinatorial differential manifolds.  Notably, we have discovered that the distinction between rational and algebraic combinatorial differential manifolds is not as pronounced as previously thought.  In the process, we have also established the relationship between the set of rational points on a combinatorial differential manifold and the set of its algebraic points.  Most notably, we have an explicit formula that calculates the number of rational points on a combinatorial differential manifold that is parameterized by a parameter r, as well as the evidence that for any finite field with a certain characteristic, the set of rational points on a particular type of combinatorial differential manifold corresponds to the set of roots of a specific polynomial equation, which can be described by its coefficients.  These coefficients themselves form another combinatorial differential manifold, offering a fertile ground for further study.  Finally, we have also established the connection between the number of rational points on this particular combinatorial differential manifold and the number of its algebraic points, as well as the evidence that the graph of the polynomial that has rational coefficients can be identified as a type of combinatorial differential manifold, which in turn allows us to apply the results we have previously obtained to demonstrate the implication that the number of its roots, when counted over any field, is finite and specifically equals the product of r, the number of algebraic points on it, and the number of its rational points.  Consequently, we have an answer to the question of how to determine if a set of equations has a finite number of solutions in any field, as well as the evidence that this information can be found within the combinatorial structure behind those equations. The peculiar supernova SN~2020jfo has been studied in depth by several researchers, and it has been classified as a rare Type Ia supernova with an abnormal chemical element abundance pattern, similar to some globular cluster properties.  To better understand this phenomenon, more SN~2020jfo spectral data and detailed elemental abundance analyses are necessary.  Another unknown aspect of this event is the solid dust grain component, which can provide valuable information about the SN~2020jfo formation mechanisms.  In this research, we used radio and mid-infrared archival data to discover solid grains in SN~2020jfo, and found a nickel to iron abundance ratio lower than typical solar values, and also determined the abundance of iron, nickel, and solid grains in SN~2020jfo.  A model of a double-degenerate SN~2020jfo formation scenario explains the observed chemical element abundance pattern, although it cannot fully account for the low nickel to iron abundance ratio observed in this supernova. Accurate prediction of halo masses in dark matter simulations relies heavily on the correct interpretation of density fluctuations from early universe scalar perturbations. By conducting high-precision simulations of cosmological evolution, researchers can test different density field interpretation methods, such as using a single density-based model, which typically results in inconsistent halo mass predictions when applying it to initial conditions with significant scalar perturbation amplitudes. A recent study simulated the cosmological evolution of a nearly uniform density field with highly amplified scalar perturbations, equivalent to an overdensity of 10 times the critical density, using two different numerical methods - SNEAKS and Gadget. By comparing the results, researchers found that both simulations accurately reproduced the characteristics of dark matter halos within dense regions, known as 'halo cores', but differed in their formation of smaller halos surrounding the main cores - SNEAKS simulations formed these surrounding halos more quickly. Although this discrepancy needs further investigation, it is essential to recognize that the core halo regime is less sensitive to the effects of gravitational forces on dark matter. A key observation from the study was the more halos formed in the surrounding region of the core when using the Gadget simulation, which resulted in a more significant mismatch when predicting halo masses based on a single density-based model, compared to SNEAKS simulations. This difference in halo formation around the core could be attributed to the more rapid formation of surrounding halos in the Gadget simulation affecting the accuracy of halo mass predictions, as it means the model is interpreting density fluctuations from the wrong stages of cosmological evolution. A significant improvement in halo mass prediction was observed when using a two-component density model that distinguishes between the density of the main halo core and surrounding regions, achieving a factor of ten higher accuracy in predicting halo masses for the specific case of large scalar perturbation amplitudes, indicating the importance of considering the evolution of cosmological densities when interpreting halo masses. This new understanding of the relationship between initial conditions and the structure of dark matter halos also highlights the limitations of using the current generation of simulations to accurately test galaxy formation models, as even the most realistic simulations overlook crucial factors, such as the formation of smaller halos, due to the overmerger of halos, and the differences between simulation methods, as seen in the SNEAKS and Gadget simulations. The simultaneous observation of gravitational and electromagnetic radiation from neutron star mergers offers unprecedented insights into these crucial astrophysical events. Despite the progress made with GW170817, the limited data available for other mergers with electromagnetic counterparts suggests that many neutron star merger electrons are scattered in a certain direction, potentially explaining the observed differences between GW and EM signals. To further explore this idea, we used the GW waveform influenced by the initial velocity of post-merger neutron stars to model GW signals, and combined them with a Monte Carlo simulation of the directional distribution of merger electrons' relativistic beams to predict a variety of EM counterparts. Our study reveals that the properties of these counterparts rely heavily on the inclination angle of the source, and observing the same direction in the sky could result in a variety of EW values, explaining the larger EW values observed for mergers with detected counterparts compared to those without, and the existence of a EW lower limit. Furthermore, we found that the majority of mergers with large EW values are likely to be detected by future telescopes such as the James Webb Space Telescope in certain extragalactic fields, and that future wide-field telescopes will likely observe many more EW values than those currently detected, with many of these remaining undetected due to too small an EW. Our analysis also highlights the need for a more comprehensive understanding of the relationships between EW values and the properties of binary neutron star mergers. Finally, our model predicts a variety of GW spectra shapes, could be tested with future detections of neutron star mergers, and may also be applied to black hole binary mergers. We address the challenge of scalable non-convex optimization for a specific problem - solving the two-block reformulation of rotationally invariant L1-PCA. This formulation is appealing due to its simplicity, yet it requires the solution of an intractable semidefinite program. To overcome this limitation, we develop an iterative method that parities the low-rank matrix between two blocks connected by a factor of the trace norm, which enables us to define a sequence of convex optimization problems that converge to the original non-convex problem. We establish the convergence properties of this method and show that it yields the same set of optimal solutions as the original rotationally invariant L1-PCA. Moreover, we derive a linear convergence rate to the optimal solution when the data matrix has a constant trace norm. To solve the resulting convex optimization problems, we employ the fast Nesterov gradient method, which we then apply to large-scale real-world datasets with impressive results. Specifically, we achieve significant improvements in computational efficiency and accuracy by transforming the method into an alternating direction embedding framework that leverages the sparse structure of the gradient matrix. This embedded method serves as a key component for the wide area network architecture, enabling distributed solution finding to the two-block reformulation. Compared to traditional approaches, machine learning methods for natural language processing that leverage additional information and incorporate structural patterns and relations have superior performance. However, the reliability of annotated data is crucial, as it serves as training data for these models. A potential issue with existing annotation evaluation methods is their inability to assess the consistency of labeled data by comparing it to the underlying distribution of unannotated text. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a method to evaluate annotated data at the paragraph level using subtask annotations such as sentence similarity comparison and categorical classification. The evaluation method scores the consistency of annotated data and refrains from making explicit categorizations, instead relying on comparative judgments. The results show that inconsistent annotations can lead to poor performance in tasks like sentence classification and that the evaluation method accurately identifies areas where the annotation is flawed and inconsistent with unannotated text. Achieving efficient and effective navigation in vast public spaces like airports and shopping centers relies heavily on accurate understanding of their layout. Current approaches to mapping these environments are limited by representing distances alone, neglecting vital local navigation information between adjacent points of interest. In contrast, a novel framework called HiTMap is proposed to capture dual-level representation, encompassing both global metrics and micro-scale trajectories between nearby points of interest. In HiTMap, each location is assigned a probability distribution of potential destinations, serving as a directed sketch of the surrounding area, and is demonstrated to enhance navigation by addressing conflicts between competing trajectories and identifying unexplored areas. Furthermore, a practical solution was developed for determining the parameters of HiTMap, including the number of required sketch components, by harnessing a Bayesian method that incorporates a prior understanding of transportation costs between locations. The proposed framework and its associated solution were put into practice using data from Uber movement patterns in Santa Monica, with results showing HiTMap to provide a more precise representation of the underlying layout, thereby enhancing navigation by addressing conflicts between competing trajectories and identifying unexplored areas. We achieved a record sensitivity in detecting a local magnetic field using atomic interferometry, at a level of $10^{-13}$ Tesla, which surpasses the quantum limit predicted by theory. This accomplishment allows for the conversion of accurate measurements of magnetic field strength into valuable information about ultra-low frequency vibrations in gravitometers with ultimate sensitivity. These vibrations would limit the ability to detect weak gravitational waves generated in certain nuclear reactions or those produced by the decay of nuclei in laboratory experiments. Therefore, our breakthrough paves the way for a new method of assessing the vibrations of extremely sensitive gravitometers and measuring the characteristics of nuclear sources of gravitational waves in nuclear electroweak reactions. Moreover, our findings also surpass the magnitude of magnetic field levels that can affect atomic clocks, providing valuable insights for achieving greater precision in time measurements. These achievements were made possible by utilizing $^1$S$_0$-$^3$S$_1$ Rb atoms, a specific atomic beam technique, and a magneto-optical trap designed especially for this experiment. We investigate a Bayesian model that employs Dirichlet processes in density estimation and a hierarchical variation of the model for recovering admixture weights. Initially, we show that placing a Dirichet process prior on densities results in a non-identifiable model with respect to admixture weights. However, by switching to a hierarchical specification, we regain weight identifiability while gaining the ability to make inferences about unobserved groups. Furthermore, this leads to a computational benefit, as it allows us to avoid labeling groups as we collect new data. Given that a group's density is shared across observations, we can also leverage this information to improve our inferences about that group by pooling the available data. We develop a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm to make inferences about unobserved groups and provide an example application using a hierarchical specification with multiple levels of grouping. Additionally, we outline the relationship between this model and the hidden multi-membership model presented by Blei and Jordan (2009), as well as the group-free topic model of Wang and Blei (2011). When the hierarchy is flat, our variation of the model is equivalent to the hidden Markov model, according to our derivation, which implies that it can recover admixture weights that span the entire range, thereby achieving the maximum possible recovery of the hidden structure, compared to the narrow range achieved by the model proposed by Blei and Jordan (2009). Nonetheless, our results also indicate that weights are non-identifiable in a way that arises specifically from the use of Dirichlet process priors, which has not been previously documented, to our knowledge. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model by applying it to both real and simulated data, where it demonstrates its ability to accurately recover unobserved group densities even when those groups are not sufficiently represented in the available data, even achieving a level of performance superior to models that require pre-specification of groups, according to our experiments. All the necessary code to replicate the results presented in this research is available in the accompanying online material. Traditional GPU memory management faces significant challenges in large-scale deep learning applications with complex dynamic memory patterns, leading to slow performance and memory waste.  To address this issue, a self-adaptive, zero-overhead array memory allocator for GPUs called DynaSOAr has been developed, leveraging a hierarchical tree structure to efficiently manage memory for arrays of varying sizes at different levels of the computation stack.  DynaSOAr's unique features include: (1) eliminating explicit memory release operations, (2) using a balance tree to optimize memory allocation and release for arrays, (3) employing a separate memory pool to reduce memory fragmentation, and (4) integrating computation task scheduling with array memory management.  Through extensive testing on real-world deep learning workloads and synthetic benchmarks, DynaSOAr has been shown to provide significant performance improvements, reduce memory fragmentation, and display excellent scalability on multi-GPU systems.  Compared to state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators, DynaSOAr delivers superior performance, memory efficiency, and lower overhead for memory management.  To facilitate wider adoption, a simplified version of DynaSOAr's source code is openly available on GitHub at the specified URL.  Future plans for further optimizing DynaSOAr's performance and expanding its capabilities have also been outlined.  Overall, DynaSOAr presents a significant breakthrough in self-adaptive, zero-overhead GPU memory management, and its advancements are expected to benefit a broad range of high-performance, parallel computing applications.  Key aspects of DynaSOAr, including its design, evaluation methods, and performance results, are detailed in this research.  The underlying technology and testing environments used are described in the appendix.  The paper concludes with key findings, implications, future work, and potential areas for further exploration.  A related demo paper titled Demo-DynaSOAr was also presented at SC21. Orbital periods for both planets are under 5 days, and their surface temperatures likely range from 40 to 60 degrees Celsius, making them unsuitable for supporting life similar to Earth. A study of 19 known mini-Neptunes that orbit hot stars also shows that these planets primarily reside in short-period orbits and have low mass densities, indicating that these planets have extensive atmospheric layers. A model simulating atmospheric loss suggests that habitable zone mini-Neptunes likely get destroyed by their host star before they reach ages similar to our Sun. However, another possible explanation is that mini-Neptunes in habitable zones get consumed by their stars in the early stages of their formation and then reincarnate as rocky planets like Earth. A statistical analysis of various stellar and planetary properties also shows that there likely exists a population of rocky planets around hot stars similar to our Sun, and these planets could potentially support life, awaiting detection with future astronomical tools. A research on the atmosphere of KELT-9b discovering a strong hydrogen escape flow around this star also highlights the importance of studying the boundaries between planets that lose their atmospheres and those that retain their layers, and how these processes affect the habitable zones around stars. A study of their orbital periods and masses indicate that both planets have unstable orbits that could end in planet-planet scattering or ejection from their system. A simulation of their formation through gravitational interactions with their host star or other planets suggests that they might have formed through migration caused by massive gravitational interactions with other planets or binary stars, and could have originated from a disk similar to the one found around Beta Pictoris. A examination of their luminosities in relation to their masses, however, indicate that they likely formed through core accretion rather than gravitational fragmentation, and could have obtained their orbits through massive stellar interactions or binary stars. We investigated the atomic arrangements of carbon and nitrogen in interstitial sites within rutile TiO2 using ab initio calculations from the VASP code. Comparing these results to those of substitutional C and N, our findings indicate that in order to minimize energy, atoms tend to occupy interstitial sites in pairs, forming a C$_2$ or N$_2$ molecule. Furthermore, we discovered that these molecules possess a significant positive charge, resulting in an electric field that causes neighboring oxygen atoms to become misaligned, thus creating F centers and allowing for the substitutionation of carbon or nitrogen in TiO2. These features are absent in substitutional C and N, distinguishing their behavior from that of pair-bonded atoms. Our study reveals that defects in the form of atomic pairs are common in wide-bandgap semiconductors and can give rise to F center formation and site-selective doping. Our predicted absorption spectra for C and N in TiO2 correspond to those reported experimentally and provide a possible explanation for the observed patterns. Lastly, our research proposes that many solid-state compounds misidentified as being doped may actually be incorrectly understood and require revisiting with an eye towards atomic pair defects. Our predictions can be tested in other materials and would offer valuable insights into their doping processes and optical properties. Our results also indicate that N$_2$ molecules can reduce to N- and N+ ions at high temperatures, which may reflect the durability of N$_2$ molecules in melilite minerals and other geological materials and provide a possible explanation for the observed distributions of N in these compounds. Our study of high-temperature reductions of N$_2$ molecules to atomic N also reveals a strong temperature-dependent phase transition in melilite minerals, which can be an important indicator of their high-temperature histories. In opposition to conventional beliefs, our research indicates that qutrit systems, which require three levels, can serve as accurate mass measures, even in noisy environments. By developing a novel phase estimation technique based on qutrits in a coherent Jaynes-Cummings circuit, we found that qutrits can precisely determine mass with minimal error, surpassing qubit systems under certain error conditions. Furthermore, our novel method exhibits greater resilience to errors caused by both faulty gate implementations and deceptive noise during measurements. Specifically, our results show that qutrit systems can better withstand frequent faulty gates and a type of measurement noise, known as amplitude damping, than their qubit counterparts. Consequently, our findings suggest that qutrit systems are more suitable for accurate mass determination in noisy environments than qubit systems. Ultimately, our research paves the way for the development of reliable phase estimation techniques, including those using qutrits in Jaynes-Cummings circuits, that can efficiently measure mass with minimal error in various noisy conditions. Our novel method also presents a notable improvement in reducing the necessary measurement times in noisy environments. Specifically, when measuring against the most demanding noisy baseline in our study, our qutrit method achieves a computational efficiency gain of one order of magnitude over the most efficient qubit method tested. In addition, our research demonstrates the potential applications of phase estimation in mass determination and identifies the suitable parameters for reliable mass measures in both qubit and qutrit systems. In the process, we developed an efficient qutrit phase estimation method that can serve as a benchmark for comparable algorithms aimed at improving the noise tolerance in mass and phase measurements. We provide a new framework for analyzing finite groups with polynomial diameter, by combining recent developments in the study of polynomial families of groups. Specifically, we explore groups characterized by a diameter of $n^c$ for some constant $c$, with a focus on those with a diameter of $n^2$ and a specific polynomial structure that incorporates both random-like and ordered aspects. Within this structure, we demonstrate how a group with a diameter of $n^2$ is comprised of: 1) a group without small non-trivial conjugacy classes, 2) a soluble subgroup with a nilpotent subgroups of bounded order, and 3) a soluble group without small non-trivial conjugacy classes, which makes up the majority of the group's order. Furthermore, we establish a significant result regarding the number of nilpotent subgroups of a given order that can exist within a group of a specific polynomial size, using a variant of the Burnside's problem as an evidence of an broader, more intricate problem. Ultimately, we establish a crucial connection between the polynomial diameter of a group and its largest nilpotent subgroup of a given order, thereby answering a question posed by Pyber, Shalev, and Talbot. Additionally, we demonstrate how this result can be applied to a variety of scenarios, including groups characterized by a diameter of $n^3$ with a specific polynomial family structure, as well as those with a diameter of $n^4$ that comprise both a symmetric group and a direct product of two cyclic groups. Moreover, we establish a significant upper bound on the number of nilpotent subgroups of a given order that can exist within a group of a specific polynomial size, thereby solving the variant of Burnside's problem mentioned earlier. Lastly, we conclude with an exploration of the limitations of our research, as well as possible future directions, such as determining whether there exists a group with a diameter of $n^3$ that is fundamentally distinct from infinite groups. Additionally, we touch on an unresolved question regarding the possible existence of a group with a diameter of $n^4$ that is essentially infinite. We hope that our research will serve as a starting point for further exploration of these intriguing topics. A statistical analysis of molecular cores within the Milky Way and nearby galaxies suggests their mass evolution may hold significant insight into massive star and giant planet formation. Using various observations and radiative hydrodynamic simulations, we developed a non-linear model to describe the mass growth of these cores. The model differentiates between two processes - mass accumulation and mass expenditure - whose rates determine the mass evolution of cores. By fitting observations of both local and extragalactic molecular cores, our model reveals a consistent picture of their mass development, characterized by an initial slow growth phase followed by a rapid expansion phase. This development is further supported by the inclusion of an additional observation of giant HII regions, also exhibiting a non-linear mass growth pattern. Our model's predictions for the mass loss and mass gain rates of these cores reveal a critical threshold mass above which they tend to escape their parent molecular clouds, often giving rise to massive star and giant HII region formations. Consequently, the distribution of core mass growth rates aligns with a broken power law, with the primary power law component indicating that cores typically remain below this threshold and form low-mass stars, while the secondary power law component indicates that a significant fraction of massive stars originate from initially massive, self-gravitating molecular cores. We demonstrate the equivalence of these networks to specific graph constructions, utilizing the power of spectral Graph Convolutional Networks. This equivalence reveals the underlying mechanics of these networks, allowing us to draw comparisons with irregular datasets represented through random graphs, and to extend the functionality of these networks to such datasets. We also establish the connection between CNNs and Graph Convolutional Networks in the spatial domain. This is accomplished by utilizing the Neumann series representation of the graph convolution operator. We then establish the connection between fully connected Neural Networks and Graph Convolutional Networks in the spatial domain, by employing a customized graph construction that incorporates node degree normalization, thereby ensuring the sparsity of connections. We also provide empirical evidence highlighting the superiority of this approach over existing methods for graph-based classification, by conducting experiments on datasets representing biological protein interactions and social relationships. We have made the code and models for these experiments available openly, to facilitate reproducibility. We have also formulated the Graph Convolution Neural Network as an optimization problem, and employed the optimization algorithm of gradient descent to train the model, which we have made available openly, to facilitate further customization. A fundamental challenge in elastography arises from the uncertainty surrounding the direction of sound wave propagation, which makes axial displacement estimation more accurate than lateral estimation, albeit still subject to significant errors. This study leverages a novel approach, known as oriented imaging, which modifies the traditional elastographic formulation to match the characteristics of ultrasound data and facilitates the estimation of axial displacements in a differential formulation based on the variation of oriented images with respect to a reference point. A critical aspect of this method involves estimating oriented images, which can be accomplished through the application of a nonlinear diffusion equation to the complex envelope of radiofrequency ultrasound data, followed by the removal of the imaginary component and normalization of the resulting images. A nonlinear elasticity model serves as the basis for elastographic simulation, which allows for the prediction of tissue stiffness based on axial displacement estimates. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of oriented imaging elastography through numerical simulations of point-like stiffness variations and comparisons with conventional elastographic methods. The results show that oriented imaging elastography yields axial displacement estimates with lower mean squared error values (1.44 χ10^-2) compared to lateral estimates (1.83 χ10^-2) and exhibits increased sensitivity to localized stiffness changes, which translates to improved estimation of tissue stiffness (mean absolute error: 1.25 kPa) in a simulation representing liver disease. The oriented imaging elastography approach also demonstrates robustness in the presence of speckle noise. The findings of this study provide a theoretical framework and practical implementation for oriented imaging elastography, which offers axial displacement estimation capabilities with increased accuracy and represents a promising non-invasive technique for the detection of localized tissue stiffness variations. The code for oriented imaging elastography is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/aliakbarahmadi/Oriented-Imaging-Elastography. This framework assesses the similarity between actual and expected outcomes based on the underlying logic underlying the pseudocodes. Our analysis reveals distinct categories of pseudocodes, including those that are inherently correct, depend on external factors for correctness, and are inherently incorrect. Furthermore, we establish a method to determine the safety of logical pseudocodes by considering the potential consequences of their execution. Our study also differentiates between two types of safety: absence of harmful effects and presence of beneficial effects. To demonstrate our approach in action, we apply it to various examples of logical pseudocodes from diverse scientific disciplines, including economics, psychology, and computer science. Our results show that a significant number of these pseudocodes are either unsafe, insecure, or both, highlighting the importance of evaluating the underlying logic of scientific claims through the use of formal methods. Various solutions exist that reduce the action space, but these are often specific to particular problems and don't offer a versatile solution. We introduce a novel method that can be applied broadly, calling it a 'coarse representation of the world'. This involves dividing the environment into distinct zones that correspond to specific actions, and has several advantages. It simplifies action selection while also making the problem more interpretable, and enables important questions about future consequences to be answered more effectively. Through thorough evaluation, our approach shows superior performance and efficiency compared to other common strategies for action selection. A key benefit becomes particularly apparent when considering long-term consequences, as it enables better evaluation of future states and allows for more informed decision-making about them. This improvement in evaluating future states and actions becomes statistically significant when the action space is particularly large and complex. Additionally, our approach demonstrates greater flexibility when considering uncertain future events, and this too shows a significant positive impact on its performance. Overall, our approach offers substantial benefits for decision-making in complex scenarios, both with and without uncertainty about the future. It is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of problems, and has been tested thoroughly in multiple different scenarios. We make our code and results available for further examination and comparison with other methods. According to this model, it's evident that the normal variations in W and Z boson distribution are influenced by "hard" interactions between fundamental particles, in addition to "soft" or universal forces that affect all particles equally and exhibit a pattern of complexity, resembling a fractal structure. These universal forces, in turn, are driven by the same fundamental principles that give rise to the properties of quarks and gluons, the basic components of protons and other hadrons. Although these findings provide a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying mechanics of hadron collisions, more research is necessary to determine how and why these universal forces affect W and Z bosons in the same way, as well as how they affect other particles and forces. In 1936, Theodor Rosser expanded upon Kurt Godel's inaugural incompleteness theorem by demonstrating that any sufficiently powerful formal system is either complete but inconsistent, or incomplete but consistent. This enhancement entails a stronger consistency claim, as it guarantees that the system is consistent relative to itself, without relying on a supersystem. We will illustrate the specifics of this extension through the context of Peano arithmetic. A notable aspect of Rosser's extension involves modifying Godel's original approach so that the associated diagonalization function behaves predictably, thereby sidestepping the complications arising from the Godel undecidability theorem. This paper delves into the specifics of Rosser's extension of the Godel incompleteness theorem within the framework of first-order logic. We will also examine how it can be viewed as an application of the fixed point theorem, as well as explore its implications for the halting problem within computability theory. Furthermore, we will analyze the relationship between Rosser's extension and the concept of arithmetical hierarchies, revealing that it is equivalent to a specific level within this hierarchy. Finally, we will discuss its connection to the syllogistic theorem, demonstrating that no formal system is capable of proving the validity of the principle that if all natural numbers are either odd or even, then there exists a natural number that is odd and also a natural number that is even. This implies that the syllogistic theorem lies outside the scope of such formal systems. This paper is an expanded version of an earlier work presented at the conference Next 50 years of Incompleteness Theorems, held in Beijing, China, from August 1-3, 2021. We have updated the presentation to better reflect the current state of knowledge, while maintaining the original structure and content. This research extends Hadamard's three circles theorem to a higher dimensional context, where a significant connection is established between this generalized theorem and the concept of monogenic functions in higher dimensions. Through a change of variable, the theorem is reinterpreted in terms of integral transforms, which helps demonstrate the existence of a specific integral transform that maps polynomials to monogenic functions. This integral transform is fundamentally linked to the Dirac operator in higher dimensions. A detailed examination of the transform's properties reveals similarities with the classical Fourier transform. Moreover, an investigation of the kernel function associated with this transform reveals that it obeys the same type of estimation bounds as the Fourier transform kernel. Consequently, this implies that the transform retains its character when it is applied to a wide range of functions, including those with smoothness properties up to a certain depth. This leads to an expansion of the Cauchy-type integral formula that can be utilized to determine the image of a given set of functions under this transform. This research also explores connections to the Riesz-Herglotz representation theorem, the inverse problem of determining the Dirac operator from its action on a set of monogenic functions, and the possibility of utilizing the transform to solve a certain type of integral equation that involves the Dirac operator. It is further demonstrated that this integral equation has a unique solution if the kernel function associated with the transform can be expressed as a sum of an analytic function and a compact operator. This condition is proven to be satisfied for a wide range of functions, thereby ensuring the existence and uniqueness of the solution for this particular type of integral equation. We propose a novel hyperbolic graph convolutional network (HGCN) called the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), which enhances existing HGCNs in both theory and practice by utilizing the unique properties of Lorentz transformations. Our LGCN advances beyond current HGCNs in two significant ways: it enhances the accuracy of node feature representations and simplifies the process of hyperbolic GCN construction. Moreover, LGCN leverages the intrinsic scalability of hyperbolic spaces by introducing a multi-resolution framework, and this framework can be seamlessly integrated with current HGCN implementations. Our LGCN and related methods are tested on extensive datasets, and the results reveal a substantial improvement in performance when utilizing our LGCN, and the simplicity of its construction is validated mathematically. Ultimately, the Lorentzian graph convolutional network presents a significant breakthrough in the design of hyperbolic graph convolutional networks. Our work is applicable to numerous graph-based machine learning applications, and the underlying concepts can be extended to other learning methods that utilize hyperbolic spaces. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/QingyuXu/LGCN. Our best model achieves an accuracy of 98.84% on the enzo5 dataset, which surpasses the current state-of-the-art performance. This study focuses on solving two significant problems involving the stabilization of inverse problems for PDEs. Firstly, we establish a Carleman estimate for the observability inequality of the semi-linear wave equation with non-zero boundary conditions, which helps us achieve unconditional uniqueness and a stability estimate for a inverse problem of identifying an unknown coefficient of the equation's partial derivative term. Secondly, we derive a Carleman estimate for the semi-linear heat equation, which enables us to obtain the unconditional uniqueness and a stability estimate for an inverse problem of determining another unknown coefficient of the equation. Thirdly, we also establish a stability estimate for an inverse problem of recovering a function from its non-zero boundary condition, which can be applied to the first two problems. Notably, these stability results are achieved without requiring any a priori assumption about the solution or its spatial regularity. Instead, the a priori assumption is replaced by an additional boundary condition, which makes the problem more well-posed. This condition can be satisfied by suitably choosing a control function in a control-observing problem of the wave or heat equation. Consequently, we prove that a simple gradient reconstruction method leads to a regularizing scheme, which, in turn, results in the convergence of an iterative algorithm with a linear convergence rate in the $H^{-1}$ norm. This convergence is achieved without any a priori assumption about the solution's regularity, provided that the a priori assumption is replaced by the additional boundary condition mentioned above. Ultimately, this implies that the iterative algorithm produces a stable and unconditional solution to the inverse problem. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this solution converges with a linear convergence rate in the $H^{-1}$ norm, which includes the $L^2$ norm as a special case. This achievement is significant because it represents a distinct improvement over the regularizing properties of the gradient reconstruction method in the $H^{-1}$ norm, which were previously known to be independent of the solution's regularity. This means that we can now recover a solution with an arbitrarily large number of spatial smoothness factors from a coarse initial guess, without resorting to any a priori assumption about the solution's regularity, which is a crucial property with important implications. Finally, we emphasize that the most significant advantage of this approach is the absence of any a priori assumption about the solution's spatial regularity, which is a major limitation of other regularizing schemes, including the one based on the gradient reconstruction method, when applied to the two problems considered here. The Tsallis distribution has extensive applications in various fields, and the Pareto distribution, a specific case of Tsallis distribution, has been widely observed in social systems, suggesting that they follow power laws. Although the Tsallis distribution can be derived from the maximum entropy principle in thermal equilibrium, its emergence in nonequilibrium situations, especially in relation to preferential attachment, is not well understood. We derive the Tsallis distribution in nonequilibrium conditions, characterizing processes that result in distribution widths less than one, and show that it arises from the maximum entropy principle among conditional distributions. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this approach applies to generating power-law distributions in social systems, including citation patterns and the ranks of athletes in Olympic games. We also introduce an adjustable parameter that allows for smoother distribution shapes, leveraging the Tsallis distribution's connection to the Renyi entropy. Our work clarifies the genesis of power-law distributions in nonequilibrium scenarios, beyond the conventional explanation of preferential attachment, and demonstrates the versatility of our approach by incorporating additional features, such as a peaked distribution. We believe that our approach simplifies the underlying mechanics of power-law distributions, making them more intuitive and readily interpretable. We also propose that the adjustable parameter our approach offers could be valuable in modeling scenarios with distinct peak ranks, such as the ranks of Olympic athletes or the distribution of movie ratings. We anticipate that our approach will be useful in modeling power-law distributions in various domains, including biology, finance, and physics, and even in understanding the complex mechanisms underlying universal scale-free patterns. We have made our analytical findings and numerical tools available at https://github.com/TsallisSociety. We hope that our work will contribute to a deeper comprehension of the intricate relationships between entropy, probability distributions, and the complex systems that exhibit them. We have made our code publicly accessible to facilitate the reproduction of our results and to encourage further customization of our approach for other power-law distribution applications. We plan to enhance our code regularly in response to user feedback. We also invite researchers to collaborate with us and explore additional implications of our work. We have established a community website at https://tsallis.society to serve as a platform for discussion, new developments, and future research guided by the Tsallis distribution. Despite the mass term's impact on the particle's properties, the number of degrees of freedom in the linearized gravity theory appears to remain unchanged. However, the presence of the mass term leads to an irreversible loss of gauge symmetry, resulting in a genuine physical degree of freedom becoming a ghost in the theory, and this phenomenon occurs across all metric agnostic theories of gravity. These theories, which include power-Yang-Mills, Einstein-Yang-Mills, and a collective of higher-derivative scalar-tensor and metric theories, inevitably suffer from the problem of ghost degrees of freedom, suggesting that the notion of a mass term in gravitational perturbations is fundamental and ubiquitous. The absence of an intrinsic mass scale in linearized gravity is thus shown to be an artifact of the metric agnostic approach, allowing for the development of a linearized gravity theory with an intrinsic mass scale. This new understanding sheds light on the linearized degree of freedom's self-interactions and provides a metric-dependent intrinsic mass scale, which can give rise to an intrinsic mass scale in linearized gravity, present in a wide range of fundamental particle theories. Our investigation focuses on four possible connections: (1) those that result from classical mechanics, (2) those associated with coherent states, (3) those connected to the classical limit, and (4) those with thermodynamic universality. We explore these linkages in both closed and open systems, discussing various examples and presenting a comprehensive classification of quantum equilibrium states. Notably, our analysis reveals distinct structures and patterns of incompatibility within the set of all quantum equilibrium states. Furthermore, we establish the equivalence of certain categories and expand on the implications of these relationships for our understanding of quantum equilibrium states. These findings contribute to our comprehension of the interplay between dynamics, thermodynamics, and the principles of incompatibility in quantum mechanics. We also highlight the significance of these investigations for ongoing and future research in the field. Our studies have been published in various papers over the years. We introduce a minimal dark sector to extend a meson-fermion seesaw model, assigning a dark parity symmetry to the extended particles. The stability of the vacuum is ensured by incorporating a dark sector that interacts with the standard sector only marginally. The dark parity symmetry is found to be approximately conserved, and the dark sector particles are heavy, with masses ranging from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-6}$ TeV, depending on the parameter values. These particles can be part of possible dark matter candidates, especially if we consider a scenario with an additional dark parity-breaking term, which facilitates their formation into dark mesons with masses around 10 TeV and explain the observed dark matter density. Furthermore, these dark mesons may be identifiable at future colliders, specifically the 100 TeV future particle collider, which could potentially reveal evidence of them through rare production processes or rare decays of heavy standard model particles. The necessary parameters for such a scenario are achievable within the existing theoretical and experimental bounds, offering a compelling idea that combines fundamental symmetries, dark matter, and a possible explanation for rare phenomena observed in high-energy physics. The key features of this model can be tested in various areas of physics, including the parameters of rare particle decays, the power spectrum of gravitational waves, and the distribution of satellite galaxies, providing potential connections with other physical phenomena and offering a unified framework that can be validated through a thorough examination of predictions in different fields of physics and astronomy. The code used to generate the results from the model is available at https://github.com/yinyanxiao/DPSSM. The model can be extended to accommodate additional dark sectors that interact with the minimal dark sector, either through fundamental forces or composite particles, offering numerous possibilities for its modification and application in various contexts. A fundamental concept in condensed matter theory, effective spin-orbit coupling, is subject to renormalization due to interactions with other physical parameters, particularly in transition metal oxides where it can be strong and uncompromised. It is essential to account for this complexity to accurately understand various interesting phenomena, including ferroelectricity and superconductivity. A recent study aims to clarify the relationship between spin-orbit coupling, interaction effects, and crystal field splitting within a general theoretical framework that can be applied to specific material cases by perturbation theory. Based on a two-level model, it has been possible to analyze the effective spin-orbit coupling in its general form, identify its fundamental components, and demonstrate that it can be influenced by both on-site Coulomb interactions and lattice vibrations. Additionally, a critical threshold for strong spin-orbit coupling has been determined, beyond which the coupling becomes quasi-frozen due to interaction-induced crystal field splitting. Consequently, the distinctive features of effective spin-orbit coupling in simple systems have been revealed, with implications for understanding its behavior in more complex and real-world situations. Moreover, the developed framework offers a practical method for calculating the effective spin-orbit coupling in specific material cases by combining first-principles calculations with the proposed theoretical model. This approach has been successfully applied to the transition metal oxides BaRuO3 and CaRuO3, both known for their strong spin-orbit coupling, and has been found to accurately describe their effective spin-orbit coupling, crystal field splitting, and related energy levels by means of a two-level model. Notably, the effective spin-orbit coupling in these two materials has been found to differ significantly, with BaRuO3 exhibiting a marginally stable spin-orbit driven middle orbit state, whereas CaRuO3 has a more pronounced distinction in spin-orbit driven crystal field splitting that could explain its unique ground state configuration and special properties. Lastly, the potential applications of this knowledge have been considered in the context of related material research, including the design of novel materials with unique properties, such as spin-orbit coupled superconductor CaRuO3. The proposed framework and the studied materials serve as a starting point for exploring the complex interplay between various physical parameters that influence the effective spin-orbit coupling in transition metal oxides, with the aim of gaining a deeper understanding of this crucial concept and its far-reaching implications for condensed matter physics. By utilizing exit paths, we establish that a subset of these relative $I$-functions exhibit interesting relationships, indicating their equivalence to a specific set of relative $I$-functions featuring a certain permutation-induced action. Furthermore, this equivalence has a direct connection to the Cox ring of the associated variety, thereby extending previous findings by Batolla, Manento, and Toso. This study explores the potential of generative models to create precise medical image representations by manipulating latent codes, building on the concept of disentangled representation. Although disentangled representation has been effectively applied in non-medical imaging tasks, our research discovers that such representation is not necessarily stable across different generative models trained on medical images. Our findings highlight the difficulty of achieving disentangled representation on medical images and the need for new evaluation metrics specifically designed for medical imaging tasks. We also propose a novel approach, guided latent code manipulation, to facilitate the manipulation of specific pathologic features in medical images. Our method combines a condition-aware encoder with a latent code generator, enabling the extraction and modification of precise pathologic representations from limited training data, outperforming existing approaches in various medical imaging tasks, including lung sound analysis and breast cancer diagnosis. We further introduce a new evaluation framework that considers both visual inspection and quantitative analysis, demonstrating the efficacy of our method in maintaining the integrity of medical images during latent code manipulation, maintaining both visual consistency and retaining diagnostic information. We make our code and evaluation metrics publicly available to facilitate future research in this area. We propose a lung sound analysis method based on our framework, showing its potential to improve accuracy by ensuring the precision of medical image representations. We highlight key takeaways from our research, emphasizing the potential of generative models to create medical image representations that are both specific and general, while highlighting the challenges and opportunities presented by this area of study. We conclude by emphasizing the need for novel evaluation metrics and more robust training data to ensure the reliability of generative models in medicine, while highlighting the potential of lung sound analysis as a promising application of this technology. We make our code publicly available at https://github.com/author/name/lcm-med. We encourage further research in this area and the development of more robust, clinically applicable methods for lung sound analysis based on medical image representations learned through deep learning techniques. We evaluate our method on a publicly available lung sound dataset, comparing it to existing classification approaches and discovering that it outperforms them in accuracy, while requiring significantly less training data. Spectral Embedding (SE), have seen significant advancements recently. However, the
interpretation of these methods can be challenging for non-experts due to the
complexity of their mathematical representations. This paper introduces an innovative
approach, called ViDaExpert, a user-friendly visualization tool designed to
facilitate the interpretation of SE for non-experts by providing a simplified,
geometric representation of high-dimensional data. ViDaExpert's user interface
allows users to explore the underlying structure of high-dimensional data by navigating
a 2D representation of the dataset, examining local neighborhoods, and identifying
anomalies. This paper also includes an empirical investigation into the efficacy
of SE in reducing data dimensionality for various real-world datasets, comparing it
to established methods like PCA and Autoencoders. Empirical results demonstrate
the effectiveness of SE in preserving the underlying structure of high-dimensional data
when compared to alternative methods. ViDaExpert's functionality is implemented
as a web application that is freely accessible online. The empirical research
underpinning this paper is published in a separate study cited herein. Through

widely recognized challenge of interpreting machine learning models as part of
feature extraction and dimensionality reduction. The code and application are
